achad-egyptian-revival-1923:
Achad turned his new key on Egypt and the tarot in his second major book of 1923. The Egyptian Revival reads the ever-coming son, a figure of the new age, in the light of the cards. Charles Stansfeld Jones writes here as Frater Achad, Crowley's breakaway student.

Egyptian gods and signs are matched to the tarot trumps by his revised scheme of the Tree. The son who ever comes stands for the god of each new age, crowned and conquering. The book carries the project of Q B L into myth and image. It is the middle panel of his Kabbalah trilogy.
aeneas-tacticus-asclepiodotus-onasander-:
A 1923 Loeb volume binds three Greek works on military science together. The Illinois Greek Club translated Aeneas Tacticus, Asclepiodotus, and Onasander into English. Greek text faces the translation in the Loeb manner throughout.

Aeneas, writing around 350 BCE, teaches how to hold a city under siege. Passwords, gates, signals, and spies fill his practical chapters. Asclepiodotus offers a drill book of formations and commands for infantry. Onasander advises generals on character, strategy, and choosing the moment of battle. Together the three founded the literature of ancient military technology. Officers and historians still read them for Greek warfare's working details.
akeley-in-brightest-africa-1923:
Carl Akeley went to Africa to kill gorillas for museums and stayed to save them. In Brightest Africa, printed in 1923, is his classic of the hunt and the wild. Akeley was the great taxidermist of his age and a sculptor of animal groups.

He tells of elephants, lions, and the mountain gorillas of the high volcanoes. His gorilla work showed the beast as shy and grand, not the fiend of old tales. The book helped turn hunters into guards of the great ape in time. Akeley's prose is as clean and bright as his museum glass.
anderson-constitutions-1723:
James Anderson wrote The Constitutions of the Free-Masons in 1723. The Grand Lodge of England had been formed six years past. Anderson gave the new body its laws and its tale of the past. The book is the root text of the craft as a world guild.

A long tale traces Masonry from Adam through kings and saints to London. The Charges then lay down the faith, morals, and peace each Mason owes. Rules for lodges, ranks, and meets fill the last part. The book fixed the shape of the craft for the age to come.
anderson-horses-men-1923:
Horses and Men, published in 1923, gathers Anderson's later stories of the American Midwest. Horses run through the book as measures of human worth: creatures of grace beside men cramped by money, shame, or longing.

'The Man Who Became a Woman' tells of a young horse-hand's frightening, tender awakening at a county fair. Other stories follow grooms, trainers, and small-town dreamers in Anderson's halting, musical prose. The racing world gave him some of his finest material. The collection confirms his gift for lives that official America overlooked, told from inside their own confusion and hope.
anderson-many-marriages-1923:
Sherwood Anderson published Many Marriages in 1923, the most outspoken of his novels. Anderson had been through divorces of his own and wrote obsessively about the gap between respectable marriage and inner desire. The book shocked some readers and was banned in places for its frankness.

John Webster, a washing-machine manufacturer in a Wisconsin town, walks through his house at midnight and confesses everything to his daughter. He tells her of his dead wife, his erotic discontent, and his plan to begin life again with his secretary. The confession takes the whole novel, part sermon and part breakdown. Anderson's plain, groping style tries to say what his characters cannot. Many Marriages remains his most daring treatment of marriage.
arxiv-2512-00023:
Hetvi Shastri, Akanksha Atrey, Andre Beck, and Nirupama Ravi survey threats in peer-run wireless networks. In these networks, individuals own and operate equipment, offering access without sign-ups for pay. Older providers earned trust over decades through scale, practice, and rules.

New owners lack that foundation, so some may be tempted to exploit the service. The survey catalogs the threats that follow from misaligned motives and weak checks. Knowing the threat list is the first step to designing networks users can trust. Monetary compensation for owners is the network's engine, and also the source of its exploitation motives.
arxiv-2512-00123:
When one curve rolls along another without slipping, a fixed point on it traces a new curve called a roulette. Osvaldo Santos-Pereira writes about these curves in a 2025 article, using two classic puzzles as motivation. They are the coin paradox and Aristotle's wheel paradox.

The article derives parametric equations for epicycloids and hypocycloids, the curves traced when circles roll outside or inside other circles. Python code produces concrete visualizations and animations of the results. The piece serves teachers and students who want geometric intuition for curves that formulas alone can make feel abstract. Epicycloids appear in gear design, which gives the old puzzles a practical afterlife.
arxiv-2512-00223:
Kagome lattices, named after a woven basket pattern, host magnetic behavior that frustrates simple ordering. Gabriel Capelo and Eric Andrade study a magnetization plateau in such a lattice in 2025. Recent observations found a plateau at one third of full magnetization in kagome-based magnets.

The authors investigate a Heisenberg model with two exchange couplings under an external magnetic field. Although the classical ground state at zero field depends on the sign of one coupling, they find the one-third plateau is robust in both cases. Robust plateaus interest physicists hunting for materials with unusual, controllable magnetic states. Magnetization plateaus are prized because they stay stable across a range of fields.
arxiv-2512-00523:
Glasses of self-propelled particles flow in sudden avalanches, much like passive materials under stress. Roland Wiese, Ezequiel Ferrero, and Demian Levis investigate avalanche statistics in active glasses with finite persistence in 2025, with and without applied shear. Persistence measures how long each particle keeps its direction.

Departing from the infinite-persistence limit, the authors explore the interplay of internal activity and external driving. They uncover when active and passive systems share avalanche statistics and where the analogy fails. The findings matter for understanding living tissues, bacterial colonies, and other active matter that yields in bursts. Finite persistence is the realistic case, since real active particles do change direction. For folks who study such stuff, the gain is a clear map. It shows when crowds of small bits surge as one, and when they do not.
arxiv-2512-00823:
Arpit Kottur, Meet Mehta, and Raka Dabhade compare age and dark matter across spiral galaxies in a 2025 astronomy paper. Dark matter is the unseen mass that holds galaxies together and shapes how they spin. The team asks whether a galaxy's age tracks how much dark matter it holds.

They study sixteen nearby spiral galaxies with well-resolved rotation curves. Each galaxy's mass is split into a central bulge, an exponential disk, and a dark matter halo. Monte Carlo fits find the mix that matches the spin data. Their results test simple stories about how galaxies grow old and gather dark matter.
arxiv-2512-01023:
Orestis Kaparounakis, Yunqi Zhang, and Phillip Stanley-Marbell improve particle filtering in a 2025 paper. Particle filters track hidden states from noisy observations and power tools in self-driving cars, drones, warehouse robots, target tracking, and patient monitoring. They keep many candidate states, called particles, and weight them by how well each matches new data.

Their weakness is representing that match, the likelihood, which can cause particles to degenerate into a few survivors. The authors approximate hard likelihood densities with deterministic arithmetic for optimal filtering. Better likelihood handling matters most for fast, resource-limited systems where filters must run in real time.
arxiv-2512-01123:
Xiaoting Kuang and Boken Lin build a hybrid system for options trading decisions in a 2025 paper. Large language models read context and qualitative nuance well. They struggle, though, with the rigorous, transparent reasoning that high-stakes quantitative domains like financial trading demand.

Their model-first architecture targets the options wheel strategy, a cycle of selling options to collect income. It combines the language model with a Bayesian network, which reasons with explicit probabilities. The language model helps generate the network, and the network keeps the reasoning auditable. Transparent decisions matter when real money rides on each trade.
arxiv-2512-01323:
Sanjay Mishra gives a full base treatment of simplicial complexes. These are shapes built from points, edges, faces, and higher kin. They are core tools in geometry and data study. Mishra stresses worked sums, clear cases, and ways to check each claim.

The path starts with finite point sets in Euclidean space. It shows when points are geometrically free of each other. That trait is proved from how their gap vectors line up. Matrix rank tests make the checks concrete. A firm base like this helps new scholars use complexes with care.
arxiv-2512-01423:
Qi Kuang, Bowen Gang, and Yin Xia offer a way to test many claims on a tight budget. Big tests often need exact p-values or e-values for each claim. Those exact scores can cost a lot to compute. Funds and time are short in genome and AI work.

Their frame uses cheap proxy scores to guide where to spend. Costly exact work goes to the claims that need it most. A shared budget is split with care across all claims. Smart splits keep error rates in check while saving compute for large scans like genome-wide studies.
arxiv-2512-01723:
Saba Kublashvili builds HistoricalML for learning from sparse historical data. Historical sets are tiny, noisy, and mixed in type. Counterfactuals are missing by nature. Answers must also be readable by human scholars. Standard machine learning fits none of those needs well.

The frame blends Bayesian inference with neuro-symbolic methods. Probability handles doubt and scarcity. Symbols keep outputs interpretable. Joint use lets the model state both a claim and its grounds. That fit serves history, where each data point is precious and each claim is debated. Interpretable outputs let historians contest a claim's grounds, which keeps the tool inside scholarly debate rather than above it.
arxiv-2512-02323:
Boltzmann machines are strong models that learn by weights and energy. But training them in the right way has long been too slow. In practice, folks settled for small, cut-down forms. Kentaro Kubo and Hayato Goto take on both blocks in 2025: fast sampling that runs in parallel, and a quick gauge of the model's heat scale.

True learning needs samples drawn by long random walks through the model's states. For rich, fully linked machines, those walks resist being run side by side. A sampler that can run in parallel, plus fast heat gauging, could reopen the full class of models. That class was set aside when a shortcut called contrastive divergence took over.
arxiv-2512-02423:
Software agents that click through real applications must learn navigation across many screens, but real apps are proprietary and complex, starving training of good environments. Haolong Yan and a large team present the GUI Exploration Lab in 2025, with multi-turn reinforcement learning to teach agents screen navigation.

The focus has shifted from single-screen tasks to long navigation challenges across PC software and mobile apps. A lab environment supplies the comprehensive information needed for training and evaluation that real products withhold. Agents that can explore interfaces patiently would automate the multi-step chores that current assistants abandon halfway.
arxiv-2512-02523:
Xueyan Li and six co-authors work on judging songs made by singing voice synthesis systems. Modern systems can now hold pitch and keep a steady style across a song. As output quality rises, fair and useful scoring of that output becomes more pressing.

Common reward systems give a single number, which misses traits like phrasing and expressiveness. Human labels for those traits cost a lot to collect. The team's generative multimodal feedback gives richer, multi angle comments instead. Better feedback could help builders improve synthetic singers and help listeners trust quality claims. Rich notes beat a lone score when a coach must say what to fix next in a take.
arxiv-2512-02723:
Palash Saha and Michał Zegrodnik study a stacked pair of atom thin crystals, molybdenum ditelluride over tungsten diselenide. At two holes per moiré cell, electron interactions and spin orbit coupling compete strongly. Such moiré bilayers are known hunting grounds for new topological phases of matter.

Their analysis finds a robust quantum valley Hall insulating phase. Long range interactions alone can drive tunneling between layers, creating topologically nontrivial bands even without single particle hopping. Interaction driven topology widens the menu of phases that layered materials might host for future electronics. A phase born of sheer push and pull, with no hop to seed it, was not on most lists till now.
arxiv-2512-02923:
Augusto E. Lassen and a large team separate two forces that can stretch a galaxy into similar shapes. In dense environments, ram pressure strips gas as a galaxy plows through hot surroundings. Gravitational interactions with neighbors can mimic those same morphological features closely.

The Size-Shape Difference method compares stellar properties to tell the two causes apart. Applying it to real galaxies tests whether the method survives messy data. Knowing the true cause tells astronomers how galaxies are quenched and reshaped inside clusters over cosmic time. Real sky data is the stern test. Clean mocks can hide the flaws that real noise and real dust will find in no time at all.
arxiv-2512-03423:
Atoms linked to light guides can be steered with care. Weijun Cheng, Da-Wei Wang, Yang Xue, Zhihai Wang, and Liantuan Xiao study such a system in this 2025 work. They use one-dimensional coupled-resonator waveguides with long-range hoppings.

By engineering each order of hopping between resonators, they build linear dispersion relations with a chiral character. Dispersion shapes how light and atoms interact over time. Precise control could help quantum networks and simulators. It also opens routes to study exotic light-matter effects in the lab. Chiral dispersion could steer single photons and atoms in future quantum links.
arxiv-2512-03523:
A young, active star flared through a week-long campaign. Isaiah Tristan and co-authors report the quiet-phase radio data in this 2025 work, the fourth in a series. The star is AU Mic, an M-dwarf known for strong flares.

The campaign ran in October 2018 across many wavelengths. This paper analyzes radio data between flares, at frequencies from twelve to twenty-five gigahertz. Quiet emission reveals the star's steady magnetic activity. Understanding it helps judge the space weather faced by AU Mic's young planets. Quiet radio emission sets the baseline against which flare bursts are judged.
arxiv-2512-03623:
Britain's Shipping Forecast is an iconic weather text. Edward Steele and a large team test whether vision language models can write it in this 2025 work. Application of multimodal foundation models to weather products is still nascent.

The team explores generating the forecast text directly from video-encoded gridded weather data. A model that reads maps and writes clear forecasts could speed up services. It could also tailor forecasts to new audiences. Careful checks remain vital, since mariners rely on these words for safety. Video encoding lets the model see weather evolve, not just a single static chart, which matches how forecasters read moving systems.
arxiv-2601-06623:
Philip Korman settles an existence question for a class of hard math problems in a 2026 paper. The problems mix a fixed linear part with a curved part. The linear part sits at a point of resonance, where small inputs can grow.

He gives a test that is both a must and enough for a solution. That is, solutions exist just when his test holds, with no gap. The test is then used on a linked heat problem in his paper. It gives a rule for when all solutions of that heat problem grow without bound. Old tools for resonance gave tests that were enough but not a must. His sharper test closes the gap for this class at last. The result is a full answer, not a one-way hint.
arxiv-2601-07223: Research by Eromanga Adermann and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with quantum error correction and detection for quantum machine learning. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. At the intersection of quantum computing and machine learning, quantum machine learning (QML) is poised to revolutionize artificial intelligence. However, the vulnerability of the current generation of quantum computers to noise and computational error poses a significant barrier to this vision. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07823:
Zhiting Mei and a large team survey how video generation models are entering robotics. These models synthesize high-quality video of agents interacting with environments. They condition on multi-modal user inputs. Their realism addresses long-standing limits of physics-based simulators. Adoption across robotics problem domains has been broad and fast. Their 2026 preprint reviews applications, research challenges, and future directions.

A survey is timely when a tool spreads faster than the field's shared understanding. The authors organize uses from training data generation to planning and evaluation. They also name open challenges, where video models still mislead or fall short. Robotics scholars choosing simulation tools are the readers. The paper helps them judge where generated video can be trusted. It maps a fast-moving area at a moment when standards are still forming.
arxiv-2601-07923:
Hao-Ran Cui and Hart Goldman study edge behavior at an odd quantum phase transition. More work now asks how quantum critical swings affect gapless edge modes. The authors take the non-compact CP model with N boson species in two space dimensions. The bosons couple to a fluctuating U(1) gauge field. Their 2026 preprint reports striking edge correlations at this deconfined quantum critical point.

Such points split phases in ways Landau theory does not allow. Edges can host their own critical behavior, richer than the bulk. Striking correlations mean edge order reacts with great strength. Measuring that response tests theories of the transition itself. The paper serves condensed matter theorists. It uses the boundary as a lens on a transition that remains hard to simulate and measure. The edge is not a mere rim here; it is where the sharpest signs of change show up.
arxiv-2601-08123: Gabriele Dessena and Alessandro Pontillo test propeller-driven vibration testing as a cheaper route to aircraft modal data. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that ground vibration testing supports certification but takes long, costly campaigns. Propeller-driven testing is an output-only option in the spirit of operational modal analysis. Taxi and flight vibration testing follow the same broad idea of using working loads. The authors assess whether a spinning propeller can excite an aircraft well enough for modal parameter extraction. If it works, smaller teams could gather certification-grade data faster.
arxiv-2601-08423: Jakub Gismatullin, Immanuel Halupczok, and Dugald Macpherson characterize simple groups definable in valued fields. Their 2026 arXiv paper proves that non-abelian definable, definably simple groups in 1-h-minimal henselian valued fields are essentially linear algebraic groups. The group is assumed to live in the home sort. A similar result holds in pure algebraically closed valued fields of positive characteristic, with an added subgroup assumption. The theorem limits how exotic definable groups can be, a core question in model theory.
arxiv-2601-08723:
Jeff Murugan and Hendrik van Zyl study how hard it is to build a quantum state step by step. This cost is called Krylov complexity. They look at a system made of two parts put side by side. Each part has its own cost when it acts on its own. The pair asks what cost the joint system has.

They prove the joint cost is at least the sum of the two part costs. In most cases it is more than that sum. They also name a tool that can count the extra part. The result shows that joined systems are more rich than their parts suggest. A reader in quantum work gets a firm bound and a way to track the extra growth.
arxiv-2601-08923:
Marco Fenucci and three co-authors trace the birth place of a small rock that tracks Earth in space. The rock is named Kamo'oalewa. A China space craft will soon fly to it to bring bits back. Its path and hue hint it may be a chunk of the Moon, blown off by a crash. One young Moon crater is a prime source guess.

The team tests that Moon source next to a plain belt source. Belt rocks drift to Earth like paths by slow pulls over long spans. Moon bits take a more direct path. A reader in space rock work gets a head to head test. The odds of each source can guide what the craft finds when it lands.
arxiv-2601-09023:
Xabier Cid Vidal and five co-authors plan a hunt for quirks at the LHCb lab. A quirk is a heavy bit tied to its pair by a tube of hid force. The tube acts like a string. As the pair parts, the string pulls them back. They swing and loop in ways no plain bit does, which makes them hard to spot with plain hunts.

Large zones of quirk mass and force are still not ruled out. LHCb, a lab at CERN built for beauty bits, may see the odd paths quirks leave. The team maps how those paths would look in its gear. A reader in core physics gets a hunt plan for a bit that could hide in plain sight.
arxiv-2601-09223:
Luigi Romano and four co-authors build a watcher for roll contact systems with unknown rub. Such a system pairs a fast spin part with a wave part that spreads down a line. Rub at the touch zone is set by a set of unknown counts in the wave rule. Those counts shift with wear and heat, so a fixed watcher fails in time.

Their watcher reads just edge marks. From them it tracks both the spin state and the spread state at once. It also learns the rub counts as it goes. Key needs are that the system stays whole in time, and that edge sense can see the state. A reader in control work gets a watcher for a hard mix of lump and wave.
arxiv-2601-09523:
Abdelrahman Abdallah, Mohammed Ali, Muhammad Abdul-Mageed, and Adam Jatowt build a benchmark for questions about change over time. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents TEMPO, a test set joining temporal reasoning with hard retrieval. It spans thirteen domains.

Older temporal benchmarks use simple fact-seeking questions over news text. Hard retrieval benchmarks, in turn, lack temporal grounding. Real questions often need both: reasoning about how things evolve and gathering evidence from several periods. TEMPO is built to measure exactly that mix. It gives retrieval systems a tougher, more realistic target than the simple fact hunts used before.
arxiv-2601-09823:
Subhajit Sanyal and nine co-authors shrink a diffusion-based image restorer to fit edge devices. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents NanoSD, a foundation model for real-time image restoration. Latent diffusion models like Stable Diffusion 1.5 carry strong priors for repairing images.

The full pipelines are too heavy for phones and embedded hardware. Lightweight variants usually squeeze the denoising network or shorten the sampling path, which warps the latent space and hurts generality. NanoSD takes a different route to stay fast and broad. Real-time restoration on the device itself would help cameras, drones, and medical tools.
arxiv-2601-09923:
Hanna Foerster and co authors study the safety of agents that use a real computer. Such agents click, type, and run tools to do tasks. Bad text on a page can trick them. A trick can make an agent leak codes or lose funds.

The team says one strong shield is known. Keep the plan step apart from what the agent sees. The plan step should use only trusted input. The view step deals with raw page text, which may be fake. The paper tests how well this split shield works in a system named CaMeLs. It asks what the split can and cannot block.
arxiv-2601-10023:
Junseok Oh and co authors test chains of small links that join two stuffs. The links are Josephson links. They are made from a layer pair of aluminium on indium arsenide. Chains of such links can act as a large coil with no loss.

The chains show this large coil trait. Their wave load tops a key quantum bound. The flat form of the links gives a high base tone. The chain acts close to an ideal coil up to a high tone. Such coils matter for quantum chips. They can shield states and help form new kinds of bits.
arxiv-2601-10123:
Aditi Anand, Dildar Ali, and Suman Banerjee add fairness to path plans for many agents. Each agent must move from start to goal with no clash. Such plans run bots in halls and drones in the sky. The task is hard to solve fast.

Fairness adds a new bind. Agents are self run and may lie about their needs. A plan that is fast for the group may be poor for one agent. The team seeks plans that share the load in a fair way. They must also cope with false claims. The work joins path math with fair share rules.
arxiv-2601-10223:
Ziqi Xu and co authors build speech tools for people who stutter. Voice tools now gate much of daily life. They run aids, log ins, and work calls. But most were trained on fluent speech. They fail for the many people who stutter.

The team made Steamroller, a team of agents for this task. It aims to hear stuttered speech as it is. It should not force it into fluent norms. The work frames the gap as a form of lock out. It seeks speech tools that serve all users, not just the fluent.
arxiv-2601-10323:
Xueyun Tian and co authors build a live aid that hears, sees, and reads at once. Such aids are named omni multimodal. They pledge one model for sound, sight, and text. But live streams are hard. Aids tend to lack full mode reach or fail to watch on their own.

The team made ROMA, a live aid for streams. It can react to what a user says. It can also act first when a stream shows a key event. That dual skill is named proactive watch. The aim is an aid that joins a live stream as a true peer.
arxiv-2601-10623:
Yongzhen Feng, Weiwei Wang, Raymond K. W. Wong, and Xianyang Zhang build a single framework for fair regression. Regression predicts a number, such as a price or a risk score. Fairness here means demographic parity, a rule that asks for like outcomes across groups. Past methods often fit only one loss or lean on hard non-convex math.

Their framework casts fair regression as risk minimization under a parity constraint. It aims to cover a broad range of regression tasks in one setup. A shared frame makes results easier to compare and reuse. The work speaks to teams that must ship numeric predictions while meeting a clear fairness rule.
arxiv-2601-10923:
Haoze Guo and Ziqi Wei present a benchmark for indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation. RAG systems ground their answers in web content, much of it user-generated. That grounding is useful, but it widens the attack surface. Hidden instructions planted in web pages can survive the ingestion pipeline and hijack the model's reply.

The benchmark, called Hidden-in-Plain-Text, tests how systems handle such attacks from social-web sources. Indirect injection and retrieval poisoning are the threats in view. A shared test set lets teams compare defenses on equal terms. The work serves builders of search assistants that read the open web and must not obey it blindly.
arxiv-2601-11023:
Yong-Shen Cao, Qi-Rong Deng, and Ming-Tian Li set up Moran-type iterated function systems. A classic iterated function system repeats the same set of contractions to build a fractal. A Moran-type system changes the set at each step, following a sequence. The authors build the basic theory: attractors, invariant probability measures, and separation conditions.

With those in place, they develop the dimension theory of Moran self-similar sets. Dimension tells how the fractal fills space between line and plane. Step-varying systems model growth that is not steady, like deposits or branching with changing rules. The framework gives analysts firm ground for fractals built stage by stage rather than by one fixed rule.
arxiv-2601-11123:
Gabriele Parisi, Fabrizio Murgana, Vincenzo Greco, and Marco Ruggieri study the elliptic flow of charm quarks in proton-nucleus hits. Elliptic flow measures how particles favor one side, echoing the shape of the hit. Charm quarks are born in the earliest stage. The initial state is modeled as a glasma within the Color Glass Condensate framework.

The glasma starts from the McLerran-Venugopalan model. Fine fluctuations enter as hotspots of constituent quarks in both the proton and the nucleus. Tracking charm through this stage shows how much flow is built in the first instants. The work helps separate early-time physics from the later fluid stage in collider data.
arxiv-2601-11223:
Shiyang Zhang, Hendrik Hildebrandt, and six coauthors hunt for dark matter clues. Their 2026 preprint uses the KiDS-Legacy survey and Fermi-LAT data. Dark matter makes up most of the matter in the Universe. Its traits can be probed through the large-scale shape of cosmic mass.

The team cross-matches two weak signals in the sky. One is weak lensing, the slight bend of light by mass. The other is the glow of gamma rays yet to be sourced. They built gamma-ray maps from 15 years of Fermi-LAT data. The maps span ten bins of energy. Cross-matching the two can bound what WIMP dark matter can do.
arxiv-2601-11523:
Christian Ellington, Paramahansa Pramanik, and Haley Robinson evaluate user feedback data. Their 2026 preprint names the tool MetaScoreLens. Electronic games have grown steadily in recent years. Their audience now spans a broad range of age groups.

Growth brings a large volume of feedback data with it. Efforts like PlayMyData compile structured sets for academic use. MetaScoreLens evaluates such feedback across entertainment systems. Digital entertainment spans more than games alone in scope. A shared lens helps compare scores across unlike platforms. The work serves researchers who mine player opinion data. Fair comparison is the base for sound claims from such data.
arxiv-2601-11823:
C. Jiang, Cody L. Covington, and Kalman Varga model what a strong laser does to a pair of HCl molecules. The laser can tear the pair apart in a burst called Coulomb explosion. They sort the burst paths by which parts fly out.

They find three main paths: one three-body path and two four-body paths. One four-body path breaks the two units in steps, and one breaks them near the same time. Which path is picked tracks how much charge the laser built up. That in turn tracks the angle of the pair to the laser field.
arxiv-2601-11923:
P. Bilha Githinji, Aikaterini Melliou, Xi Yuan, and a large team map how proof has grown for Traditional Chinese Medicine as an add-on to radiotherapy. Use of such add-on care in cancer wards has grown for about twenty-five years. That span is since joint cancer care took formal shape.

Their sum traces how the proof base has matured over that time. Such a map can show which uses rest on firm trials and which rest on thin proof. It can guide new trials to gaps. It also helps clinics weigh claims with care.
arxiv-2601-12123: Hanwen Liu and Ibrahim Sabek ask if quantum computing is ready to speed up live database choices. Databases face hard choice tasks on each query, such as join order and index tuning. Those picks can make a query fast or slow by a large factor. Live use adds a strict time cap, since a slow plan costs more than it saves. The study weighs quantum tools against that cap and against strong classical tools. Its verdict guides where quantum help is real today.
arxiv-2601-12223:
Chandra M. Varma argues that Berry phase effects can yield a flux quantum of h over e in metals. Berry curvature does not show in phase links between points in a metal by default. It can show when fermions loop in momentum space, such as round lone impurities.

Those links fade past the diffusion length, like Bloch phase links. Varma sets out where the coherence can hold. A halved flux quantum would be a clear sign of Berry effects. The work is a theory note on metals and phase.  The claim rests on phase links round lone defects.
arxiv-2601-12323:
Yin Cai, Zhouhong Gu, JunTao Zhang, and Ping Chen train language models to reason via social interaction. Humans learn judgment in daily social acts. Most model training uses fixed text or set problems. That gives no lived sense of interaction, negotiation, or competition.

Their method, named MARO in the work, learns from social plays. Models gain from outcomes of talks and contests, not just from text. Social training could yield more robust judgment in open tasks. The work tests that claim on reasoning tasks.  Social plays give stakes that plain text lacks.
arxiv-2601-12423:
Antonin Clerc and five co authors work on stereo matching, the task of pairing points in two camera views. Stereo depth faces occlusions, motion, and warped images in real use. The task gets harder when features are sparse, as with facial landmarks. Sparse points give far less context for a match than dense pixels do.

Settings of the method can also sway results a lot. The team bring in optimal transport, a math tool for moving mass at least cost. Their method, called HOT-POT, uses that tool for the sparse case. Uses named in the work span self driving cars, robotics, and face analysis. A robust sparse matcher would help all three fields at once.
arxiv-2601-12523:
Cem Suulker and a large team work on eversion robots, soft robots that grow from their tip. Such robots turn themselves inside out to extend, like a vine. That growth lets them reach remote spaces through narrow gaps. Steering them around tight bends, though, remains a hard problem in practice.

Past fixes add artificial muscles to the body or active steering at the tip. Those additions work, but they add complexity and bulk. They also undercut the softness and compliance that make eversion robots special. The team use constrictive bands that induce buckling at chosen spots. Buckling on demand lets the robot take high curvature turns. The route aims to keep the robot soft while giving it real control.
arxiv-2601-12723:
Yuhiro Ono, Tomohiro Harada, and Yukiya Miura build a way to generate benchmarks for optimization algorithms. Benchmarks are fundamental for judging how well an algorithm performs. Artificial benchmarks often miss the diversity and irregularity of real world problem structures. Benchmarks built from real problems fix that, but they are costly and hard to construct.

Their framework evolves new benchmarks automatically with help from a language model. The model acts as a generative operator inside an evolutionary loop. Candidate benchmarks are created, tested, and bred over generations. The system is called an LLM driven evolutionary benchmark generator. Richer benchmarks could expose weak algorithms that toy problems let pass.
arxiv-2601-12823:
Belal Shaheen and a large team measure tree trunks from the air with Gaussian splatting. Foresters need DBH, the diameter of a trunk at breast height, for carbon and timber estimates. Aerial remote sensing surveys large areas efficiently. Accurate direct measurement of single objects in complex natural scenes stays difficult, though.

Learned radiance field methods, like NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, have raised reconstruction fidelity. The team build TreeDGS, an aerial Gaussian splatting method for distant DBH measurement. Denser geometry from posed imagery could let drones measure trees without ground crews. That would scale forest inventories to whole landscapes. The work links 3D vision with climate relevant forestry.
arxiv-2601-12923:
Nikita Popov, Eric Shen, and Ilya M. Spitkovsky study Kippenhahn curves of low rank partial isometries. A partial isometry is a matrix that preserves lengths on part of its space. Its Kippenhahn curve traces the boundary of its numerical range, the set of attainable field values. Circular components inside that curve are the focus here.

They establish conditions for rank three partial isometries to have such circular parts. They describe the matrices in this class whose numerical ranges are circular. They also show a named conjecture, the Gau Wang Wu conjecture, holds for these matrices. Results began in a capstone project under supervision. The work serves operator theory and matrix analysis.
arxiv-2601-13023:
Jamie Incley and Laura Wolz trace how neutral hydrogen gas changed over cosmic time. They start at the end of the Epoch of Reionization, when the first stars had cleared much of the early fog. They end with the large web of matter seen today.

The pair look for the mark of that shift in one faint radio line. It is the 21 cm line, shifted to long waves by the stretch of space. They use the SKA-Low array as their tool. Their range spans redshifts from three to seven, a span when the gas moved from a near smooth state to clumps tied to young galaxies. The work helps plan how such maps can read that change.
arxiv-2601-13223:
Patrick J. Wong, Zackary White, and Alexander V. Balatsky ask how curved space time shifts quantum phases in two model systems. The play of Einstein's gravity with quantum stuff is a live field. Most work looks at small bits, though. Work on wide quantum systems in curved space is thin.

The team fills part of that gap. They study two famed one dim chains. One is the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain, a model topological insulator. The other is the Kitaev wire, a model superconductor. They ask how a broad curved space from Einstein's rules moves the phase lines of each. The work ties two fields that meet too rarely.
arxiv-2601-13323:
Charlie Drury and co-authors run a guard service for rocks that may hit Earth with scant warn. The service is called the Meerkat Asteroid Guard. It is built and kept by the European Space Agency's Near Earth Object hub. Its job is to flag soon impactors, rocks whose path may end in a hit.

Such rocks show as short tracklets on a check page. Short arcs make the path hard to pin. The tool uses systematic ranging, a scan of all paths that fit the arc. From that scan it can warn while data is still thin. For Earth guard teams, hours of warn can move scopes to the right sky in time.
arxiv-2601-13523:
A. Elbaroudy and co-authors grow hybrid films of aluminium on indium gallium arsenide and watch them bead and facet. Hybrid superconductor and semiconductor stacks can host bound states in the gap. In topological phases, a zero energy class of such states may show, called Majorana bound states. Such states draw wide hunt.

The team grows aluminium films by molecular beam on In0.75Ga0.25As at near room heat. They track how the film dewets as a solid and how facets form. Film form sets if bound states can live at all. For Majorana teams, growth facts on the base stack are ground work, not a side note.
arxiv-2601-13823:
Van Chien Le and Kristof Cools set up a new equation for how waves scatter off mixed objects in 2026. The case is time-harmonic electromagnetic scattering by composite dielectric objects. Composite means the object joins parts with distinct traits. The classic Müller equation handles single objects well.

Their multi-trace Müller formulation extends it to composites. A key step uses the Stratton-Chu representation in the complementary region, known as the extinction property. The final block system is built only of second-kind operators. Such systems tend to solve in a stable, fast way for antenna and radar work.
arxiv-2601-15123:
Andrey Moskalenko, Danil Kuznetsov, and a team of co-authors test how well promptable image models hold up. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with models such as SAM, which cut objects out of images from a user prompt. A prompt can be a point, a box, or a line of text.

Boxes work especially well in practice. They often beat points and cost far less effort to draw. The authors set out BREPS, a way to gauge how robust box prompts are. It checks what happens when the box is loose, shifted, or drawn in a slightly off way.
arxiv-2601-15323:
Solving systems of nonlinear equations gets a new iterative method in a 2026 arXiv paper. The work starts from a three-point method built for a single scalar equation. That method is then adapted to systems, where many equations in many unknowns must hold at once.

Using Taylor's theorem for functions of several variables, the author shows the new method keeps a strong rate. It has a sixth order of convergence. That means the error shrinks very fast near a solution. Fast convergence matters a great deal when each function evaluation is costly to run.
arxiv-2601-15523:
Tyler Kharazi and three co-authors build a quantum method for reaction rates in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Fokker-Planck equation models rare events across the sciences. Its high-dimensional form strains classical computers. Quantum algorithms for such dynamics face their own flaw. Their success probability often decays exponentially, wasting runs.

The authors introduce a quantum algorithm that gets past that flaw. It computes reaction rates in sublinear time, per the title. Reaction rates govern how often rare shifts occur, from chemical change to protein folding. A faster route to those numbers would aid many fields. The paper targets the high-dimensional cases where classical tools stall. That is where a quantum edge, if real, matters most.
arxiv-2601-15823:
P. Jelínek, M. Karlický, and S. Belov model a solar filament that fails to erupt in a 2026 arXiv paper. Solar filaments are cool, dense threads held in the Sun's corona. They often link to eruptions and coronal mass ejections. Sometimes the ejection halts midway. The result is a failed eruption. What happens after the filament destabilizes is poorly understood. Yet it matters for space weather, since near-eruptions still shake the corona.

The authors study a current-carrying filament balanced by gravity. They follow its post-destabilization evolution in that model. Oscillations after a failed ejection are part of the story, per the title's theme. A filament that falls back can sway for hours. Reading those sways tells physicists about the forces that held it.
arxiv-2601-16623:
Weerayut Buaphet and coauthors build one bench and model for word form fixes in Asian tongues. Their 2026 preprint, named MultiLexNorm, deals with social text. Social text is rich but wild in form and word use. Wild forms break tools built for clean text. Word form fix maps wild words to a set clean form.

Asian tongues add script and form traits past work oft missed. One bench lets teams weigh fix tools fair on those traits. A seed model in the work gives a base score to beat. Fair tests serve chat, search and guard tools. The work widens fix craft past West tongues.
arxiv-2601-16823:
Leonard Pleiss, Maximilian Schiffer, and Robert von Weizsäcker use chess to test what chatbots truly know. Chatbots ace many tests, but why is unclear. They may recall vast text by heart. Or they may reason from first rules each time. Their 2026 preprint sorts these two gifts with chess boards.

Chess gives a clean test bed with strong judge tools. The team sorts boards from famed to brand new. Famed boards can be solved by recall of past games. New boards call for fresh thought on the spot. Gaps in scores then show where recall ends. Such tests help labs build bots that truly think.
arxiv-2601-16923:
Nick Fischer, Marvin Künnemann, and Mirza Redzic sharpen bounds for a classic pick task. The task picks k sets to cover the most ground. Ground here is a pool of items to claim. Their 2026 preprint ties the task to a twin task on rule graphs. That twin picks points that rule most of a graph. Cuts that drop rule depth link the two.

Their bounds are tight if a famed guess holds. Such tight bounds close long hunts in pick math. They tell coders when to quit the hunt for speed. Pick tasks sit in ads, sensors, and team choice. Sharp bounds guide all those fields at once.
arxiv-2601-17123:
Daehwa Kim and Chris Harrison give sight-text bots a new sense: sound maps. Plain clips join shots with one flat sound track. Their 2026 preprint adds acoustic field video to the mix. Such video paints sound strength across the scene. Each spot in view gets its own loud mark. Bots can then tie sounds to the things that make them.

A dog's bark can pin to the dog in view. A far siren stays faint at the frame's edge. This ground truth helps bots read scenes with more sense. It may aid guide tools for the blind. It adds a sense that flat tracks lack.
arxiv-2601-17323:
The SkyReels Team presents SkyReels-V3, a model that makes video from mixed inputs. Video work is a core test for world models. A strong model must infer what should happen from text, images, and sound cues. SkyReels-V3 uses one shared frame for that in-context learning. It is built on diffusion Transformers, the current workhorse for video.

The model is conditional, so users steer output with the inputs they give. One frame for many input types cuts the need for split tools. Such models serve film, ads, and training worlds for robots. The tech report lays out the design. It shows where this line of models stands now.
arxiv-2601-17623:
Alexander Plakhotnikov frames Ricci flow in the language of categories. Ricci flow smooths the shape of a space over time. It is the tool that helped prove the Poincaré conjecture. Plakhotnikov treats the flow as a sequence of functors. Functors map between categories while keeping structure. His maps link stacks of Riemannian metrics to geometric decompositions.

Singular flow spacetimes handle the points where smoothness breaks. To make the domain rigorous, he adapts differentiable stacks to Banach manifolds. A categorical frame can unify split results in flow theory. It may also move tools from algebra into geometry. The note is a proposal, framed with care. It invites geometers to test the frame.
arxiv-2601-17723:
Tayyab Nasir, Daochang Liu, and Ajmal Mian run an empirical study of continuous single image super-resolution. Implicit neural representation is now the standard for arbitrary-scale upscaling. No study had systematically tested existing methods as a set. Training recipes also lacked study. Scaling laws, objective design, and optimization choices all vary by paper.

A shared empirical base lets the field compare fairly. It shows which gains come from method and which from recipe. Super-resolution serves photos, medical scans, and satellite views. Arbitrary scale fits zoom tools users expect today. The study gives builders a tested menu of choices. It can end cherry-picked claims in the subfield.
arxiv-2601-17823:
Pranav Kasela and co-authors present DIETA, a compact model for translating between Italian and English. Their 2026 preprint describes a decoder-only transformer with half a billion parameters. That is small next to the giant models in wide use. The team trained it for this one language pair. They built a large parallel corpus of about 207 million sentence pairs to teach it.

A focused model can be cheap to run and easy to host. It can also be tuned with care for the quirks of one pair of languages. The paper covers both the data work and the model design. For groups that need Italian-English translation, a small specialist may beat a huge generalist on cost.
arxiv-2601-17923:
Ali Najar teaches a game agent skills that it can carry to new fights. His 2026 preprint uses the action game Dark Souls III as the test bed. Lifelong agents should grow in skill over time. They should not need retraining from scratch, nor should new skills wipe out old ones. The author maps combat as a directed graph of skills, where each node is a move or tactic and edges show how they chain.

Training follows a staged curriculum over that graph. New parts are added in a set order, and only chosen parts adapt at each stage. That selective update helps old skills survive. Games with real-time control make a harsh but clear test of the idea.
arxiv-2601-18023:
Runjie Song, Kengo Deguchi, Genta Kawahara, and Yongyun Hwang look for hidden order inside shear-flow turbulence. Their 2026 preprint studies flows like those in pipes and channels. Many efforts seek simple patterns in the chaos, such as travelling waves or periodic orbits. The authors show that multiscale features need richer states. They focus on solutions that are quasi-periodic in time, repeating with more than one rhythm at once.

Such states can be computed well with a quasi-linear model. That keeps the cost sane while the structure stays rich. Richer building blocks may explain more of what real turbulence does. The work helps the long search for a skeleton beneath turbulent flow.
arxiv-2601-18223:
Jiaqi Liu, Zhenzhen Lou, and Vilmar Trevisan find the graphs with the smallest spectral radius for a fixed matching size. Their 2026 preprint takes up the Brualdi-Solheid problem. That problem asks which graph in a class hits the extreme spectral radius, largest or smallest. The class here is all graphs with a given order and matching number. A matching is a set of edges that share no vertices, and its size limits how a graph can spread.

The authors aim to identify the spectrally minimal graphs in that family. Extremal results show which shapes sit at the edge of what is possible. Spectral radius links to walks, spread, and network behavior. The work adds a solved case to a classic problem.
arxiv-2601-18323:
Weishi Mi and co-authors ground video generation so its plans can drive a real robot. Their 2026 preprint presents TC-IDM. The vision-language-action paradigm gives strong robot control, but it feeds on large sets of costly robot data. Generative world models promise an alternative: dream the scene, then act. The gap is that pixel-level plans are not yet physical actions a robot can run. TC-IDM aims to close that gap for zero-shot robot motion, with no task-specific training.

Executable plans would let one world model serve many robots. The grounding step is where many embodied AI ideas fail. Success here would loosen the field's dependence on hand-collected robot data.
arxiv-2601-18523:
L. A. S. Evangelista and A. F. Santos work out how gravity could bend a classic smash of bits and anti-bits. In their setup an electron and its anti-twin meet and make a new pair of like bits. The trade is run not by light or by charge, but by a graviton, the guessed bit that bears the pull of gravity. They frame gravity in a weak form that looks much like the maths of magnets and charge.

That frame lets them write the odds for each path the new pair can take. The odds are far too small for a lab test now, but the maths still counts. It shows how a weak-gravity frame would mark even a clean bit smash. Such work tests the reach of the frame and its ties to the charge world. It may guide hunts for where the frame breaks.
arxiv-2601-18723:
Mengyuan Liu and six colleagues call for a more trust-worthy way to grade robot arm work. Arm tools now learn by copy: they watch a pro and learn to act the same. Grades for such tools rest most on a plain pass count. Did the arm stack the block or not? That count says nought about trust. A lucky pass and a firm pass count the same.

The team set out a new test set and auto grade paths that weigh more. Their grades ask where the skill came from and if the tape of the run is true. They also weigh how the arm acts when the task shifts a bit. A richer grade could help firms pick arms they can trust on a line. It could also show which skills are firm and which are luck.
arxiv-2601-18823:
A study takes on a flaw in a kind of smart tool that learns to squeeze data down and build it back up. Such a tool, called a variational autoencoder, learns a small code for each case. Once taught, it should flag new cases whose codes look odd, since odd codes may mark faults or fraud. But as the code grows in dims, its space swells fast. That swell can warp the codes and hide the odd ones.

The work bends the code space in-to a ball form, in which all codes sit on a shell of set span. A shell has no far waste space for codes to drift in-to. Codes that break the shell's form then stand out with more ease. A sharper flag could serve banks, plants, and scan tools. The work tests the ball form on that hunt.
arxiv-2601-18923:
Manthan Patel and seven co-authors tackle a gap in how robots learn from depth sensors. Depth cameras are now common on robots, and fake depth data made in sims can train skills that work in the real world. Yet learned depth features lag far behind those for color images, where big base models lead the field.

The authors build a base model for depth, called DeFM, meant to be reused across tasks. A shared depth model could cut the need to train from scratch for each new robot job. The work treats depth as a sense that earns its own large scale training, much like sight through color.
arxiv-2601-19423:
Zijie Lei and six co-authors fold four kinds of signals into one encoding for model based recommendation. Language models have shown promise for recommending with text and images. Real recommendation signals run wider: free text, images, categorical facts, and numeric values all speak at once.

That mix is hard for a language model to swallow evenly. Their unified encoding, UniRec, gives each kind a place in one frame. Recommenders that read all four signals as fluently as text could use the rich records that shops and platforms already keep on items and users.
arxiv-2601-20023:
The CMS Collaboration reports production rates for three closely related mesons in proton collisions. The particles are the Upsilon states, bound forms of a bottom quark and its antiquark. Their production cross sections test quantum chromodynamics in a clean setting. The data come from collisions recorded by the CMS experiment in 2022.

The team measures how the cross sections vary, using a large sample from that run. Differential measurements, split by momentum and angle, are far more constraining than a single total. They test the calculations theorists use to predict heavy quark production. Any mismatch points at gaps in our picture of the strong force. The results feed global fits of collider data.
arxiv-2601-20223:
Aral de Moor and eight colleagues introduce control models for AI code completion inside JetBrains development tools. These are classifiers that decide when to trigger a completion and which suggestions to show. The goal is to match suggestions to what a user wants and to cut needless model calls.

The authors test boosting and transformer designs on real completion data from dozens of users. Each wasted call costs money and can annoy the user with a poor suggestion. Filters of this kind sit between the user and the model, and they shape how helpful code completion feels in daily work.
arxiv-2601-20423:
Zhiqing Zhang gives an invited overview of tau lepton physics. He also makes the case for a super tau-charm factory, a planned collider in the energy range where tau particles are produced. The talk uses the tau's discovery and its precision measurements as examples of why this energy region matters.

Zhang reviews the current status of the major physics topics for the tau. He then points to open issues and the chances a super tau-charm factory would bring. Precision tau data test the standard model of particle physics and can reveal cracks where new physics hides.
arxiv-2601-20523:
Haiyan Wang and Melinda Wang find necessary and sufficient conditions for a unique solution to a gamma moment closure of the stochastic Ricker equation. The Ricker equation is a classic model of population size, where each generation grows and then is checked by crowding. Here random perturbations multiply each step.

Moment closure approximates the full distribution by tracking a few of its moments, and the gamma closure assumes a gamma shape. Knowing exactly when that closure has one solution tells ecologists when the shortcut is safe. Population forecasts for fisheries and pests lean on such approximations.
arxiv-2601-20623:
Hongyi Cai studies listwise reranking for documents that mix images and text. Recent retrieval work shows promise in joining visual and textual signals. Yet reranking image-text documents stays hard, because of the modality gap and a scarcity of aligned datasets. Existing approaches often use very large models with reasoning-based distillation.

That size brings heavy compute cost while focusing mostly on text. Cai's work questions whether the visual side gets its due in reranking. Better multimodal reranking would sharpen search in commerce, media libraries, and any archive where pictures and words travel together.
arxiv-2601-20723:
Emrah Akyol and Marcos Vasconcelos study how a network of agents can learn to coordinate when their messages get garbled. Their 2026 paper uses binary coordination games played over a graph. Each agent picks one of two actions. News of neighbors' actions arrives through noisy links. The noise can flip a bit or erase it.

The team models each link as one of two classic channels. One flips bits at random; the other drops them. Agents update their play with log-linear learning, a standard rule for such games. The authors analyze two working regimes and describe the shape of the learning dynamics that result. The work matters for systems that must agree while talking over poor connections.
arxiv-2601-21123:
Tianyi Chen and a large team of co-authors give computer-using agents a library of reusable skills. Their 2026 paper presents CUA-Skill. Computer-using agents aim to operate computer systems autonomously for real-world tasks. Existing systems remain hard to scale and lag behind human performance. A key limitation is the absence of reusable, structured skill abstractions. Humans rely on such skills for graphical interfaces. Agents mostly improvise each step anew.

CUA-Skill captures how humans interact with interfaces as named skills. An agent can then compose those skills for new tasks. Reuse turns one-off tricks into dependable tools. It also makes agent behavior easier to inspect and fix. The paper targets the gap between agent demos and office reality. Structured skills are a step toward agents that learn like apprentices.
arxiv-2601-21523:
Bang Giang Le and Viet Cuong Ta fix credit assignment when robot teams or game agents share one team reward. A shared reward is noisy, since every agent's acts are mixed into it. Each agent still needs to learn which of its own acts helped.

The authors give each agent explicit local rewards shaped by a dependence graph. The graph records which agents actually affect each other. Local signals tied to real links should cut through the team noise. Clearer credit means faster learning for teams, from warehouse robots to traffic control, where joint rewards are the only honest score.
arxiv-2601-21623:
Stanislav Budzinskiy and seven co-authors speed up language model inference with mixed numerical precision. Modern AI runs on a blend of number formats, some cheap and coarse, some costly and fine. The blend is a hallmark of current systems and helps models run locally.

The paper studies the floating-point math behind functions built from many composed parts. It focuses on transformer inference, where such compositions pile up. A look-ahead method chooses precision step by step with the road ahead in view. Smarter precision choices can cut cost without letting small errors grow into wrong answers.
arxiv-2601-21823:
Zihan Huang and co-authors try to give spiking neurons a sense of prediction. Spiking neural networks save energy because they compute only when spikes occur, in short events. Their training is hard, though, because spikes cannot be differentiated smoothly, and designers face trade-offs among accuracy, efficiency, and realism.

The authors note that mainstream spiking networks ignore predictive coding, a core idea about how the brain works. Predict the input, then encode only the error. Their 2026 preprint proposes a general self-prediction enhancement for spiking neurons built on that idea. If prediction can be woven into spiking models cleanly, the networks could keep their energy edge while closing the accuracy gap with ordinary deep networks.
arxiv-2601-21923:
Elisabeth Wybo and co-authors mix quantum and classical methods to solve a classic graph problem. The maximum independent set problem asks for the largest set of vertices with no edges between them. It appears in scheduling, coding, and network design, and it is hard to solve exactly at scale.

Their 2026 preprint studies a hybrid algorithm for regular graphs. It combines the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm, using angles computed in advance, with a minimal-degree classical greedy method. The quantum part guides the search while the classical part finishes the job cheaply. Honest tests of such hybrids matter because they show where today's small quantum processors can genuinely help rather than merely participate.
arxiv-2601-22023:
Juntao Wang, Mei Wang, and William Zuluaga Botero prove an equivalence between two categories in mathematical logic. One category holds certain c-differential residuated distributive lattices that satisfy a condition called CK. These lattices are algebraic models of substructural logics, systems that drop some usual rules about reusing assumptions.

The other category holds plain residuated distributive lattices. The authors show an exact match. The first category is the image of the second under Kalman's equivalence. That classic construction is adapted here to first-order substructural logics. Equivalences like this let results proved on one side transfer to the other. Their 2026 preprint extends the reach of a powerful method in algebraic logic.
arxiv-2601-22123:
Winfried Ripken and co-authors teach neural networks to leap through molecular time. Simulating how a Hamiltonian system evolves over long times is limited by the tiny steps that stable numerical integration demands. A simulation that must take millions of small steps cannot reach the timescales chemists care about.

The team introduces a framework for learning Hamiltonian flow maps, functions that jump the system forward in large steps. A consistency condition on the mean flow keeps those jumps honest. Their 2026 preprint targets molecular dynamics, where folding, binding, and reactions unfold over times that brute-force integration reaches only on supercomputers. Learned large steps could open those processes to routine study.
arxiv-2601-22223:
C. N. Kimmig and co-authors ask whether a passing star can permanently tilt a young planetary system. When a star flies by a protoplanetary disk, it can warp the disk and excite spiral arms. Observations suggest that warps in disks are common, which raises the question of how long such damage lasts.

The team investigates fly-by effects across different trajectories. Their finding, announced in the title, is that warps survive beyond the fly-by encounter itself; the disk does not simply settle flat again. Their 2026 preprint also links the models to observations. Lasting warps would give astronomers a fossil record of stellar encounters in the crowded nurseries where most stars, and their planets, are born.
arxiv-2601-22323:
Qi Cao and five co-authors route each user query to the model that fits it best. Cheap models can take easy asks, while hard asks go to strong, costly ones. Their 2026 preprint argues that most routers pick from a fixed short list, which dates fast as new models land.

Their method reasons ahead of the choice, a step they call pre-hoc reasoning. It aims to adapt as models and budgets change. Good routing can cut spend a great deal while holding quality high. The work speaks to any team that serves models at scale.
arxiv-2601-22823:
Mathieu Petitbois, Rémy Portelas, and Sylvain Lamprier study offline learning where style matters as much as success. An agent learns from logged data, without fresh trial and error. The goal is a policy that both performs well and follows a target style, labeled on parts of past behavior.

Style and reward often pull in opposite ways, and offline data shift makes the clash worse. Past methods, despite many definitions of style, often fail to balance the two. Workable style control matters for robots and games that must act well in a set manner.
arxiv-2601-22923:
Gracinda M.S. Gomes, Victoria Gould, and Yanhui Wang characterize a class of algebraic structures called left Ehresmann monoids. These structures generalize groups by allowing operations that need not be reversible. The class studied here is picked out by certain universal properties and a proper basis.

Every such monoid is known to have a cover built from a monoid acting on an ordered set. Their abstract characterization clarifies exactly which monoids arise this way. Results like this organize the landscape of semigroup theory, a field used in automata and language theory.
arxiv-2601-23123:
Francesca Zanichelli and six co-authors build a compact resonator that couples light strongly to magnetic waves. Cavity magnonics usually pairs a bulky three-dimensional resonator with a thick magnetic crystal. That standard platform is hard to shrink or adapt.

Their loop-gap resonator is modular and tuned for thin magnetic films instead. Thin films are the form used in modern spintronic devices. Strong coupling in a film-friendly package could bring hybrid quantum devices closer to practical chips. Thin films are the advance: earlier cavity magnonics platforms were built around bulk crystals, not device-ready layers. The loop-gap design is modular, so the resonator can be adapted to different films and setups.
arxiv-2601-23223:
Hao Xu, Alisa Liu, Jonathan Hayase, Yejin Choi, and Noah A. Smith study prompts that end mid-token. Language models are trained on token sequences, but users type raw text. When a prompt stops inside the model's expected next token, predictions can skew badly.

The authors call this the partial token problem and study it practically. It affects everyday tools, since people paste, truncate, and edit text mid-word all the time. Naming and measuring the flaw is the first step to interfaces that handle it gracefully. Distorted next-token predictions are the measurable harm, appearing whenever user text and model tokenization fall out of alignment.

Alexandre Bertrand wrote his Traite du somnambulisme in French in 1823. Somnambulism, sleepwalking raised by magnetism, is his whole subject. Bertrand sorts its forms and the changes each one brings. His treatise is the first systematic French pathology of magnetic sleep.

broad-scientific-thought-1923:

He examines space, time, matter, and cause as the new theories rebuilt them, asking which older notions can survive. His manner is slow, exhaustive, and scrupulously fair to every side. Philosophers treated the book as the standard survey of the questions. It shows analytic philosophy learning to take modern physics seriously, concept by concept.
bruce-evolution-arthurian-romance-vol1-1:
James Douglas Bruce published the first volume of The Evolution of Arthurian Romance in 1923. His aim was to map the whole Arthurian tradition from its start to the year 1300. The book surveys sources, poets, and prose cycles in careful order.

buckland-reliquiae-diluvianae-1823:

He read the caves of Kirkdale and other sites as dens of hyenas, swept by the flood. His scheme tied all such finds to the one flood and left no room for an old age of man. All who came next and claimed deep time for man had to fight his frame first.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-1-182:
Gilbert Burnet, a Scottish bishop who lived at the center of power, wrote the History of His Own Time. The work was published in 1724 to 1734, after his death. Volume one here opens the Oxford edition of 1823. The edition runs to six volumes, with passages once suppressed now restored. Burnet's span covers the Restoration and the Glorious Revolution.

Burnet writes as a Whig and a churchman who knew Cromwell's heirs, Charles II, and William III in person. His pages mix high politics with gossip, character, and sharp moral judgment. The result is the great eyewitness history of his age, partisan and priceless at once. Volume one sets that crowded stage.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-2-182:
Volume two continues Gilbert Burnet's History of His Own Time in the Oxford edition of 1823. Burnet's history, first published in 1724 to 1734, covers the later Stuart age from a bishop's seat near the throne. The 1823 edition runs to six volumes and restores passages that earlier editors had cut.

Burnet knew the men he judges: kings, ministers, generals, and plotters passed through his life. His narrative of the Restoration and the road to revolution in 1688 is vivid, frank, and openly Whig in sympathy. Scholars quarrel with his bias and quarry his facts in the same breath. Volume two keeps the eyewitness record rolling through a dangerous reign.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-3-182:
Burnet's History of His Own Time reaches volume three in the Oxford edition of 1823, the six-volume set with suppressed passages restored. Gilbert Burnet published the history in 1724 to 1734, drawn from his own diaries and his place at the heart of affairs. He had advised William of Orange and helped prepare the revolution of 1688.

Volume three holds the middle of his long story, from Restoration intrigue toward open crisis. Burnet's pen portraits of the age's leaders are bold, warm, and sometimes unfair, always alive. His history is the great Whig counterpart to Clarendon's royalist epic. Reading both gives the age in stereo. This volume keeps Burnet's side loud and clear.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-4-182:

Burnet writes history as a participant with strong loves and hatreds, which is both its spice and its warning. Courts, parliaments, and churches fill his pages, judged by a man who served in all three. The Glorious Revolution, his great cause, draws near as the volumes advance. Volume four carries the crisis forward in the bishop's brisk, knowing voice.
burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-5-182:
The History of His Own Time moves through volume five in the Oxford edition of 1823. Gilbert Burnet's work, published in 1724 to 1734, narrates England's passage from Restoration to revolution through the eyes of a bishop at the center. Volume five stands deep in the reign-shaking events Burnet helped to shape. His account blends state papers, private talk, and his own sermons and counsel to princes.
