Perry's July report came days after the Seven Days battles ended in Virginia, when European papers were full of Union retreat. His task in Madrid was to keep Spain from drawing the worst conclusions. Reports home also described Spanish policy in Mexico and the state of feeling at court. Seward read such letters from every post before framing his replies, so each one shaped, in a small way, the Union's voice abroad.
frus-1862-d523:
On 13 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. The instruction is Document 523 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Five days after his last Dutch order, Seward was back at the same desk, a measure of how much detail the Hague file carried. The standing business included Dutch colonial ports in the West Indies, where the rules for belligerent ships had daily consequences. Pike's blunt reporting had made The Hague one of the Department's trusted smaller posts. The instruction shows the relationship in its mature form: frequent, factual, and free of ceremony, between two men who wrote as plainly as they thought.
frus-1862-d623:
On 18 September 1862 Jacob S. Haldeman sent this report from Stockholm to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 623 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the Swedish file's last paper of the year.

Haldeman wrote the day after Antietam, in complete ignorance of it, as every minister in Europe did that week. His letter reported the north as he found it: friendly, neutral, and watching. When the battle news and the emancipation order reached Stockholm soon after, they fell on prepared ground. The dispatch closes a small, serene file, and its very calm is data. In the war's most dangerous month, the Union's northernmost European post had nothing to fear. It had little to ask.
frus-1863p1-d123:
From the London legation on 19 March 1863 came this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 123 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late-March reports from London charted a tense season. The ship question neared a head, and the South's friends in Britain pressed their case in the open. Adams's mail weighed each sign for Washington. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day, part of the flow that made his legation's file the fullest in the volume.
frus-1863p1-d223:
From Washington on 29 June 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 223 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d23:
On 1 January 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams held the American legation in London. The letter is document 23 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, twin to the one before it.

Two sheets in one day split a post's business by topic, a habit on both sides of this exchange. Adams had much to sort: British feeling on the war, the South's agents, and the first word of the new year at home. This letter is the second half of his New Year's Day work, and it keeps the file's pace into 1863.
frus-1863p1-d323: On 14 November 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 323 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d423:
In Washington on 24 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 423 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d523:
21 May 1863 is the date on a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d623:
Dated 24 September 1863, document 623 is a letter from William Stuart, Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d123: Alexander Kirk, now styled Minister in Egypt, wrote to the Secretary of State on November 12, 1943. His dispatch is Document 123 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Kirk's Cairo post made him the host government's closest American watcher, and his messages in the summit fortnight carried the local scene. The record names the parties and the date. The dispatch is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d223:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt cabled Washington late on 16 November 1943, in telegram 1884, about a talk with Soviet ambassador Sergey Vinogradov in Ankara. The two men had met the day before and traded pleasure at the outcome of the Moscow conference.

Vinogradov said he had kept away from Foreign Minister Numan so the British ambassador could test whether Turkey cared more about the military or the political side of joining the war. He stressed that early entry would count as a real gift to Allied victory, while late entry would count for little. Steinhardt concludes that Vinogradov had orders to stand back from the Anglo-Turkish talks, ready only if Numan asked him about Soviet aims in the Balkans.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d23: A second Churchill message to Roosevelt bears the same date, August 11, 1943, and follows as Document 23 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two notes in one day was nothing unusual for the prime minister, who ran much of his war by letter and telegram. Why this one was needed, the catalog does not say. It is kept in the Foreign Relations series, on the eve of the Quebec Conference.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d323:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 411/2 at Cairo on 26 November 1943, listing the points on which Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek's agreement should be obtained before he left for China. Lord Mountbatten drafted the list, and the chiefs amended and approved it that day.

Since the 535 extra transport aircraft for the Mandalay plan cannot be found, Mountbatten's plan from the first plenary session stands. Chiang's demand for a seaborne operation in March is noted for the world review of amphibious operations a week later. A strong fleet will gather in the Bay of Bengal by March. Mountbatten may divert no more than an average of 1,100 tons a month from Hump tonnage to the Burma campaign. Meanwhile the airlift strives for the full 10,000 tons into China by late winter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d423:
Louis Dreyfus, the American minister in Iran, telegraphed Secretary of State Hull from Tehran on 8 December 1943. His telegram, number 1096, reports the Soviet explanation for an early publication. The Declaration on Iran had appeared ahead of time in the Soviet Embassy's Persian newspaper.

The Soviet chargé told Dreyfus he had heard the Iranians meant to release the text on the morning of 5 December. His embassy therefore rushed its own publication to avoid being left behind. In a separate talk, the Soviet press attaché denied all knowledge of any release-date agreement and hinted he had not understood the declaration to form part of the general release. Dreyfus calls the two statements conflicting and both implausible: the chargé could simply have warned his colleagues, and the attaché had sat in the 4 December meeting where the release was arranged. He has not pressed the point.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d523:
Ambassador Averell Harriman cabled President Roosevelt directly from Moscow on December 20, 1943. Harriman, a businessman turned envoy, had Roosevelt's ear and used a direct channel to the President for his most important reports. The State Department printed the cable in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Three weeks after Tehran, Harriman's task was to judge how the new partnership looked from inside the Soviet capital: what Moscow expected, and where its patience might run short. His reports shaped Roosevelt's handling of Stalin more than almost any other source. For readers, this cable is front-line evidence from the embassy that watched the alliance's most difficult partner.
frus-1944-quebec-d123:
A second State Department briefing paper for Quebec, titled "U.S. Relations With the Soviet Union," takes a cooler look at the alliance. It states the American goal plainly: the closest, most cooperative relationship possible with Moscow. But it says wartime needs had put cooperation itself ahead of agreeing the principles cooperation must rest on.

The paper calls recent Soviet policy on Poland and the Baltic States far from encouraging. It warns that Moscow might mistake friendliness for weakness. Washington should show more firmness and speak more frankly, the authors argue, without risking military cooperation against Germany. Enduring cooperation, they conclude, cannot be bought by swallowing policies America judged destructive.
frus-1944-quebec-d223: An editors' note points forward in the volume. For the memorandum of agreement on lend-lease to the United Kingdom, initialed by Roosevelt and Churchill at Quebec on September 15, 1944, readers are directed to page 468. The note itself records no discussion; it simply keeps the conference's paper trail connected, linking the lend-lease debates printed earlier to the signed text printed later.
frus-1944-quebec-d23:
On August 10, 1944, Churchill sent a further message to Roosevelt. He kept up the near-daily rhythm of that month. The letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

By August 10, the German army in France faced encirclement. The alliance's arguments were shifting from survival to settlement. Churchill's letters pursued British interests through that shift. He wrote with his usual energy. For readers, the message forms part of a written bridge. It links the Normandy campaign to the Quebec Conference. There the two leaders would settle the war's remaining course. They would try to do so face to face.
frus-1945-50-intel-d123:
Tamm wrote to Hoover on 10 August 1946, two days after the authority's letter to Clark. The FBI's inside papers kept pace with the fight's public moves. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Tamm's memorandum gave Hoover the bureau's private reading of the ruling and its costs. Inside papers at such moments often plan the next step: acceptance, appeal, or quiet resistance. Readers following the FBI thread should read this beside the letters of 8 August. The public record shows what the bureau was told; Tamm's paper shows what the bureau told itself, and the difference is where institutional history lives.
frus-1945-50-intel-d223:
On 19 September 1947, the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) sent a memorandum to the National Security Council. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 223 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d23:
Alfred McCormack, the secretary of state's special assistant for research and intelligence, wrote to General Magruder of the Strategic Services Unit on 4 October 1945. McCormack had just inherited the OSS's analysts at State. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The two men now held the two halves of the dead OSS between them, one at State and one at War. Their letters had to settle how the halves would still work together. This early exchange shows the heirs feeling their way, polite on paper and jealous in fact. Readers can follow the McCormack and Magruder thread as the volume's clearest view of the divided inheritance. Of the men who knew it could not stay divided for long.
frus-1945-50-intel-d323:
Minutes record the 15th Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board on 31 July 1947. It is document 323 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act was moving through Congress that year, and it would soon replace the wartime setup with the CIA.

No speeches fill these pages; the form is a tight note of points made and ground covered, kept for later use. Staff in other offices then worked from this record, treating its lines as the settled word. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d423:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 5, dated 12 December 1947, is document 423 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Council issued the early directives in a group, in the first winter of the CIA's life. Each one fixed a piece of the shared system, so that no agency could claim the whole field. Readers can watch a government invent a new kind of office and then fence it round with written rules. Read in order, the December directives show a full system being sketched in a single week.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d123:
Churchill reported his Moscow talks with Stalin in this top secret message of 22 October 1944. The excerpts printed in the Malta and Yalta volume cover the future partition of Germany. Churchill had just come from sitting with the Soviet leader, whom the cables call “U. J.”

Stalin, he writes, wants Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary to form a belt of free, anti-Nazi, pro-Russian states. Against his earlier view, Stalin would gladly see Vienna head a federation of south German states, taking in Austria, Bavaria, Württemberg, and Baden. Churchill likes the Danubian idea, which has always drawn him, but he would add Hungary. To that, Stalin is strongly opposed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d223:
War-significant equipment and true rebuilding credits must travel apart, Grew cabled Harriman on 26 January 1945. His secret instruction, number 173, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. State, Treasury, and the Foreign Economic Administration all agree on the separation, he reports.

Separate cables will carry the reply on the Fourth Protocol and the answer to Molotov's aide-mémoire, with its bearing on the 3-C agreement. This message gives background on postwar credits. A departmental study puts Russia's war loss at sixteen billion dollars of fixed capital. That is about a quarter of the prewar total, with stocks down perhaps four billion more. Even without foreign loans, the study reckons, Moscow could regain the prewar level of capital by 1948.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d23: Churchill kept the exchange moving with a message to Roosevelt on 19 November 1944, the third letter in three days. It is document 23 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering Malta and Yalta. Read in sequence, these November messages show the Anglo-American partnership working at full speed while arrangements for the winter conferences slowly came into focus.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d323:
America's Joint Chiefs gathered at Yalta on the morning of February 4, 1945, to set their agenda for the three-power talks. Admiral Cooke summed up the staff work done with the United States Military Mission from Moscow. Two large items stood out: linking operations in the field with the Soviet armies, and dealings with Moscow on the Far East.

The first item, Cooke noted, involved British, American, and Soviet talks together. Papers before the chiefs pulled months of exchanges with Moscow into one place. The session shows the American military team clearing its decks hours before the first full meeting with Stalin that afternoon.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d423:
Stettinius reported no Polish deal yet when the plenary met on February 9, 1945, in Bohlen's minutes. The President called on him as the day's chairman of the foreign ministers. Stettinius described the long debate on the Polish governmental question, held on the basis of an American paper. The presidential committee idea had been dropped, following Molotov's proposal.

On the formula itself, Molotov wanted time. He would put the new American considerations before Stalin before speaking finally. The ministers agreed to continue the discussion later and to report no agreement so far. Bohlen's record shows the conference's centerpiece still stuck, two days from the end.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d123:
Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled Ambassador Winant in London on July 5, 1945, with the senior names of the American delegation. The telegram is document 123 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, answering the Foreign Office's request after it shared its own roster on June 29.

Winant may tell the Foreign Office that the State Department delegation will include Byrnes himself, Assistant Secretaries Dunn and Clayton, and Ambassadors Murphy and Harriman. H. F. Matthews, who directs the Office of European Affairs, will also come, along with several specialists on European and Far Eastern political and economic matters. The exchange let the two Western delegations line up their experts before the meeting opened.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d223:
A briefing book paper warned Truman about Churchill's Commonwealth role, in a paper dated July 4, 1945. The paper is document 223 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It belongs to the set of studies prepared to ready the President for his first meeting with the other two leaders.

The summary makes a legal point with practical weight. At Big Three meetings Churchill may give the impression that he speaks for the whole British Commonwealth. In fact he represents only the United Kingdom. He has no authority to commit Canada, Australia, South Africa, or New Zealand, and Ireland has stayed neutral and is not in the United Nations. The Dominions are kept informed and consulted when time permits, but their consent is not his to give. The paper taught a new president the limits of his partner's signature.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d23:
Announce after departure, not before: Truman's message to Stalin of May 22, 1945, explains the publicity plan for the Hopkins trip. He was most pleased with Stalin's wire about the visit. He judged it wiser to announce the mission only after Hopkins left the United States. Announcing earlier risked a leak becoming press speculation.

Hopkins planned to leave the next morning, May 23. Later that day, Truman proposed to tell the press the mission's purpose. Hopkins was proceeding to Moscow with Harriman, to talk over matters then in discussion between the Soviet and American governments. The White House statement followed as planned. The cable shows secrecy being managed, not merely kept.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d323:
An airgram from Washington to Ambassador Harriman, dated June 29, 1945, reports a new fight over Rumanian oil. Soviet military authorities in Rumania, the Department had learned, had advised taking oilfield equipment from British-owned companies, calling it war booty. British officials in Bucharest had already protested to the Control Commission.

London meant to carry the protest to Moscow itself. Its case rested on three points: the removals broke Soviet pledges given in January, they harmed a clear British interest, and they would cut Rumanian oil output and so world supply. The airgram kept Harriman ready to support the British stand.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d423:
Churchill's answer to Truman's coal message arrives in Winant's cable from London of July 3, 1945. The Prime Minister's reply is quoted in full: personal and top secret. Churchill writes that he is in full agreement in principle with the President's proposal. A similar directive to Field Marshal Montgomery is being prepared.

One reservation follows. Certain points, Churchill notes, are being taken up by the Foreign Office with the State Department. London would like those points considered before its own telegram is despatched. The short cable thus records British assent to the coal drive, with details still to be squared between the two foreign offices.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d523:
Agreed points on aid to Poland are cabled to Ambassador-designate Lane on July 12, 1945, after Department discussions in which Lane took part. First, the United States will give full support to UNRRA in fulfilling the contemplated Polish program. That tentative program is substantial: almost half a million tons of supplies for the third quarter of this year, and a similar quantity for the fourth.

Even if more aid were available, the cable warns, shipping and port facilities probably could not move a larger program. Real difficulties may even be met in delivering the supplies UNRRA will have ready to send with American support. The cable closes with UNRRA's plans for a permanent mission chief for Poland.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d623:
Robert Murphy, the political adviser in Germany, reported oil needs from Hoechst on June 30, 1945. His secret wire is document 623 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It answers Edwin Pauley's query about supplies for U.S. forces in Germany.

Murphy cites figures given in confidence by a SHAEF supply officer, Colonel Vissering. Strict military needs in the U.S. zone would run near 200,000 tons of gasoline and like goods a month by December 1945. With 400,000 troops in a quiet zone, the need would drop to about 50,000 tons a month. Austrian crude, refined on the Danube, could serve where no combat was expected. Murphy stresses that these figures cover military needs only, not the least German civil needs. SHAEF, he adds, is keen to get any oil Austria, Hungary, or Rumania can spare.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1023:
Philip Mosely drafted this memorandum for the Secretary of State on July 16, 1945. It weighs plans to create a separate Rhineland-Ruhr unit. All such plans assume that western control of the area's resources would guard Allied security. Mosely lists the hard questions the other governments are bound to ask.

If Ruhr steel and coal still feed factories across Germany, what does controlling raw materials gain? If the area turns west, what trade shifts must western lands accept? If millions of Germans are crowded into a rump state, how will it live? And can France, Belgium, and the Netherlands, even together, really run so large a region? Britain joining in, he adds, would build a western bloc against Russia.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1123:
Carmel Offie, deputy political adviser at Allied Force Headquarters, reported to the Secretary of State on 20 July 1945. His post sat where the army's rule met civilian policy. The headquarters ran Allied operations in its theater and dealt daily with the lands the armies had freed.

Offie's message linked the officers who governed freed Europe with the envoys planning its future at Potsdam. What the summit decided on paper, men in his position had to carry out in towns and ports. His voice is the field command's part in the record. It grounds the high talks in the facts of rule on the ground.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1223:
Foreign Minister Togo of Japan cabled Ambassador Sato in Moscow on 17 July 1945, the day Potsdam opened. The pair's exchange forms one of the most telling threads in the volume. Japan, beaten but not surrendered, was seeking a way out of the war through Soviet doors.

Tokyo hoped Moscow would mediate, or at least hear an envoy, before the Allies closed in. Sato's task was to open that door. American codebreakers read this traffic as it passed, a fact Tokyo never knew. The cable opens the exchange that Potsdam's leaders watched in secret while they set Japan's terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1323:
Ickes, the Petroleum Administrator for War, wrote to Pauley, the reparations envoy, on 25 July 1945. Harold Ickes ran America's wartime oil policy from Washington. His letter joined the oil desk to the man valuing Germany's wealth for the peace.

Oil touched reparations at several points: German fuel plants, stocks, and the claims of nations whose fields the war had wrecked. Ickes's word gave Pauley the oil side of that ledger. This message shows the home agencies feeding the summit's money fight with their own facts. It is the energy desk speaking in the reparations record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1423:
A third Soviet text dated 14 July 1945 completes the set Moscow tabled before the Potsdam Conference opened. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Read together, the three texts of 14 July show the breadth of the Soviet program: land, money, and power were all on its pages. The other delegations spent the next two weeks answering them. This closing piece of the set lets readers finish the opening picture before turning to the bargaining itself. The editors placed the run at the volume's end, where the conference's raw materials sit beside its results.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-123:
The United States delegation at Potsdam issued this memorandum on July 27, 1945. It belongs to the dense staff traffic of the conference's last week. Memoranda at that stage often carried near-final positions. Teams used them to align before the closing sessions. The paper was preserved and printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Late-conference memos have a special edge. The time for open options was shrinking. Writers knew their words might feed straight into agreed texts. Readers see the American machine tightening its lines. The memo helps explain the firmness the delegation showed as the end approached.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-23:
A rapporteur's report by Eden covers the foreign secretaries' meeting of July 19, 1945, at Potsdam. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. Eden reported the morning's work to the plenary session of the heads of government.

Two items lead the report. First, the United States wished to amend the redraft of paragraph 3 of its Council of Foreign Ministers proposal. The meeting agreed to send that point to a drafting committee. Second came Germany's political questions. The secretaries had given further study to the political section of the draft agreement on principles for treating Germany. A revised draft, marked Flag A, was now submitted to the heads of government. Beyond clarifying the draftsmanship, the report signals steady, detailed progress on the German settlement's core text.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d723:
Joseph Grew, the Acting Secretary of State in Washington, wrote to Byrnes at Potsdam on July 16, 1945. Document 723 shows the home office at work while the leaders traveled. Grew, a veteran diplomat, kept the Department running. His letter reached the Secretary as the conference opened in Germany.

The Acting Secretary's letters form the spine of the Washington-Potsdam link. Grew passed news, flagged problems, and held lines at home. Readers see the Department as a two-front operation in July 1945. The document honors a quiet truth: summits rest on the staff who stay behind and keep the machine turning.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d823:
A second Barnes letter from Bulgaria bears the date July 27, 1945, as document 823. Two reports in one day from Sofia mark pressing business. The representative wrote to the Acting Secretary of State in both. This one was printed in the second Potsdam volume beside the first.

Paired letters let a post divide its load. One may press a case while the other reports a fact. Barnes's pair shows a mission working at full stretch in the last week. Readers gain two dated points on Bulgaria's line. Together they sharpen the picture of a country whose fate the conference was sealing.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d923:
The Economic Sub-Committee sent this second report to the foreign ministers at Potsdam on July 24, 1945. The printed text is an extract. It regrets that long talks on German, Austrian, and Italian reparations ended without agreement. The questions go back to the ministers for decision.

The members did accept that all three countries owed reparations. For Germany, they agreed the sum should be substantial. They split only on the method for carrying out such a program. The report thus marks the point where staff-level talks gave up and the dispute rose to the heads of government.
frus-1964-1968-congo-vol-23:
Volume twenty-three of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1964 to 1968 in fact covers the Congo from 1960 to 1968. The Office of the Historian compiled it from declassified records. The Congo's independence in 1960 set off a crisis that drew in the United Nations, Belgium, and both Cold War camps.

The documents follow Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba's fall and murder, the Katanga secession, and the UN intervention. Later files cover the Simba rebellion, the hostage rescues of 1964, and the rise of Mobutu to lasting power. Washington's fear of a communist Congo drives page after page. The volume is the official record of a new nation's violent birth.
gao-gaoreports-b-297323: L-3 Systems Company Wescam Sonoma took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Defense firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298123: Capitol Supply tripled its June 2006 protest — three case numbers, one supply fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Triple filings get one careful answer. Three dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299523: Head Inc. took its June 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest. Short name, full hearing: every bidder gets the same fair-play ruling.
gao-gaoreports-b-299723: Forensic Quality Services-International took its May 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the claims against procurement law. Even forensic deals get the full fair-play hearing in the protest system.
gao-gaoreports-b-299923: K9 Operations took its August 2007 dog-team contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's pick was unfair; the call tests the protest and rules. Even the government buys guard dogs by the rulebook — and GAO enforces it.
gao-gaoreports-b-310023: This 2008 GAO ruling is about light Refreshments for National Trails Day at Forest Service. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-b-310823: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Global Computer Enterprises, Inc. Decided January 31, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-b-311423: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Eastern Medical Equipment, Inc.; Omnicare. The 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-123: Energy's big project contracts needed muscle in 2005, and GAO's report says further actions were required to strengthen management. The review demands the discipline. The megaprojects deserved the watch. The watch had to be steady. The discipline was demanded. The muscle was needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-223: Credit report know-how was thin in 2005, and GAO's report says the basics landed, though sharper teaching could help. The review grades the knowledge. The borrowers deserved the smarts. The borrowers deserved the smarts. The teaching had to sharpen. The knowledge was graded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-323: Uncle Sam's sales pitch abroad was a jumble in 2005, and GAO's report says the teams lacked a shared script. The review calls for one clear voice. The nation's voice deserved the harmony. The harmony was missing. The script was missing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-823: Mexicali power plant emissions got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says estimated emissions were low, though health impacts were unknown. The findings balance the numbers and the unknowns. The report warns that the border air deserved honest measuring. The impacts had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-23: Financial product sales to troops needed stronger safeguards in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were needed to better protect military members. The findings demand the shield. The report warns that the uniformed borrowers deserved honest products. The protection had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-423: Chip and software jobs were moving to Asia in 2006, and GAO's report says U.S. industries increasingly produced in China and India. The findings map the migration. The report warns that the offshoring wave had consequences. The trend had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-623: The Coast Guard's rescue system buying needed oversight in 2006, and GAO's report says management and oversight of the acquisition wanted improvement. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the lifesavers' gear should be bought right. The acquisition had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-723: The uranium company's data delays hindered oversight in 2006, and GAO's report says USEC's slow responses blocked the Energy Department's watch. The findings target the stonewalling. The report warns that the atomic deal's books should be open. The data had to flow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-823: Immigration enforcement's computers were aging in 2006, and GAO's report says ICE was beginning to address the infrastructure modernization. The findings track the start. The report warns that the digital border needed modern tools. The modernization had to proceed. The digital border needed modern tools.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-523: American school aid abroad needed better teamwork and scorecards in 2007 — GAO's report calls for tighter coordination and real results measures. The findings demand proof of learning gains. The report's standard: chalk and books bought with tax dollars should show learning.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-923: Chernobyl's crumbling sarcophagus needed a new cover in 2007 — and GAO's report says the shelter project was slipping behind. The findings track the delays dogging the international effort to entomb the reactor. The report is a slow-motion alarm: the world's worst nuclear scar still waited for its shield.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1123: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at rural Economic Development: Collaboration between SBA and USDA Could Be Improved. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-223: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at state and Local Government Retiree Benefits: Current Funded Status of Pension and Health Benefits. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-23: This 2007 GAO report finds the State Department's get-out plans for its far-flung posts needed work. With embassies dotting shaky regions, GAO asked if the exit drills were real, fresh, and fit for a true crisis. The report lists the soft spots — and warns that a bad plan only shows its cracks when the shooting starts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-623: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at border Security: State Department Should Plan for Potentially Significant Staffing and Facilities Shortfalls Caused by Changes in the Visa Waiver Program. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-723: The Government Accountability Office dug into health Resources and Services Administration: Many Underserved Areas Lack a Health Center Site, and the Health Center Program Needs More Oversight in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-823: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at voluntary Organizations: FEMA Should More Fully Assess Organization's Mass Care Capabilities and Update the Red Cross Role in Catastrophic Events. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
garland-book-american-indian-1923:
Harper issued The Book of the American Indian in 1923, written by Garland and pictured by Frederic Remington. A scout image from Remington's A Bunch of Buckskins fronts the volume. Garland had spent years visiting reservations and hearing Native leaders at length.

Accounts of Plains Indian life and history fill the book, told with care and respect. Garland also records the harm that white settlement brought to Native peoples. Part report and part plea for justice, the work defends its subjects with rare sympathy for its time. It remains a window on how one famed prairie writer tried to set the record straight.
goldman-my-disillusionment-russia-1923:
Emma Goldman published My Disillusionment in Russia in 1923. Goldman had sailed to Soviet Russia in 1919, deported from the United States as a dangerous radical. She went as a friend of the revolution and left, two years later, as its critic.

Goldman described the crushing of free unions, the jailing of anarchists, and the Kronstadt sailors' revolt and its bloody end. She told how Bolshevik power, in her account, replaced one tyranny with another. The book was among the first breaks with Bolshevism from within the revolutionary left. Her firsthand scenes and names gave the account weight that later histories have confirmed in large part.
goldsack-selections-muhammadan-tradition:
William Goldsack was a missionary scholar in Bengal who translated Islamic texts for Christian and general readers. His Selections from Muhammadan Traditions, published in 1923, offers classified English selections from the six canonical hadith collections. Hadith are the recorded sayings and deeds of the Prophet Muhammad.

Goldsack arranges traditions from Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, and others by subject, from prayer to trade to family life. A reader can see what the tradition teaches on a topic without searching the vast Arabic collections. The book served missionaries and students as a handy, ordered gateway to Islam's second source.
gregory-hellman-hesperopithecus-1923:
William K. Gregory and Milo Hellman, two New York men of dental science, restudied the famed Nebraska tooth in 1923. The tooth had been named Hesperopithecus, a first ape man for America, the year past. Their notes deal with the type tooth and its true kind.

With fine care they set out the tooth's crown, roots, and wear, point by point. Bit by bit, the ape man marks fade, and a more lowly beast takes their place. The paper is the start of the slow walk back from the Nebraska man claim.
gregory-hellman-molars-hesperopithecus-p:
William K. Gregory and Milo Hellman, with a note by Gerrit S. Miller Jr., took the Nebraska tooth row a step more in 1923. Their theme is the back teeth, the molars, of two claimed ape men. One is Hesperopithecus of Nebraska, the other Pithecanthropus of Java.

Tooth by tooth, the team sets the worn Nebraska molar by the Java man's teeth. The match fails, and with it the claim of an ape man in America fades fast. The dry notes close the case that a year of press noise had blown so large.
hemingway-three-stories-1923:
Ernest Hemingway was a twenty-four-year-old newspaper correspondent in Paris when Three Stories and Ten Poems appeared in 1923. A tiny press printed only three hundred copies. It was his first book, and almost everything he later became is visible in it.

The lead story, Up in Michigan, tells of a young woman's rough sexual awakening in a lumber town. Two more stories introduce Nick Adams, the hero of his later fiction, fishing and soldiering. The ten poems, snapshots of bullfights, executions, and war, are frankly apprentice work. The plain style that would change American prose is already forming. This slim Paris debut is where Hemingway began.
isaac-the-syrian-wensinck-1923:
Isaac of Nineveh, a seventh-century bishop who gave up his see for the desert, wrote the mystic treatises translated here by A. J. Wensinck in 1923. Isaac wrote in Syriac, and his works traveled across the Christian East in many tongues. Wensinck's was the first complete English rendering of this contemplative classic.

Isaac writes on prayer, tears, humility, and the stillness of the mind before God. His pages prize mercy above all: a merciful heart, he says, burns for every creature, even snakes. Monks of Mount Athos and the Russian tradition kept his words close for centuries. The translation made the desert father's voice plain to English readers at last.
jersey-devil-evening-journal-1909-01-23:
Panic grips two states in the Evening Journal pieces of January 23, 1909, from Wilmington. For a week, folk from New Jersey to Delaware swore a winged beast flew by night: hoof prints in snow, hens slain, and a shape like a crane with a horse's head. The Journal prints fresh tales: a church meet broke up in dread, and a crop of new tales from each town in its reach.

The tone veers from fear to wry doubt, day by day. These scraps are the wave as it broke, raw and live. They are prime sources on the famed scare.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-23:
Volume 23, from 1898, finds the Hurons in 1643 facing a bleak war. Iroquois wins multiply with each new season of fighting in the woods. Thwaites prints letters that read like reports from a doomed fort under siege.

Faith and hard realism fight for space on nearly every page. The priests see the danger in full, name it plainly, and stay. They tend the sick, teach the young, and guard the chapels at night. Supplies fail, allies waver, and still the daily work goes on. Few volumes show plain duty under hopeless odds with such force.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshwi-al-ukbar:
Meshwi al-'Ukbari was the founder of the Jewish sect called Al-'Ukbariyyah, or the Okbarites, named for the city of 'Ukbara near Bagdad where he is said to have lived. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Karaite writer Ḳirḳisani is a main source for what is known of him.

His real name was Moses, the article says, until opponents twisted it into Meshwi, meaning one whose ideas are confused. He broke with both Karaites and Rabbinites, ruling that the Day of Atonement must always fall on a Sabbath and that prayer should face west, not toward the Temple. He also barred Sabbath sacrifices in the Temple and reportedly allowed his followers to eat fat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mihaileni-10823:
Mihaileni, a small town in the Rumanian district of Dorogoi, was founded by Jews in 1792 under a written bargain with the land's proprietor. Richard Gottheil and E. Schwarzfeld tell its story in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Prince Alexander Moruzi confirmed the deal, which gave the founders free ground for a synagogue, a bath, and a cemetery.

In 1835 Prince Michel Sturza made the town his district capital and turned on its people, beating a leading Jew and jailing his son while trying to rewrite the old agreement. Relief came through law: new artisans won five rent-free years, and an 1838 settlement, negotiated with seven Jewish representatives at the table, freed the synagogues and bath from rent for good.
journal-of-discourses-vol-23:
Volume Twenty-Three, also from 1883, finds the crusade at its cruelest. Leaders sit in prison, families scatter, and church funds face seizure. The Saints' suffering peaks in the sermons gathered in this book.

Preachers frame the pain as fire that refines, not breaks, the faithful. Discourses console the jailed men's wives and fatherless homes directly. A people drinks its Gethsemane, in their own stark biblical phrase. Endurance becomes the chief virtue preached from every stand in Utah. The record of those who bore the cup fills this grim, moving volume. Consolation, not complaint, is the note its preachers strike most often.
julian-works-wright-vol3-1923:
Wilmer Cave Wright's third Loeb volume of Julian's works came out in 1923, ten years after the first two. It holds the emperor's letters and the fragments of works that survive only in pieces. Julian wrote these texts in the brief reign when he tried to turn the empire back to its old gods.

The chief piece is Against the Galilaeans, his case against the Christians, kept in quotes by Cyril, the church writer who answered it. Julian mocks the claims of the Bible and defends Greek religion and learning. The letters beside it show his rule in daily detail. The volume completes Wright's English Julian.
jung-psychological-types-baynes-1923:
C. G. Jung published Psychological Types in German in 1921. The English text here is H. G. Baynes's translation of 1923. Jung sorts people by two attitudes: introversion, turned inward, and extraversion, turned outward. He adds four functions: thinking, feeling, sensation, and intuition. Combinations of these form his famous types.

Jung draws examples from history, literature, and his patients. The book became the source of all later personality typology, including popular tests used today. Jung warns that types are tools, not boxes for souls. His aim was to explain why thinkers see the same facts so differently. The work remains a classic of personality theory.
keynes-tract-monetary-reform-1923:
Keynes's Tract on Monetary Reform, published in 1923, tackles the money chaos that followed the First World War. Prices in Europe had swung wildly, and several nations saw their currency collapse. Keynes asks how a state should manage money in such a world.

He applies the quantity theory of money to wartime and postwar inflation in plain, forceful terms. He faults the gold standard, which ties a nation's money to a fixed stock of gold. His call for managed money pointed toward the policies he would urge for the rest of his life. He writes for citizens as much as for bankers, in brisk, quotable prose.
kierkegaard-selections-hollander-1923:
Soren Kierkegaard's selected writings appear here in L. M. Hollander's translation of 1923, the first broad English gateway to his work. Kierkegaard was a Danish thinker of the 1800s who wrote under many pen names. The selections cover dread, faith, and the stages of life. Aesthetic, ethical, and religious ways of living stand in sharp contrast.

Kierkegaard defends the leap of faith against cold systems of thought. He insists truth for faith is personal and inward. Later thinkers named him a founder of existentialism. Hollander's volume let English readers meet him at length for the first time. It remains a useful door into a demanding author.
lawrence-birds-beasts-flowers-1923:
D. H. Lawrence wrote most of Birds, Beasts and Flowers during his travels in Italy, New Mexico, and Australia. The collection appeared in 1923, after he had left England for good. Lawrence arranged the poems by their subjects, as the title announces.

The poems watch plants and animals with fierce attention. A snake drinking at a trough in Sicily shames the poet's fearful education. Figs, bats, kangaroos, and dark Bavarian gentians all appear, each treated as a living otherness to respect. Lawrence rejected smooth traditional forms for free, breathing rhythms. Many readers call this his finest book of poems.
lawrence-kangaroo-1923:
Lawrence and Frieda spent months in Australia in 1922, and Kangaroo grew directly out of that stay. Published in 1923, it follows Richard Somers, a writer much like Lawrence, settling near Sydney with his wife Harriet.

Somers is courted by 'Kangaroo', a charismatic lawyer building a paramilitary movement of returned soldiers, and by socialists who want him too. He refuses both, and the novel becomes a reckoning with politics, loyalty, and Australia itself. Long passages simply watch the sea and bush with fierce attention. It is the antipodean chapter of Lawrence's search for a new life and a new faith.
lawrence-ladybird-1923:
The Ladybird, published in 1923, gathers three long stories from Lawrence's post-war years: 'The Ladybird', 'The Fox', and 'The Captain's Doll'. Each turns on power and surrender between men and women in a Europe broken by war.

In the title story, a wounded German count draws an English lady toward a dark, chthonic faith. 'The Fox' sets two women farming alone against a young soldier and the fox that haunts them, toward a shocking end. 'The Captain's Doll' plays the same tensions as comedy. These are among Lawrence's most perfectly made tales, written at the height of his powers.
lawrence-studies-classic-american-1923:
Lawrence's 1923 criticism took on the classic American writers and read them against the grain. His essays on Franklin, Cooper, Poe, Hawthorne, Melville, and Whitman became the most famous single book of American literary criticism by an outsider.

Lawrence claims that American literature hides a dark secret: a continent won by violence, and a soul split between innocence and blood. He distrusts what these writers say they mean and hunts what their tales confess. The style is wild, funny, and prophetic. Scholars have argued with his readings ever since, and few have matched their force. The book remade how America read itself.
li-bai-the-works-of-li-po-the-chinese-po:
Li Bai, called Li Po in this 1923 English version by Shigeyoshi Obata, was China's most loved poet. He sang of wine, moonlight, high mountains, and friends far away. His Tang dynasty lyrics date from the eighth century, China's golden age of verse.

Obata chose and Englished the poems with a scholar's care and a poet's ear. Parting, longing, and drunken joy recur like notes in music. Li Bai's ease hides deep craft, and his freedom still startles readers. This selection carried his genius to the West and helped fix his name among the supreme lyric poets of the world.
lizerand-dossier-affaire-templiers-1923:
Georges Lizerand, a French scholar, built Le Dossier de l'Affaire des Templiers in 1923 as a working file of the case. The Knights Templar fell in 1307, when the French king's men seized them across the realm. Lizerand prints the core papers of that fall in one volume.

Readers get the arrest order, the long interrogations of the brothers, and the acts that ended the order in 1312. Grand Master Jacques de Molay's own words sit among the records. The dossier lets the case be read from its papers, not from legend. Students of the Templar trial still start with this file.
llull-lover-beloved-peers-1923:
Ramon Llull was the Catalan mystic of the 1200s. His Book of the Lover and the Beloved is a string of 366 short prose poems, one for each day of the year. E. Allison Peers translated the work into English in 1923, with an essay on the life of Llull and his famous Art. The poems stand inside his great romance Blanquerna.

The Lover seeks the Beloved, who is God, through forests of signs, questions, and joy. Each piece is a spark: a dialogue, a sigh, a small parable of longing and praise. Llull drew on the Sufi poets he had read in Mallorca. The book is the sweetest fruit of Catalan mysticism, still read day by day.
machen-christianity-and-liberalism-1923:
Machen's Christianity and Liberalism, published in 1923, is the fundamentalist manifesto of the American church fights of the 1920s. Its claim is blunt: liberalism is not a kind of Christianity but a different religion entirely. Machen wrote it while Princeton Seminary slid toward the split he would soon lead.

He compares the two faiths on God, man, the Bible, Christ, salvation, and the church, finding them opposed at every point. Liberalism, he says, rests on naturalism, the denial that God acts in history in supernatural ways. The book still anchors conservative arguments about the boundaries of the faith.
millay-harp-weaver-1923:
Edna St. Vincent Millay published The Harp-Weaver and Other Poems in 1923, and it won the Pulitzer Prize for poetry. Millay was the first woman to win that prize. The book catches her in her prime, when her sonnets were being memorized across America.

The title ballad tells of a poor mother who weaves fine clothes for her son on a magic harp as she dies. Behind its fairy-tale shape sits real poverty Millay knew from her own childhood. The volume also holds a celebrated sonnet sequence on love and loss. Ballads, lyrics, and sonnets together make this the fullest single display of Millay's gifts.
monroe-doctrine-1823:
President James Monroe laid out his doctrine in a message on December 2, 1823. The Seventh Annual Message to Congress holds the famed passage. Europe's monarchs are warned to keep hands off the Americas.

The Western Hemisphere, Monroe declares, is closed to fresh colonization. Any bid to crush the new Latin republics will count as hostile. The young republic thus claims a sphere of its own age. The statement became the base stone of foreign policy for a century. Later presidents stretched its reach far past Monroe's first intent in 1823. The doctrine's few lines grew into a creed of hemispheric power.
muir-life-mohammad-weir-1923:
William Muir built The Life of Mohammad from Arabic sources, first in 1861 and revised by T. H. Weir in the 1923 edition. Muir read Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Hisham, Waqidi, and Tabari at first hand, a rare feat for a Victorian writer. His critical biography follows the Prophet from Mecca to Medina to the conquest of Arabia.

Muir admired his subject's power while judging the faith by his own Christian lights, and readers have argued with him ever since. The book long served English readers as their fullest life of Mohammad from the sources. It also stands as the public-domain stand-in for the early Sira in English.
openalex-w1595049023: Malaria got gametocytaemia-determined, and this epidemiology article covers Papua New Guinea. The pages detail the blood findings. The epidemiologists get their paper. The parasitaemia was and-Age. The paper was epidemiologist. The Guin were New. The vivax were P.
openalex-w1985667523: An invasive tree reshapes whole communities. A 2012 study compared the local impacts of its spread in native and non-native ranges. The comparison revealed how the invader changes ecosystems abroad — and which native species suffer most.
openalex-w2040593023: A giant toxic plume off Peru feeds life on chemistry. A 2013 study found a giant sulfide plume in Peru's low-oxygen zone supports sulfur-eating microbes. The work traced life living on sulfur instead of sunlight.
openalex-w2068794323: Chagas treatment needs a parasite counter. A 2009 report describes a real-time PCR method for tracking parasite loads in Chagas patients' blood. The method measured Trypanosoma cruzi DNA from repeat sequences in blood samples — a treatment yardstick.
openalex-w2073840323: Reinventing government became a verb. Kelnert and Silva's 1993 review covers Osborne and Gaebler's 'Reinventing Government' — the book that made 'reinventing the public sector' a sensation. The review traced the entrepreneurial-spirit wave sweeping American government.
openalex-w2092288223: People carry diseases with their footsteps. Stoddard and colleagues' 2009 review covers the role of human movement in transmitting vector-borne pathogens. The work showed movement across scales shapes exposure and disease dynamics worldwide — from commutes to migrations.
openalex-w2119721623: Outbreaks need early detection — statistics can find them. A 2005 paper introduced a space-time scan statistic for disease outbreak detection. The method needs only case counts, no population data — watch made simple and fast for health teams.
openalex-w2316628323: Winemakers traditionally rely on Saccharomyces cerevisiae — but wild yeasts like Hanseniaspora vineae can ferment too. This 2016 research article, published in Frontiers in Microbiology, compares fermentations and the resulting wines from the two yeasts side by side. The comparison reveals how the choice of yeast shapes a wine's character, from aroma to alcohol.
openalex-w2742149023: As socio-environmental conflicts grow more visible, scholars are bridging history and anthropology to understand them. This 2017 article in Luna Azul (in Spanish) stages interdisciplinary dialogues between environmental history and anthropology on nature-culture relations. The essays explore, from multiple disciplinary angles, how humans and nature shape each other.
openalex-w2898493623: Fermilab's MiniBooNE experiment keeps seeing something it shouldn't: an excess of electron-like neutrino events. This 2018 Physical Review Letters paper analyzes 12.84×10^20 protons on target — double the previous data — and the excess persists. The stubborn anomaly keeps the sterile-neutrino hypothesis alive.
openalex-w2949716623: Do neutrinos and antineutrinos oscillate differently? This 2019 Physical Review Letters paper reports NOvA's first measurement of oscillation parameters using both — including a 4.4-sigma signal of electron antineutrino appearance in a muon antineutrino beam over 810 km. The result tightens the hunt for CP violation in the lepton sector.
openalex-w3004109123: Pseudomonas aeruginosa makes pyocyanin — a blue-green pigment with uses in medicine, agriculture, and the environment. This 2020 Scientific Reports paper isolates a potent producer and characterizes the nutrient-dependent pigment's dye and agrochemical properties. The bacterial colorant proves surprisingly versatile.
openalex-w3006366423: Why do some people resist severe malaria? This 2019 Nature Communications genome-wide association study of 17,000 individuals from Africa, Asia, and Oceania — severe cases and controls across 11 countries — hunts the human genetic factors of resistance. The findings illuminate the host side of humanity's oldest plague.
openalex-w4360603423: Corporations shape health — through products, marketing, and lobbying. This 2023 Lancet paper, by Gilmore, Fabbri, Baum and colleagues, defines and conceptualizes the commercial determinants of health. The framework names the business forces behind disease.
openalex-w4366091323: This 2023 Artificial Intelligence Review paper surveys deep learning modelling techniques: current progress, applications, advantages, and challenges. The review covers how multi-layer nonlinear transformations are revolutionizing evidence-based decision-making across sectors.
openalex-w7128498023: Immune thrombocytopenia thins the blood's clotting cells, and bleeding shapes daily life. This study linked bleeding severity to quality of life in adults with ITP. The authors measured how symptoms erode well-being. A patient-centered study of a rare blood disorder's real cost.
openalex-w7204939723: Police work is going airborne in northern Brazil. This article examines how the military police of Para are putting drones to work: surveillance, search operations, and monitoring hard-to-reach areas. The authors place the technology within the broader digital revolution reshaping public security. Part technology survey, part institutional case study, it shows what happens when a state police force adopts eyes in the sky.
openalex-w7206151423: Artificial intelligence is entering classrooms, and this article asks what it means for students with disabilities. The authors review the teaching possibilities AI opens up, the ethical limits that must be respected, and the conditions schools need so digital tools genuinely help every student participate and learn. Balanced rather than boosterish, it treats inclusion as the test of whether classroom AI is worth having.
osty-supernormal-faculties-in-man-1923:
Eugène Osty, a French doctor who led a Paris institute for psychical study, published Supernormal Faculties in Man in 1923. Osty reported tests with people said to know facts they could not have learned in normal ways. He used the term supernormal for powers beyond the usual senses.

Case studies follow subjects through sittings where they described hidden objects, past events, and distant scenes. Osty tried to rule out fraud and lucky guessing, and he set out rules for such tests. His work reflects the French branch of psychical research, which leaned toward careful case work in the lab and the study room.
otto-idea-of-holy-1923:
Rudolf Otto was a German theologian whose Idea of the Holy, in this 1923 English edition, changed the study of religion worldwide. Otto argues that religion rests on an experience that reason alone cannot capture. He names that core the numinous, from the Latin word for divine power.

The numinous, he says, is a mystery at once fearful and fascinating, the mysterium tremendum that makes worshippers tremble and draw near. He finds it in Hebrew prophets, Hindu hymns, and the silence of Quaker worship alike. His book founded the modern phenomenology of religion, the study of faith as it is felt.
parry-second-voyage-northwest-passage-18:
Parry's second Arctic voyage, from 1821 to 1823, sought the passage by Hudson Bay and the straits beyond. His Journal of a Second Voyage appeared in 1824. Two winters in the ice gave the work its special value.

The crews wintered at Winter Island and then at Igloolik, where they lived beside an Inuit community. Parry records Inuit dress, hunting, family life, and language with unusual care. That makes the book a landmark of early Arctic ethnography as well as a voyage narrative. The passage stayed hidden, but the human record of those winters endures. Plates of Inuit dress, tools, and homes give the text lasting worth.
peirce-chance-love-logic-1923:
Charles S. Peirce's essays were gathered in Chance, Love, and Logic in 1923, the first anthology of his work. Morris Cohen edited the volume. Peirce, who died in poverty in 1914, founded pragmatism and much of modern logic. The essays cover his theory of meaning, belief, and inquiry.

Peirce argues that a belief is a habit of action and truth is inquiry's long-run aim. Other pieces defend chance in nature and an evolutionary love as a cosmic force. His terms tychism and agapism name those bold ideas. The anthology rescued Peirce for a new generation. It is still a good first Peirce.
perry-children-of-the-sun-1923:
W. J. Perry wrote The Children of the Sun in 1923. Perry was a keen fan of the spread school of G. Elliot Smith. The book makes Egypt the well of all high culture on Earth. Its title comes from the sun kings he saw at the root of each great land.

Stone graves, gold hunts, and sun rites trace his claim round the globe. He holds that bands from Egypt bore these traits to Asia and the New World. The claim drew fire then and still splits views now. The book is the grand plea of the spread school at its peak.
plaw-118-11-2023: Congress passed this federal law, the Pala Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act, in 2023. The short title states its purpose; the enrolled text holds the binding details. It is kept here as part of the lasting public-law record.
plaw-118-12-2023: Enacted in 2023, this federal law designates the clinic of the Department of Veterans Affairs in Indian River, Michigan, as the “Pfc. Justin T. Paton Department of Veterans. The operative clause states exactly what Congress authorized. It is kept here as part of the lasting public-law record.
plaw-118-5-2023: Enacted in 2023, this federal law provides for a responsible increase to the debt ceiling. The operative clause states exactly what Congress authorized. It is kept here as part of the lasting public-law record. The full text sits with this description in the library.
plaw-118-7-2023: Enacted in 2023, this federal law modifies the age requirement for the Student Incentive Payment Program of the State maritime academies. The operative clause states exactly what Congress authorized. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
plos-pbio-0020123:
Nicholas T. Ingolia modeled a patterning network in the fruit fly in PLOS Biology in 2004. In the fly embryo, genes in the segment polarity network lock each body segment into its final form. The author used math models to test how the network holds its pattern when parts are noisy or stressed.

A good network must be robust: it should give the same neat stripes even when gene levels wobble. The models show which links in the network carry that stability. Work of this kind turns a wiring diagram into predictions that lab tests can check. It shows how embryos get reliable shapes from sloppy parts, a puzzle at the heart of development.
plos-pbio-0020423:
Peiman Hematti, Bum-Kee Hong, Cole Ferguson, and their team compared gene therapy vectors in primates in PLOS Biology in 2004. Vectors based on MLV and SIV viruses carry new genes into blood stem cells. Each virus inserts its cargo into the genome at spots of its choosing.

The study found the two vectors favor distinct kinds of insertion sites in primate stem cells. That difference matters for safety. Insertions near growth genes can raise cancer risk, a harm seen in early gene therapy trials. Choosing a vector with a safer insertion pattern is thus a practical design step. The paper gives trial planners hard comparative data, not just theory.
plos-pone-0000023:
Karen Aboody, Rebecca Bush, Elizabeth Garcia, and co-authors worked in 2006 on aiming cancer treatment only at the cancer. Metastatic cancer, disease that has spread to new sites, is what usually kills. Drugs that reach it also poison healthy tissue. The team developed a tumor-selective approach meant to treat the spread while sparing the rest of the body.

A selective method changes the arithmetic of therapy: stronger attacks become safer when they concentrate in tumors. The paper reports the design of the approach and its early performance against metastatic disease. Work of this kind laid ground for later targeted and cell-based cancer treatments, where the whole point is to hit the tumor and leave the patient standing.
plos-pone-0000123:
Laure Perchepied, Thomas Kroj, Maurice Tronchet, and colleagues published this plant genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2006. Their subject is Arabidopsis thaliana, a small weed used as a model plant. They asked why some plants resist the bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas syringae better than others.

The authors traced the partial resistance to two major spots in the genome, called QTLs, that together control much of the natural variation. Work of this kind shows breeders and biologists where resistance lives in the DNA. It also helps explain how wild plants vary in fighting off disease without any human help.
plos-pone-0000223:
Michael S. Akhras, Sreedevi Thiyagarajan, Andrea C. Villablanca, and colleagues published this diagnostics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents PathogenMip, a multiplex pathogen detection assay. One test can identify many disease-causing microbes at once, instead of running a separate test for each suspect.

Doctors facing a fever often must guess which pathogen to test for. A multiplex assay screens a panel of candidates in one run. The authors describe and evaluate their assay's design. Faster, broader detection can shorten the time to the right treatment, a gain that matters most in serious infections.
plos-pone-0000323:
Anson W. Lowe, Mari Olsen, Ying Hao, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pancreatic tumors are among the deadliest cancers and among the hardest to study. The authors compare gene expression patterns across pancreatic tumors, cultured cells, and tissues to find which patterns are truly characteristic of the cancer.

Cell lines drift from the tumors they came from, so cross-checking them against real tissue matters. The authors sort expression signals by source. Their patterns provide candidate markers for a cancer that is usually found too late, and a check on which lab models deserve trust.
plos-pone-0000423:
Melanie T. Cushion and colleagues read the gene activity of a lung fungus at the height of infection, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pneumocystis carinii infects the lungs, and its fulminate stage is the most severe. The team profiled the transcriptome, the full set of genes switched on, during that stage, with attention to carbohydrate metabolism.

How a parasite fuels itself inside the lung may explain how it thrives there. From the expression pattern, the authors develop the idea of a compatible parasite, one well matched to its host niche. That framing could guide the search for drug targets in an organism that is hard to grow and study in the lab.
plos-pone-0000523:
Frédérick Barreau and colleagues showed a gut sensor is needed to keep lymphoid tissue in balance, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. CARD15/NOD2 is a protein that detects bacterial pieces inside cells; its variants are famous as Crohn's disease risk factors. The team found it is required for Peyer's patches homeostasis in mice, the steady state of the gut's immune outposts.

Peyer's patches sample gut contents and train immune responses. If a bacterial sensor is required to maintain them, Crohn's-linked variants may distort the gut's immune training from early life. Mouse findings like this give the human genetics a mechanism to test.
plos-pone-0000623:
Anders Krarup, Russell Wallis, Julia S. Presanis and co-authors studied one protease with two jobs, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. The complement system helps the immune system recognize and clear foreign bodies. One of its three activation routes, the lectin pathway, depends on a protease called MASP-2, attached to mannan-binding lectin.

Their title reports that MASP-2 switches on two systems at once: complement and coagulation, the blood-clotting cascade. That link ties immune defense to clot formation through a single enzyme. Immunologists and blood researchers both have reason to care, since a shared trigger could shape how the body answers infection and injury together.
plos-pone-0000723:
Joseph K. Jun and Dezhe Z. Jin modeled how circuits learn to fire in precise time patterns, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neurons in many brain areas produce spike sequences timed to within small fractions of a second, spanning hundreds of milliseconds. Examples appear in songbird premotor areas, cat visual cortex, and primary motor cortex. Synfire chains, networks where groups of neurons trigger the next group, are a proposed structure.

The model grows such chains through spontaneous activity, axon remodeling, and synaptic plasticity. In plain terms, practice and rewiring tune the timing. Explaining how precise sequences develop speaks to bird song, movement, and any behavior that lives or dies by timing.
plos-pone-0000823:
Morgane Rolland, David C. Nickle, Wenjie Deng and colleagues asked which parts of HIV the immune system actually targets, in PLOS ONE in 2007. HIV-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes preferentially target specific regions of the viral proteome, but the viral features driving that recognition were not well understood. One hypothesis holds that similarities between HIV and human proteins shape the targeting, since immune cells learn to spare self-like shapes.

Their title states the relationship they found: recognition of HIV-1 peptides by host CTL is related to HIV-1 similarity to human proteins. If self-similarity shields viral regions from attack, vaccine designers should aim at the regions that look least human.
plos-pone-0000923:
Ana Paula Trombone, Celio Silva, Karla Lima and colleagues followed a DNA vaccine ingredient through the cell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. DNA vaccines can raise both antibody and cell based defenses against many targets. Yet what happens to the injected DNA once inside a cell is still being mapped.

The team studied a vaccine built around Hsp65, a stress protein. They report that uptake of the DNA changes the acidity of late endosomes and lysosomes, the cell's sorting and recycling compartments. That shift interferes with antigen presentation, the step that shows targets to immune cells. Details like this decide whether a vaccine design works in practice, not just on paper.
plos-pone-0001023:
Seif Shekalaghe, Chris Drakeley, Roly Gosling and colleagues tested a drug add on to clear lingering malaria forms, in PLOS ONE in 2007. After treatment with the standard drug pair, some malaria parasites persist as gametocytes, the forms mosquitoes pick up. Those hidden forms can keep transmission going even after a patient feels cured.

The team measured whether a single dose of primaquine clears submicroscopic gametocytes that survive the standard treatment. Clearing them could cut spread from treated patients, a benefit beyond the individual cure. The study weighs that gain for malaria programs deciding whether to add primaquine routinely.
plos-pone-0001123:
Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited heart disease in which the heart muscle grows too thick. Niels Volkmann and co-authors studied one of its best-known causes in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The cause is a mutation called R403Q in the beta-myosin heavy chain, a motor protein of heart muscle.

Mutations in nearly every protein of the cardiac sarcomere, the muscle's contractile unit, have been linked to this disease. The authors examined what the R403Q change does where myosin meets actin, the interface that produces force. Their title reports that the mutation causes disorder at that interface, which helps explain how a tiny change weakens the heart.
plos-pone-0001223:
Recognizing a familiar face feels instant, but how personal familiarity changes face processing speed is not settled. Benjamin Balas, David Cox, and Erin Conwell tested the effect using faces people knew in real life, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Earlier studies of familiarity and face judgments had given equivocal results across different tasks and stimulus sets.

The authors measured how fast information is processed for personally familiar faces versus unfamiliar ones. Real-world familiarity is stronger than the lab kind, where a face is merely repeated. Their results speak to what familiarity actually buys the visual system: speed, accuracy, or both.
plos-pone-0001323:
Practice improves performance on sensory tasks, but the improvement is usually specific: train on one stimulus and the gain does not transfer. Ben Webb, Neil Roach, and Paul McGraw report an exception, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. When sensory judgments are particularly challenging, improvements are normally tightly coupled to the trained task and configuration.

The authors describe perceptual learning in the absence of task or stimulus specificity. That is, training improved performance broadly rather than narrowly. The specificity of learning is usually taken as a clue to where in the brain it happens; a general transfer points somewhere else.
plos-pone-0001423:
Katia Bassichetto and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on HIV risk in young people in São Paulo, Brazil. Spotting fresh infections is key to tracking how HIV spreads in a region. The team compared people with fresh infection to others in their data. They asked which traits marked a higher risk of recent infection.

Their results point to a raised risk for teens and young adults in the city. Youth focused outreach may thus matter more than broad plans alone. The study also shows the worth of tests that can tell fresh from old infection. Such tests help health teams aim scarce funds where spread is active now.
plos-pone-0001523:
Nicola Martinelli and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on clotting genes and heart attacks. Heart attacks are the main clot outcome of artery disease. Most work had looked at one clotting gene at a time. The team instead weighed the joint effect of several such variants in patients with advanced artery disease.

Joint tests can catch risks that single gene tests miss. The study maps how these variants add up, or fail to, in real patients. That joint view fits how clotting truly works, as a team of factors. It may refine risk scores for patients who already have grave artery disease.
plos-pone-0001623:
Troels T. Marstrand, Jes Frellsen, Ida Moltke, and their colleagues introduced a computer framework named Asap in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The tool tackles a common task in gene research: finding spots where transcription factors bind DNA more often than chance would explain. Transcription factors are proteins that switch genes on and off, so their binding sites help show how genes are controlled.

As sets of genes thought to be co-regulated grow larger, testing whether they share a common binding pattern takes fast, sound statistics.
