Asap was built to run those over-representation tests in a structured way. The full text describes the method, how it compares with earlier published methods, and the kinds of gene sets it can check. It is aimed at researchers who study gene regulation with large gene lists.
plos-pone-0001723:
Elodie Gaulin, Mohammed-Amine Madoui, Arnaud Bottin, and their co-authors catalogued the genes of a plant pathogen in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Aphanomyces euteiches is an oomycete, a water mold, that causes seedling blight and root rot in legumes such as alfalfa and pea. Its genus sits apart from better-studied oomycetes like Phytophthora, and its species attack plants and water animals alike.

The team sequenced the pathogen's transcriptome, the set of genes it switches on, to find putative pathogenicity factors and metabolic pathways. The full text gives the gene catalogue and the candidate attack proteins. A parts list for this mold's infection machinery gives crop science new targets for resistant pea and alfalfa varieties.
plos-pone-0001823:
Aranzazú Rosado, Fabian Zanella, Beatriz Garcia, and their co-authors built a screening platform for cancer drug candidates in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Inhibiting Akt signaling is considered one of the most promising therapeutic strategies for many cancers. Cell-based drug screens, though, had historically been compromised by the absence of suitable controls to judge selectivity.

Their dual-color fluorescence platform identifies selective inhibitors of Akt signaling, comparing treated pathway activity against a built-in reference. The full text gives the cell system and the screen results. A screen that reports selectivity from the start saves the common failure of finding a potent drug that is toxic to everything.
plos-pone-0001923:
Fumiko Hoeft and co-authors built a fake version of a brain tool for fair tests, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, pulses the brain through the skull and is used to prove links between brain areas and acts. It is also in trials as a treatment for ills such as depression.

Fair trials need a sham tool that feels real but does not stimulate, so patients and staff stay blind to who got the true dose. The team's sham can be switched on and off by electronics, which makes blinding strict. Good shams are what let TMS trials prove that gains come from the pulses, not from hope.
plos-pone-0002023:
Silke Lissek and co-authors scanned brains during cooperation and deceit, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Theory of mind is the mind's tool for picturing what others intend and expect. It shapes social life and helps us judge whether a partner will cooperate or defect for gain.

The team used brain scans as people played social tasks that called for teamwork or for trickery. As the title states, cooperation and deception recruit different subsets of the theory-of-mind network. One network, split by intent: the split may explain how the brain keeps track of friends and frauds in unlike ways.
plos-pone-0002123:
Nathan Cannon and co-authors studied the hepatitis C virus in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They tracked how the virus changes during drug treatment. The standard therapy at the time, pegylated interferon plus ribavirin, failed in about half of patients with genotype 1, the most common type. Failure came either as no response at all or as a relapse after a strong first drop in virus levels.

The authors followed the virus across its full open-reading frame, the long stretch of its genome that codes for proteins. By watching how the virus population shifts during therapy, they aimed to learn why treatment works for some people and fails for others.
plos-pone-0002223:
Akio Nakashima, Yoshiko Maruki, Yuko Imamura, and co-authors found a new role for a growth pathway in yeast, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The Tor pathway is a master control of cell growth. The drug rapamycin blocks it, halting cells in the first phase of the division cycle. Whether Tor also acts at later stages of the cycle was largely unknown.

The team reports that Tor signaling helps run the shift from the G2 phase into mitosis, the stage where chromosomes are pulled apart. The link runs through polo-kinase, a key driver of mitosis. The finding widens the reach of a pathway already targeted by drugs.
plos-pone-0002323:
Dilip Mahalanabis and co-authors ran a randomized trial of an oral cholera vaccine in Kolkata, India, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A killed, whole-cell cholera vaccine had been used in Vietnam since the 1990s. It was reformulated to meet World Health Organization requirements so other countries could use it.

Adults and children in a cholera-endemic area received the bivalent vaccine, covering both main cholera strains, or a placebo, assigned by chance. The team assessed safety and the strength of the immune response. A cheap, safe oral vaccine that passes a placebo-controlled trial is a strong candidate for public vaccination campaigns.
plos-pone-0002423:
Kerse and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Ngaire Kerse, Leon Flicker, Jon J. Pfaff, among others. Its subject is falls, Depression and Antidepressants in Later Life: A Large Primary Care Appraisal. Depression and falls are common and co-exist for older people.

Safe management of each of these conditions is important to quality of life. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002523:
Gibbs joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Adrian J. Gibbs, Kazusato Ohshima, Matthew J. Phillips, among others. Its subject is the Prehistory of Potyviruses: Their Initial Radiation Was during the Dawn of Agriculture. Potyviruses are found world wide, are spread by probing aphids and cause considerable crop damage.

Potyvirus is one of the two largest plant virus genera and contains about 15% of all named plant virus species. When and why did the potyviruses become so many? The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002623:
Thai Nho Dinh and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was adaptation of saccharomyces cerevisiae cells to high ethanol concentration and changes in fatty acid composition of membrane and cell size. The catalog record names Thai Nho Dinh first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Microorganisms can adapt to perturbations of the surrounding environment to grow. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002723:
Xiujuan Wang and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was seventeen new complete mtDNA sequences reveal extensive mitochondrial genome evolution within the demospongiae. Authorship is credited in the record to Xiujuan Wang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Two major transitions in animal evolution–the origins of multicellularity and bilaterality–correlate with major changes in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) organization. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002823:
Chin-Tong Ong and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was notch and presenilin regulate cellular expansion and cytokine secretion but cannot instruct Th1/Th2 fate acquisition. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Chin-Tong Ong, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Recent reports suggested that Delta1, 4 and Jagged1. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002923:
Hongquan Wan, Erin Sorrell, Haichen Song and co-authors tested H9N2 bird flu viruses in ferrets in 2008. H9N2 viruses are common in poultry across much of Eurasia and have infected people in Asia repeatedly since 1998. Judging their pandemic potential means testing how well they grow and spread in mammals.

Ferrets are a standard model for human flu. The PLOS ONE study measured replication and transmission efficiency of these viruses in ferrets. Public health readers get experimental evidence, rather than guesswork, on how close H9N2 sits to a virus that could spread widely in people.
plos-pone-0003023:
Sharad Adekar, Tsuyoshi Takahashi, R. Mark Jones and co-authors reported a human antibody that neutralizes botulinum toxin in 2008. Botulinum neurotoxins are category A bioterror agents and the most potent biological toxins known. Cloned antibody treatments hold promise, but antibodies binding the toxin's light chain faced doubts about usefulness.

Their monoclonal antibody is specific for that catalytic light chain and still neutralizes the toxin, as the title states. Published in PLOS ONE, the result expands the target options for antibody therapy. Botulism has few treatments, so each validated route matters. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003123:
Matan Oren, Marie-line Escande, Guy Paz and co-authors report this 2008 PLOS ONE study of Botryllus schlosseri, a colonial sea squirt. This animal has a rare system for telling self from non-self. When two colonies that do not match touch each other, they mount a rejection response much like inflammation. The team also noted a surprising number of genes like those vertebrates use for blood clotting.

The work tests whether those clotting-like parts switch on during the rejection response. Readers see how a simple marine animal uses tools linked to a far more complex system. That makes the study useful for tracing the deep roots of immunity and clotting.
plos-pone-0003223:
Marco Cassano, Stefano Biressi, Amanda Finan and colleagues study a growth factor variant for muscle in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatocyte growth factor is a cytokine of mesenchymal origin with many roles. It drives cell growth, survival, motility and shape change. Its high affinity receptor, the tyrosine kinase Met, is expressed by many cell types, among them the cells that build muscle.

The team describe Magic-Factor 1, a partial agonist of Met. In the title, it induces muscle hypertrophy by protecting myogenic progenitors from apoptosis, or programmed cell death. Readers get a tuned growth signal that protects muscle precursors. A partial signal may give the gains with fewer side effects than a full one.
plos-pone-0003323:
Anuja Mathew, Joel O'Bryan, William Marshall and colleagues test a weakened vaccinia vaccine in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Vaccinia viruses have been used as a model for viral disease and as a protective live vaccine. The team investigated the immunogenicity of an attenuated strain of vaccinia virus engineered to inactivate the N1L gene, called vGK5. Using the intranasal route, this recombinant virus was far less virulent.

The title reports robust intrapulmonary CD8 T cell responses and protection with the N1L deleted virus. Readers see safety improved while lung T cell protection stayed strong. That trade-off is the central problem of live vaccine design.
plos-pone-0003423:
Roberto Burioni and colleagues tried a mirror-image vaccine idea against HIV in this 2008 study. HIV enters cells by gripping a protein called CD4. The team built antibodies shaped like that grip site. Injected into rabbits, these mimics were meant to train the immune system.

The rabbits did produce responses aimed at HIV itself. Training with a mimic avoids handling the whole virus. Such anti-idiotype approaches copy the target's shape, not the germ. The results support this roundabout route toward an HIV vaccine. Work with such mimics had long been a side road in vaccine research, and this study gave it fresh support.
plos-pone-0003523:
Cheng Wang, Jie Yu, and Caleb B. Kallen ruled out two DNA switches near a key gene in this 2008 paper. PCNA is a protein vital for copying DNA and running the cell cycle. High PCNA levels mark poor outlook in breast cancer. Estrogen raises PCNA production in MCF7 breast cancer cells.

Two estrogen response elements sat near the gene as prime suspects. Testing showed they are not responsible for the estrogen boost. Negative results like this redirect the search for the true mechanism. They also warn against trusting sequence guesses without experiments.
plos-pone-0003623:
Nicholas P. Tucker, Matthew G. Hicks, Thomas A. Clarke, and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It examines NsrR, a protein that switches genes off in many kinds of bacteria. The question was how NsrR detects nitric oxide, a toxic gas bacteria must survive.

The team showed that nitric oxide acts on NsrR through a small iron-sulfur cluster built into the protein. Contact with the gas changes the protein and lifts its grip on target genes. That direct sensing helps explain how harmful and harmless bacteria alike respond when nitric oxide attacks.
plos-pone-0003723:
Francine Noel, Sapna Mehta, Yuwei Zhu, and colleagues published this health study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Since 1999, the GHESKIO center in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, has worked with the health ministry to cut mother-to-child HIV spread. Data on delivering full care in such a setting were limited.

The team examined outcomes for infants of HIV-infected women in this developing country program. They tracked what the program achieved for the babies and where care fell short. The study measures what it takes to improve survival for infants born into the epidemic's hardest conditions.
plos-pone-0003823:
E. J. Dettman and Monica J. Justice published this cancer genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Certain inbred mouse strains develop blood cancers when a leukemia virus inserts itself in their DNA. Those insertions flag nearby genes that may drive cancer. The strains have flagged many candidate oncogenes before.

In lymphoblastic lymphomas with viral insertions at a site called Evi32, the gene Prdm14 was overexpressed. Prdm14 carries a zinc finger and a SET domain, both tied to gene control. The finding nominates Prdm14 as a player in lymphoid cancers worth testing in humans.
plos-pone-0003923:
James W. Wilson, C. Mark Ott, Laura Quick, and co-authors studied Salmonella grown in spaceflight in 2008. Conditions in space mirror some stresses germs face during infection. Germs grown in flight had shown changes not seen with standard lab methods. How the cells sense those flight-linked changes was unclear.

Their PLOS ONE article shows the growth medium's ion mix steers the response. Changing ions altered how Salmonella set its control and virulence genes. That finding gives labs a way to mimic flight effects on the ground. It also flags food and water safety questions for long space missions.
plos-pone-0004023:
Jimmy Susanto, Yu-Hsing Lin, Yun-Nan Chen, and co-authors studied a pump protein in embryonic stem cells in 2008. Stem cells renew themselves many times without losing flexibility. That demands strong defenses to keep their DNA stable. A transport protein called ABCG2 helps guard cells from toxins.

Their PLOS ONE article links ABCG2 to porphyrin balance in stem cells. Porphyrins are pigment building blocks that can harm cells in excess. Keeping them in check supports healthy self-renewal. The work names one defense stem cells use during long growth. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004123:
Joseph-Omer Dyer and colleagues published this neurology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It looks at how reflex pathways in the spinal cord change after a stroke. Earlier work had shown changes in muscles that work together or against each other at one joint. Far less was known about pathways linking muscles at different joints.

Those cross-joint routes are called heteronymous pathways. The team measured how signals travel through them in stroke patients and how the changes relate to poor coordination of movement. Their findings link altered spinal wiring to the clumsy movement many patients face, which matters for planning rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0004223:
Sandra Dupouy and colleagues published this breast cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neurotensin is a small signalling molecule, and its high-affinity receptor, NTSR1, had been proposed as one of the factors driving tumour progression. In breast cancer cells, the switched-on receptor coordinates growth signals.

The team examined the neurotensin receptor-1 pathway in human ductal breast cancer, the most common form of the disease. They report that this pathway contributes to the cancer's progression. A pathway that helps a tumour advance is also a pathway that drugs might block. Ductal breast cancer starts in the milk ducts of the breast.
plos-pone-0004323:
Guo-Qiang Wu and colleagues published this heart rhythm study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Heart rate variability analysis rests on a classic paradox. Do the characteristic high- and low-frequency peaks in its power spectrum represent random noise, or chaotic order? Resolving that question is key to unravelling the mechanisms behind heart rate variability and healthy heartbeat control.

The team looked for chaotic signatures in heart rate data and its power spectrum across health, ageing, and heart failure. How the heartbeat's rhythm changes with age and disease can reveal the control system failing. Their approach treats the heart as a dynamical system, not a metronome.
plos-pone-0004423:
Three targeted drugs, taken in pairs or all at once, are weighed in a 2009 PLOS ONE study of chronic myeloid leukemia by Natalia Komarova, Allen Katouli, and Dominik Wodarz. This blood cancer is treated fairly well by the drug imatinib. Trouble comes when the cancer mutates and stops responding to the drug.

Two more targeted drugs were ready to add, so the key question was how to combine them. Using math models of how resistance grows, the authors compared pairs against the triple mix. Their answer, given in the title, is that two drugs together can improve therapy, but three cannot. That kind of result helps doctors plan drug use and slow the rise of resistant cancer.
plos-pone-0004523:
Gene-based cancer markers found in one study often fail in the next, and Joseph Lucas, Carlos Carvalho, Julia Ling-Yu Chen, and co-authors tested why, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Microarray studies use gene activity as a common currency across many human diseases. In cancer genomics, the hope is that a signature found in one group of patients will predict outcomes in another.

The team evaluated cross-study projections: taking a genomic biomarker built in one data set and applying it to others. They checked when the projection survives and when it collapses. Reliable projection is the difference between a lab curiosity and a test a clinic can use. Their evaluation gives cancer genomics a sober measure of how far its signatures really travel.
plos-pone-0004623:
HIV makes liver cells easier to kill with a death signal, show Challagundla Babu, Kanitta Suwansrinon, Gary Bren, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Patients infected with HIV have increased susceptibility to liver disease from hepatitis B and C viruses, alcohol, and fatty liver. Clinically, this limits options for antiretroviral therapy and accelerates liver disease rates.

The death signal is TRAIL, a protein that can order cells to self-destruct. The team shows HIV induces TRAIL sensitivity in hepatocytes, the main liver cells. Cells that would normally shrug off the signal become vulnerable. That mechanism may help explain why livers fail faster in HIV patients, and it points to the TRAIL pathway as a place where protective drugs might act.
plos-pone-0004723:
Marco van Eijk and colleagues showed that cutting fatty sugar lipids in fat tissue restores insulin response in obese mice, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fat tissue plays a key role in the insulin block that comes with obesity. Past work showed that a drug that lowers these lipids sharply improves blood sugar control.

The team then studied how the drop changes fat tissue itself. They tracked insulin response, new fat cell growth, and inflammation signs. All three moved in a better direction after lipid lowering. The work supports lipid control as a route to treat diabetes linked to obesity.
plos-pone-0004823:
Christopher Lortie and colleagues proposed cage matching head to head competition tests for invasive plants from different regions, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many hypotheses predict why some plant species become invasive. Yet no standard approach compared the breadth of studies or sorted rival claims. Most hypotheses also lacked direct tests that pit native and introduced groups against each other under matched conditions.

Head to head cages standardize such comparisons. Differences between regions can be tested directly. Invasion biology needs comparable evidence across species. The framework helps design stronger tests. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail.
plos-pone-0004923:
Cells stay alive by importing small molecules from their surroundings. When conditions change, cells adjust that intake. Maria Werner, Szabolcs Semsey and Kim Sneppen modeled this response system. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. It asks how cells alter the uptake and use of many molecules at once.

Their model follows a network motif. That motif shows up again and again in cellular response systems. It shows uptake and metabolism being coordinated, not handled molecule by molecule. The picture helps explain a general skill of cells. They tune what they take in to match a changing environment.
plos-pone-0005023:
In performing arts, posture is both tool and artwork. Ballet poses obey the body's biomechanical limits. They also follow strict rules set by tradition. Elena Daprati, Marco Iosa and Patrick Haggard studied this mix in PLOS ONE in 2009. They tracked aesthetically relevant changes in dancers' postures.

The team measured how poses shift across a performance. Some changes serve expression, others serve beauty. Viewers respond to those shifts, often without knowing why. The measurements link biomechanics to aesthetics. Science can probe what makes a pose feel right on stage. The work bridges movement science and art. It may also help dancers train the expressive side of technique.
plos-pone-0005123:
Glioblastoma is a deadly brain tumor. Drugs that block VEGF starve it briefly. Tumors escape, and the survival benefit fades. Emmanuelle di Tomaso and colleagues tested an escape route in PLOS ONE in 2009. The suspect was PDGF-C, another growth signal. They used a glioblastoma model.

PDGF-C induced maturation of the tumor's blood vessels. Mature vessels respond less to anti-VEGF treatment. The tumors reroute their plumbing around the drug. The finding names the escape hatch behind a promising therapy's failure. Blocking PDGF-C alongside VEGF might extend the benefit. The study shows why single-signal attacks fail. Tumors keep spare signals ready. Combination therapy is the logical answer.
plos-pone-0005223:
Silvestrol is a natural compound from trees in the genus Aglaia, and it can kill cancer cells. It belongs to a family that blocks the start of protein production in cells. Cencic and colleagues detailed how silvestrol works in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The compound targets eIF4A, a helper protein needed to start reading many cell messages. Jamming that step starves cancer cells of proteins they need to grow. Knowing the exact target and mechanism helps chemists judge whether this tree compound can be shaped into a usable cancer drug.
plos-pone-0005323:
When DNA replicates, the two new strands come out tangled and must be unlinked before division. The enzyme topoisomerase II alpha does that unlinking, and drugs that block it are common cancer treatments. Wray and colleagues found a resistance factor in breast cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Cells watch their tangling status and can trigger checkpoints when unlinking lags. The protein Metnase mediates resistance to topoisomerase II inhibitors, as the title states. Knowing the resistance factor gives drug designers a second target to restore the power of these widely used drugs.
plos-pone-0005423:
Anna Melchers and colleagues used mice to study DNA repair in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The NBN gene makes nibrin, a protein that helps find and fix breaks in both strands of DNA. The gene is so vital that mammals cannot live without it.

The team used mice in which the gene could be switched off in part of the body. After the mice were exposed to radiation, the team mapped which proteins changed in amount. Those protein shifts chart how cells react when a key repair tool is missing and DNA breaks build up.
plos-pone-0005523:
Antonia Vitalo and co-authors studied healing in rats raised alone, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Being raised alone harms health and slows healing in rats, much as stress does in people. A rich, stimulating home setting is known to lift brain levels of oxytocin, a hormone tied to bonding.

The team compared two helps: material to build nests with, and oxytocin itself. Both sped wound healing in the isolated rats by a similar amount. The match hints that simple comforts at home may aid healing through the same hormone path. Simple comforts are cheap and safe, so a real healing gain from them would be easy to use in care.
plos-pone-0005623:
Rose-Anne Romano and co-authors studied a protein isoform in skin cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The deepest layer of skin makes two keratin proteins, K5 and K14, in a tightly matched way. That pairing is a hallmark of the layer's stem-like cells.

The team found that a shortened form of the protein p63 actively drives both keratin genes. It also guides what fate those skin cells take as they mature. Knowing the driver helps explain skin development and diseases where the outer layer fails to form properly. The same keratins are faulted in some blistering skin diseases, which gives the control story a medical side.
plos-pone-0005723:
Jens Franzen and co-authors described a near-complete primate skeleton from Germany in 2009. The fossil comes from Messel, a site famous for whole Eocene mammals, ringed then by warm rain forest. Primates were oddly rare there, known from just eight broken finds before this one.

The new skeleton let the team study the animal's form and way of life in rare detail. It was widely covered as a possible early link in primate history. Whatever its exact place, a whole body beats fragments for reading how early primates moved and ate. The paper lays out the bones and the case in full.
plos-pone-0005823:
Pascal Lapébie and co-authors used a sponge in 2009 to study one of development's oldest signal systems. Sponges branch near the base of the animal tree, so their patterning tools are ancient. The WNT and beta-catenin pathway patterns bodies from sponges to humans.

In the sponge Oscarella, the team traced where this signaling acts in epithelial patterning. Activity in a simple sponge hints the pathway organized tissues before true organs existed. That deep origin helps explain why the same pathway runs so much of later development, and why its faults cause disease. The sponge offers a clean window.
plos-pone-0005923:
Drug hunters who target the bacteria behind tuberculosis face a basic question. Will blocking a given enzyme kill the germ, or only pause it? In 2009, Parvinder Kaur, Saurabh Agarwal and Santanu Datta set out to sort mycobacterial targets into those two classes, using a switchable antisense method in PLOS ONE.

Their tool lets them turn a target gene down on cue and watch whether the bacteria die or merely stop growing. That split matters most in slow-growing germs like these, where weak tests can mislead. The study gives drug teams a clearer way to pick targets worth the long work of building a new drug.
plos-pone-0006023:
Epstein-Barr virus hides for life in memory B cells, dodging the immune system. Ingrid Ruf, Jennifer Houmani and Jeffery Sample asked in 2009 whether a related immune skew in Burkitt lymphoma needs the virus at all. Their PLOS ONE paper studies UBP43, a protein that damps interferon signals, and how its mis-set level alters genes those signals control.

Even without the virus, wrong UBP43 levels bend the interferon-driven gene program, the title reports. That matters because it parts the lymphoma's immune tricks into virus-made and cell-made shares. A drug aimed at the cell-made share could work in cases where the virus plays no part, widening the reach of lymphoma treatment ideas.
plos-pone-0006123:
An enzyme with several trades may do different work in different rooms of the cell. Soner Gundemir and Gail Johnson mapped those rooms for transglutaminase 2 in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies TG2, an enzyme that cross-links proteins and also binds and burns GTP, and tracks its intracellular localization and conformational state against its known role in cell death.

Where TG2 sits and which shape it holds may decide whether a cell lives or dies, yet opinion on the details was far from settled. Placing the enzyme precisely is the first step to judging its death role fairly. The work serves cancer and brain disease research alike, where TG2 keeps appearing at the scene.
plos-pone-0006223:
Chemical messengers help animals learn which actions bring reward and which bring harm. Laura Kaczer and Hector Maldonado studied octopamine, a messenger likened to noradrenaline in backboned animals, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on the crab Chasmagnathus. Insect studies had cast octopamine as the reward signal in pleasant learning.

In the crab, the messenger played contrasting roles in pleasant and unpleasant learning. One chemical can thus push learning in opposite directions depending on the task. The finding cautions against simple one-messenger labels. It also widens the picture of how simple brains weigh reward and danger.
plos-pone-0006323:
New sequencing machines read millions of short DNA pieces, ideal for measuring gene activity. Nicola Palmieri and Christian Schloetterer tested how accurately those short reads map back to the genome, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Platforms differ in read length and cost, and longer reads were thought safer.

Mapping errors can fake differences in expression, especially between species. The authors quantify accuracy and its implications for quantitative expression profiling. Their results guide platform choice and analysis settings. Careful mapping is the difference between a real biological signal and a technical mirage.
plos-pone-0006423:
Xiao-yun Cai and co-authors used PLOS ONE in 2009 to study why some people in China live to a very old age. Long life has many causes, and genes play a part. The team focused on mitochondrial DNA, the small set of genes inside the cell's energy-making parts, and on the groups formed by its variants.

They ran a population-based case study of extreme longevity. They asked whether some mitochondrial DNA groups appear more often in the very old. Work like this can point to parts of our inherited makeup tied to aging. It also adds data from a Chinese population to a mostly Western field.
plos-pone-0006523:
Young Kwang Chae and colleagues examined estrogen receptor gene variants and prostate cancer risk in PLOS ONE in 2009. Estrogen may be involved in the development of prostate cancer, though the disease is usually linked to androgens. The team studied genetic polymorphisms of estrogen receptors alpha and beta. These variants differ between people and could alter receptor behavior.

They assessed the association between the variants and the risk of developing prostate cancer. Genetic association studies can flag pathways worth deeper study. Even small risk shifts matter when a cancer is common. The work adds to efforts to predict prostate cancer risk from DNA.
plos-pone-0006623:
Satoru Onodera and T. Philip Hicks compared a midbrain nucleus across species in PLOS ONE in 2009. The human red nucleus is comparatively less well-studied than that of cats or monkeys. Given the functional importance of reticular and midbrain structures in control of movement, that gap matters. The authors present a comparative neuroanatomical study of the red nucleus of the cat, macaque, and human.

Comparing the same structure across species shows what evolution enlarged or reduced. The red nucleus helps control limb movement. Human differences may reflect our reliance on other pathways, like the corticospinal tract. Careful anatomy still anchors functional brain research.
plos-pone-0006723:
Tamas Szikra and co-authors studied calcium control in cone cells of the eye in PLOS ONE in 2009. Calcium is a messenger ion governing nearly all cone functions. It even controls release of signal at the cone's synapse. Cone output spans a range wider than one calcium entry route explains. That hint suggested another calcium source helps set the signal.

The team examined interactions between internal calcium stores and membrane ion channels. Stores inside the cell can release or absorb calcium on demand. Channels in the plasma membrane control entry from outside. Together they regulate calcium homeostasis and shape cone signaling. Understanding the balance helps explain how cones handle bright and dim light.
plos-pone-0006823:
Jayson Gutiérrez modeled how gene pairs clash or help each other as embryos grow in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genes turn into traits through layers of control webs. Each layer reads the code of the layer below. One gene change can thus play out in ways a lone-gene view would miss. Such pair effects are called epistasis.

He took a whole-system view of those pair effects. Computer models of embryo control webs served as the test bed. Gene changes were set loose inside those model embryos. The web's shape decided which pair effects showed up. That helps explain why one gene change acts so unlike from strain to strain. It ties gene science to the growth of the embryo itself.
plos-pone-0006923:
Andrea Granstedt, Moriah Szpara, Bernd Kuhn, and colleagues described a new brain research tool in PLOS ONE in 2009. Studying coordinated activity in nerve circuits had been hard for a simple reason. No method could report both activity and wiring at the same time. Their answer used pseudorabies virus, which spreads between connected neurons.

The virus was engineered to express a fluorescent signal inside infected cells. That glow let the team watch living neural activity in place. It also mapped which neurons connect to which. The approach opened a way to link circuit structure with real-time function in the living brain.
plos-pone-0007023:
Avital Tidhar, Yehuda Flashner, Sara Cohen, and colleagues hunted plague virulence factors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Yersinia pestis is the bacterium that causes plague. The team had earlier isolated a weakened mutant with a disrupted gene called pcm. They now investigated the genes around that locus and their role in disease.

Their work identified the NlpD lipoprotein as a new virulence factor. It proved essential for plague to develop fully. Each essential factor is a possible point of attack. Knowing them helps design vaccines and treatments against a historic killer.
plos-pone-0007123:
Acely Garza-Garcia, Richard Harris, Diego Esposito, and colleagues studied a regeneration protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. Newts and salamanders can regrow a lost limb. Cells at the injury site first dedifferentiate, stepping back to a state able to rebuild. A surface protein called Prod1 is part of that system. It belongs to the three-finger protein family.

The team solved Prod1's structure in solution. They also placed it in its family tree by phylogenetics. Knowing the shape of a regeneration signal helps decode limb regrowth. That knowledge may one day inform repair medicine in humans.
plos-pone-0007223:
Veiko Krauss, Carina Eisenhardt, and Tina Unger examined DNA methylation in a stick insect in PLOS ONE in 2009. The insect is Medauroidea extradentata. Methylation adds chemical marks to cytosine in DNA and appears in many eukaryotes, from simple organisms to humans.

In vertebrates, methylation helps control development and disease. It can suppress the start or extension of gene activity. The authors report that this insect genome is strongly methylated within genes and repetitive DNA. Their finding widens the picture of where heavy methylation occurs in animal genomes more broadly. The result places stick insects among animals with heavy gene methylation.
plos-pone-0007323:
Erno Lindfors, Peddinti V. Gopalacharyulu, Eran Halperin, and colleagues hunted molecular paths to type 1 diabetes in mice in 2009. Clinical evidence suggested lipid and amino acid metabolism matter in early, pre-autoimmune stages. Those stages precede the immune attack that destroys insulin-producing cells in the pancreas of patients.

The authors study the Non-Obese Diabetic mouse, a standard diabetes model. They detect molecular pathways linked to insulitis, the pancreatic inflammation that precedes disease. Their PLOS ONE analysis maps early changes before diabetes appears. Such paths could become markers or targets for prevention.
plos-pone-0007423:
Ecologists Jasmin Godbold, Rutger Rosenberg, and Martin Solan published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on why diverse communities use resources well. The link between species variety and healthy ecosystem function was already widely accepted. What remained unclear was the mechanism behind it. Two rival explanations were on the table, and the team set out to test them.

One idea said species split shared resources into separate niches, so little is wasted. The other said each species simply brings its own distinct traits to the task. Their results favored the second view. What each species is, rather than how species divide resources, drove the effect. That finding sharpens how ecologists explain the value of biodiversity.
plos-pone-0007523:
Valeria Antico Arciuch and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Akt1, a signaling protein that guides cell growth and survival. Akt is switched on by growth factors and by oxidative stress in two steps. The team followed where Akt1 travels inside the cell. To their surprise, it cycles through the mitochondria, the cell's power plants, not just the cell surface and interior.

That intramitochondrial cycling proved crucial to how the cell reads its redox state. Redox balance, the tally of oxidants and antioxidants, helps decide whether a cell divides. Akt1's trips into the mitochondria let that balance steer cell cycle progression. The finding puts mitochondria at the center of growth decisions. It also reframes Akt1 as a messenger between the power plant and the nucleus.
plos-pone-0007623:
Lindsay Young and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on plastic pollution and the Laysan albatross. These seabirds forage across vast stretches of the Pacific. Animals should gain the most energy for the least effort when they hunt. But the ocean now carries growing amounts of plastic debris, which birds mistake for prey. The team asked whether a colony's foraging range decides how much plastic its members swallow.

Colonies feeding in debris-heavy waters ingested more plastic. The birds bring that trash home, feeding it to their chicks. A colony's address thus shapes its exposure to a man-made hazard. Optimal foraging, tuned over ages, now leads birds into a trap. The study ties a global pollution pattern to the map of daily bird movements. It shows conservation must think about where animals eat, not only where they breed.
plos-pone-0007723:
Rachel Skilton and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It watches a major human pathogen respond to penicillin. Chlamydia trachomatis lives only inside host cells, where it follows a set growth cycle. Inside a pocket called an inclusion, it shifts from an infectious form to a growing form.

Using high-quality time-lapse video, the team tracked that cycle under penicillin. The drug pushed the bacteria into a persistent, stalled state rather than killing them outright. Persistence may help chlamydia survive treatment and return later. Seeing the process clearly helps researchers design better therapies.
plos-pone-0007823:
Pawel Zajac and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It speeds up the reading of short tandem repeats in DNA. Tandem repeats are short motifs copied back to back. Labs use them as genetic markers in forensics and medicine.

Most studies need many repeats checked at once. The authors test a parallel method called trinucleotide threading, or TnT. Many repeats are amplified and read in one scalable run. Their results show the approach is feasible for routine use. Faster repeat analysis can cut the cost of genetic fingerprinting and diagnosis.
plos-pone-0007923:
Ning Yu and Hong-Bo Zhao published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines how support cells tune the ear's built-in amplifier. Outer hair cells in the cochlea change shape with electric signals, a power called electromotility. This prestin-based motor boosts hearing sensitivity and sharpens frequency tuning.

In the living ear, Deiters supporting cells cradle each outer hair cell. They are well linked by gap junctions, channels that connect cells directly. The authors show these supporting cells and junctions modulate the motor's action. Hearing thus depends on teamwork in the cochlea, not on hair cells alone.
plos-pone-0008023:
Neetu Israni and colleagues studied two genes together in type 1 diabetes patients from North India for PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease strikes when the immune system kills the pancreas cells that make insulin. One gene in view steers the immune response; the other handles vitamin D.

Certain pairings of variants in the two genes tracked with higher risk than either gene alone would suggest. Genes, like people, can amplify each other. The pairing hints that vitamin D paths play a real part in this autoimmune disease, at least in the group studied.
plos-pone-0008123:
Elliot Freeman and Preeti Verghese asked why some stacked patterns hide each other and some do not, in PLOS ONE in 2009. One pattern laid over another usually makes both harder to judge, an effect called masking. Their test patterns were plaids, grids crossing at angles.

Cues that told the brain the two grids were two things, not one cloth, eased the masking and let each be seen. Context thus acts as a sorting tool for the eyes. The result bears on how displays and signs should be drawn so layers do not blur together.
plos-pone-0008223:
Keith Al-Hasani and colleagues studied a Shigella toxin in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Shigella flexneri causes severe diarrheal disease. Its SigA enterotoxin sits on a pathogenicity island in the genome. SigA is a protease that the bacterium secretes on its own. Earlier work showed it harms cultured human cells and helps disease.

The team showed that SigA binds to HEp-2 cells, a human cell line. Inside intoxicated cells, it triggers redistribution of fodrin, a structural protein. That change helps explain how the toxin damages the gut lining. The work adds detail to how Shigella makes people sick.
plos-pone-0008323:
Fikret Er and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about heart arrest caused by a lung clot. A clot that blocks the lung's blood flow is called a pulmonary embolism. When it stops the heart, death is close at hand for most. Drugs that melt clots might help, and doctors hoped for proof. Few studies had tested clot drugs while chest pumps were in use, since such cases are hard to study.

The team checked what clot-melting drugs did for these patients as CPR went on. Proof in this dire case can guide crews who must act in minutes. If the drugs help, care rules should say so in plain terms. The work fills a real gap in rush care.
plos-pone-0008423:
Gilbert Greub and colleagues presented a shortcut for pathogen discovery in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. New sequencing technologies boosted bacterial genome projects greatly. Completing a chromosome still needs costly, time-consuming gap closure. Repetitive elements make finishing especially hard. Incomplete draft genomes, though, already contain most genes.

Their dirty genome approach uses draft sequence plus proteomics to find immunogenic proteins. Skipping completion speeds the hunt for vaccine and diagnostic targets. A new pathogen can thus be characterized faster during outbreaks. The method trades polish for speed where speed matters.
plos-pone-0008523:
Carlo Rossi and co-authors characterize rat muscle stem cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Satellite cells are progenitors that grow, repair, and maintain skeletal muscle after birth. They sit in a unique niche on mature muscle fibers. They were once thought to be a uniform, single-fate stem cell pool. The team clone single satellite cells from rat muscle. They then compare the clones in detail.

Clones differ intrinsically in proliferation, metabolism, and differentiation. That heterogeneity is built in, not just imposed by environment. Distinct satellite cell types may serve distinct repair tasks. The finding reshapes how muscle regeneration should be studied and harnessed.
plos-pone-0008623:
Francesca Scolamacchia and co-authors survey cattle infections in Cameroon in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Brucellosis, leptospirosis, and Q fever are important livestock infections. They cause abortions and reduced fertility in herds. All three are also zoonotic, infecting people who work with livestock or consume their products. The team test Bos indicus cattle in Cameroon for antibodies to each agent. Serological patterns show past or current exposure in the herd.

They find patterns indicating all three infections circulate in those cattle. That circulation poses risks to herders and consumers alike. Surveillance of zebu cattle can guide vaccination and hygiene measures. The study gives baseline data for a region with little prior coverage.
plos-pone-0008723:
Stephanie Sansom, Vimalanand Prabhu, Angela Hutchinson, and colleagues modeled a preventive step against HIV. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trials in Africa showed circumcised men caught HIV less often than others. Those trials involved grown, heterosexual men. The authors asked what newborn circumcision might do in the United States.

Their model projected a boy's lifetime HIV risk with and without the procedure. It also tallied medical costs on both sides. A small risk cut may still save money across a lifetime. The numbers give policymakers a U.S.-specific basis for debate about newborn circumcision.
plos-pone-0008823:
Sylvain Giroud, Martine Perret, Peter Stein, and colleagues watched a tiny lemur ration its body during food shortage. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The grey mouse lemur of Madagascar faces lean seasons yearly. Under steady calorie limits it holds energy balance well. Only wintering animals slip into torpor, a deep rest state. Which fuel the body spares, fat or protein, was the puzzle.

The lemur's sparing strategy switched with the season. At times it protected fat, at others it protected protein. Seasonal flexibility may explain its success in a harsh climate. The work informs broader studies of fasting and hibernation.
plos-pone-0008923:
Stephan Funk and Julia Fa argued that saving nature's regions needs a full armoury, not one magic method. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Conservation planners rank ecoregions to decide where money helps most. Many ranking schemes exist, and they often disagree. Most lean heavily on endemism, species found nowhere else. Relying on any single scheme risks blind spots. Global data let the authors compare schemes head to head.

Different schemes highlighted different regions as top priorities. No single method captured all conservation values at once. Planners should combine several schemes like tools in an armoury. That advice tempers fashion-driven swings in conservation planning.
plos-pone-0009023:
Eva Untersmayr and co-authors found an allergy receptor where few expected it, in PLOS ONE in 2010. IgE antibodies drive allergies and play a big role in gut disorders. Their strongest docking point is the receptor Fc-epsilon-RI. Whether the gut lining itself carries that receptor was the open question.

The team examined human intestinal epithelial cells, the gut's surface layer. The cells did display the receptor, including its IgE-binding chain. So the gut lining can catch IgE directly, not just via immune cells. That may change how food allergies and gut inflammation are understood.
plos-pone-0009123:
Jeroen Smaers and co-authors measured frontal white matter across monkeys and apes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The frontal lobe runs planning, control, and other executive work in the brain. Its wiring to other brain areas may explain primate brain evolution. Yet broad measurements of that frontal wiring tissue had been missing.

The team measured white matter volume in the frontal lobe of many species. Larger brains carried proportionally more of this frontal wiring. More white matter also went with richer links across the whole brain. Growing a bigger primate brain, it seems, means investing heavily in wiring.
plos-pone-0009223:
David Hone and colleagues published this dinosaur study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It looks at Microraptor gui, a small four-winged dinosaur from Early Cretaceous China. The type fossil is ringed by a halo of preserved feathers. Flight feathers attach to both its front and hind limbs, but how far the plumage spread was questioned.

The team examined the fossil under ultraviolet light. UV can reveal soft tissue traces that normal light misses. Their check measured the true extent of the feathers preserved around the body. Knowing the full feather coverage matters for judging how this dinosaur moved, and whether it glided or truly flew.
plos-pone-0009323:
Juhi Bagaitkar and co-authors published this gum disease study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Smokers suffer worse gum disease than non-smokers, yet their gums often look less inflamed. That paradox pointed to some blunting of the immune alarm. The gum bacterium Porphyromonas gingivalis was the team's focus.

They found that tobacco exposure raises the bacterium's fimbrial proteins, the hairs it grips with. Those changes make an immune sensor, TLR2, respond less strongly. A muted sensor explains the quiet look of smokers' gums while damage deepens. The work links a habit, a bacterium, and a silenced alarm into one chain.
plos-pone-0009423:
Ranjan Mannige and Charles Brooks published this virus design study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most viruses protect their genes inside a spherical shell, the capsid. Capsids come in many sizes, all built from protein subunits. The rules that shape their design through evolution were unclear.

The authors arrange capsid forms into a kind of periodic table. Patterns in that table reveal the pressures natural selection puts on shell design. A periodic table does for viruses what Mendeleev's did for elements: it shows gaps, families, and rules. Engineers designing artificial virus-like shells can read the same rules for guidance.
plos-pone-0009523:
Phan Luu and co-authors explored how perception loops back on itself in PLOS ONE in 2010. Seeing is not a one way flow from eye to mind. The brain compares fresh sensory data with stored experience. Signals run forward and then back again, a pattern called reentrant processing. The team studied this looping in the setting of intuitive perception, where a scene makes sense at once.

Their work supports the idea that quick, sure perception depends on those feedback loops. Without them, raw data would stay a jumble of features. The account helps explain how we grasp a scene in a flash. It also bears on disorders where perception breaks down.
plos-pone-0009623:
Lilian Bueno and co-authors studied immune brakes during malaria in PLOS ONE in 2010. The malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax infects red blood cells. The immune response must be strong enough to control it, yet not so strong that it harms the host. Regulatory T cells provide the braking force. The team measured those cells in infected patients and compared them with parasite levels in the blood.

As parasite levels rose, regulatory T cells rose with them in a direct relation. That close tie suggests the brakes engage in step with the threat. Understanding the balance could help design vaccines that do not overshoot. It also clarifies how this malaria species and its host negotiate a truce.
plos-pone-0009723:
Knee osteoarthritis wears down joint cartilage and makes walking painful. Masahiro Nakajima and colleagues hunted for gene variants that raise the risk of the disease. Their genome-wide association study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

A genome-wide hunt scans the whole DNA code for variants tied to a trait. The team found new variants in the HLA region, a stretch of DNA known for immune genes. The variants were linked with susceptibility, meaning higher odds of getting the disease. That result adds immune genes to the arthritis risk map. It may also hint that inflammation plays a bigger role than expected.
plos-pone-0009823:
Tuberculosis bacteria can keep growing or sit dormant, and telling the two states apart is hard. Paul Carroll and colleagues built brighter tools for spotting gene activity in mycobacteria. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The tools are far-red reporter genes, markers that glow in far-red light when a gene is on. Optimized reporters raised sensitivity under both replicating and non-replicating conditions. Far-red light cuts through background glow better than other colors. Better detection helps researchers study dormant bacteria, a key obstacle in tuberculosis. Mycobacteria include the germs behind tuberculosis and leprosy.
plos-pone-0009923:
Type 1 diabetes damages more than blood sugar control, and the skin keeps a record of it. Franco Folli and colleagues read that record in patients' skin using proteomics. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Proteomics catalogs the proteins a tissue is making. The team found novel oxidative and glycolytic mechanisms at work in diabetic skin. Normalized means the protein patterns returned toward healthy levels. Those changes were normalized by kidney-pancreas transplantation, which restores insulin production. Skin thus mirrors deep metabolic damage, and its repair after transplant. Skin is easy to sample, unlike deeper organs.
plos-pone-0010023:
Priya Prahalad, Sivanesan Dakshanamurthy, Habtom Ressom, and co-workers studied breast cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tumors need a blood supply to grow and spread, so they build new vessel networks. Retinoic acid, a vitamin A based signal, had shown effects on that process in the team's earlier work.

The study traced how retinoic acid controls network formation through a protein called COUP-TFII. It also linked the signal to VE-cadherin, a vessel wall protein, through a growth factor receptor pathway. Mapping those links may point to ways of choking off a tumor's blood supply.
plos-pone-0010123:
The authors were Samuel García-Nieto, Ramneek Johal, Kevin Shakesheff, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study worked with dendritic cells, the immune system's scouts. These cells sample sites where microbes enter the body. They then meet T cells in lymph nodes, starting an immune response against what they found.

The team grew dendritic cells on two proteins, laminin and fibronectin, found in body tissues. Cells raised that way took up material with superior endocytic capacity, meaning they swallowed samples better. Better sampling cells could improve vaccine and immune therapy design in the laboratory.
plos-pone-0010223:
Thomas Webb, Edward Vanden Berghe, and Ron O'Dor mapped where ocean life has been recorded in 2010. Knowing the distribution of marine biodiversity is a first step to managing ocean ecosystems well. New databases now gather location records from marine surveys worldwide. Their PLOS ONE study assembled that global picture and looked for gaps in coverage and effort.

They found the deep open ocean, far below the surface, has barely been explored at all. Most records cluster near coasts and shallow zones. The title calls this gap biodiversity's big wet secret, a warning for conservation planning built on patchy data.
plos-pone-0010323:
Sushila Maan, Narender Maan, Piet van Rijn and a large team sequenced a bluetongue virus strain for PLOS ONE in 2010. Bluetongue harms farm animals, and in September 2008 sick cows appeared on three farms in the eastern Netherlands. Signs included sore, inflamed hooves. Oddly, two farms had already used a vaccine against a different strain, type 8.

Lab work showed the new cases came from serotype 6, a distinct form of the virus. The team read its full genome, letter by letter. They then compared that code with field strains and with vaccine strains. Such comparisons can reveal where a virus came from and how it changed. For animal health officials, knowing the exact strain guides vaccine choice.
plos-pone-0010423:
Brian Lindshield and co-workers fed three popular nutrients to rats with prostate tumors for PLOS ONE in 2010. Many men with prostate cancer take lycopene, selenium, or vitamin E supplements. Whether those nutrients truly slow tumors was unclear. The team used a transplantable rat prostate tumor that grows steadily. They tested each nutrient's effect on that growth.

Selenium slowed the tumors; lycopene and vitamin E did not. That split result warns against lumping supplements together as equally useful. It also tempers the hope that diet pills can substitute for treatment. Rat results do not settle human questions, but they rank candidates for trials. Only selenium earned further attention here.
plos-pone-0010523:
Eva-Maria Ratai and colleagues used brain scans to show a common antibiotic protects primate brains in a NeuroAIDS model for PLOS ONE in 2010. Even with strong HIV therapy, brain problems tied to the virus remain common. The team used a fast-moving monkey version of the disease to test help quickly. Minocycline, a cheap oral antibiotic, was their candidate. They measured brain chemistry with magnetic resonance spectroscopy, a scan that reads molecules in living tissue.

Treated animals showed signs of protected brain tissue on those scans. A safe, cheap drug showing brain benefit in primates merits human attention. Scan-based measures also let future trials track benefit without biopsies. The study bridges animal work and a real unmet need in HIV care.
plos-pone-0010623:
Barbara Penolazzi and colleagues tested gentle brain stimulation and memory in PLOS ONE in 2010. Volunteers viewed pictures that were pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral. While they watched, a weak electric current passed over front and side areas of the scalp for twenty minutes.

Later memory tests showed the stimulation changed what people remembered about the emotional pictures. The effect depended on which side and direction the current flowed. Calmer and charged images were not affected in the same way. Findings like these may shape future attempts to strengthen memory in people with early memory loss.
plos-pone-0010723:
Alexandra Tobler and H. Frederik Nijhout studied wing growth in the tobacco hornworm, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A caterpillar's wings develop as flat disks inside the body. Two hormones, insulin and ecdysone, tell those disks when and how fast to grow.

In dishes, the two hormones worked far better together than either alone. Partway through development, the control switched: the disks answered the pair in a new way. That switch times wing growth to the body's overall growth. Moths must emerge with wings matched to body size, so a control switch of this kind keeps the proportions right.
plos-pone-0010823:
Ivan Martínez-Forero, Antonio Peláez-López, and Pablo Villoslada simplified the math of chemical reaction networks, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Networks of reactions govern everything from drug action to cell signaling. Their behavior settles into steady states that scientists need to find. Even small networks yield tangled equations that resist standard solving.

Their analytical method detects steady states with far less machinery than usual routes. Test networks confirmed the shortcut gives the same answers. A simpler method lowers the entry cost for biologists who need steady states but lack heavy math support. It also speeds the large models used in systems medicine.
plos-pone-0010923:
Larry Chang, Joseph Kagaayi, Gertrude Nakigozi and co-authors ran this AIDS care trial in Rakai, Uganda, published in PLOS ONE in 2010. Delivering antiretroviral therapy in poor regions is limited by a shortage of health workers. The trial tested whether trained community peers, themselves living with HIV, could support patients through counseling, clinic help, and home visits.

Fifteen clinics were assigned at random to add peer health workers or continue usual care, and more than thirteen hundred patients were followed for up to four years. The main measures were pill adherence and the risk of the virus rebounding above a set level. Chang and colleagues found the model worth testing rigorously rather than assuming goodwill guarantees results. Their trial design gives programs a fair way to judge task-shifting before spending scarce funds.
plos-pone-0011023:
Alessia Zamborlini, Noémie Renault, Ali Saïb and co-authors published this foamy virus study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Foamy viruses are odd retroviruses: their particles carry mostly RNA, yet also infectious DNA made by reverse transcription late in the cycle. Which nucleic acid actually starts a new infection was unsettled, so the team tracked both in the first hours after entry.

Using sensitive PCR methods, with and without the blocking drug AZT, they found an early round of reverse transcription within hours of infection is absolutely required for productive infection. Adding more virus could partly overcome AZT's block, and circular viral DNA appearing by four hours was already able to direct gene expression. Zamborlini and colleagues redraw the foamy virus timetable, showing early DNA synthesis, not the packaged DNA alone, launches infection.
plos-pone-0011123:
Stevens, Pavoine and Baguette examined animal movement in PLOS ONE in 2010. They compared how far individuals travel within a species and between close relatives. Movement, called dispersal, decides how species spread, mix genes and respond when habitats change.

They found very high variety in travel distance, even among members of the same species. That variety was larger than many models assume. It makes forecasts of shifting ranges harder, yet also more realistic once included. For conservation, it means protecting a species may require planning for both stay at home and far ranging members.
plos-pone-0011223:
Faure, Richard and Berridge separated wanting from liking in rats for PLOS ONE in 2010. A brain hub for reward can generate both drive to get a reward and pleasure in having it, plus their dark opposites. The team used two chemical systems in that hub to pull those states apart.

One system mainly drove motivation, while the other shaped pleasure and dread responses. That split wiring matters for addiction, where wanting can grow even as liking fades. Treatments that target the right system could restore balance. The study gives addiction science a clearer map of this small but powerful brain region.
plos-pone-0011323:
Kantelhardt, Caarls, De Vries and colleagues imaged brain tumor cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gliomas blend into healthy brain, making surgery hard: too little removed leaves tumor, too much harms function. The team achieved specific visualization of glioma cells within living tissue from low grade tumors.

Seeing tumor cells distinctly in living tissue could guide surgeons in real time. More precise removal should lower recurrence while sparing healthy brain. The method is an early step that must prove itself in the operating room. Still, it addresses the central dilemma of brain tumor surgery directly.
plos-pone-0011423:
Ariane Mogha and co-authors found in 2010 that ultraviolet light raises the activity of a cancer-linked virus living on skin. Merkel cell polyomavirus is common and usually quiet, but it is tied to a rare and aggressive skin cancer. Sunlight is the main risk factor for skin cancers generally, and the team asked whether it also wakes this virus.

After UV exposure of living skin, the message for the virus's small T antigen, a protein that can push cells toward cancer, increased. That rise links sun exposure directly to the virus's cancer-linked machinery. The result adds a viral chapter to the story of sun and skin cancer. It suggests that in people carrying the virus, sun protection guards against two threats at once: direct DNA damage and activation of a resident virus.
plos-pone-0011523:
Jasveer Virk and co-authors explored in 2010 whether a mother's stressful life events around pregnancy can program type 1 diabetes in her child. Early-life programming holds that conditions before and just after conception shape lifelong disease risk. The team examined whether severe stress in the preconception and prenatal periods links to later diabetes in the children, using population records.

Their analysis connects that early stress window to the disease, pushing its roots back further than the usual story of childhood triggers. A root before birth changes prevention thinking: support for mothers under severe stress becomes a possible child-health measure. The link needs care in interpretation, since stress travels with many other hardships. Even so, the study widens the timeline on which diabetes prevention might begin, to before the child exists.
plos-pone-0011623:
Markéta Faustová and co-authors examined tiny water fleas of the genus Eubosmina in PLOS ONE in 2010. These animals alternate between cloning themselves and breeding sexually, a cycle once thought to blur the borders between species. In some lakes, several distinct Eubosmina forms live side by side.

Combining shape analysis and genetic evidence, the authors show the coexisting forms make up a young species flock formed since the last ice age. A recent burst of splitting like this is rare and valuable to study. It lets biologists watch how new species arise and stay distinct despite a breeding system that might mix them.
plos-pone-0011723:
Jens Jensen and co-authors presented two shortcuts for measuring gene activity, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Real-time quantitative PCR is a workhorse of research and clinical labs, but it normally needs control samples for comparison. The team aimed to broaden what the method can do while dropping that requirement.

Their approaches use tiny standard curves built into each run, and a direct relative method that needs no control samples. Run-specific values come from inside the run itself. The control-free recipe makes routine gene measurement simpler and cheaper for busy laboratories.
plos-pone-0011823:
Marianne De Paepe and co-authors watched twin germs drift apart under virus attack, in PLOS ONE in 2010. How an outbreak spreads rests not just on the mean output per host, but also on a few highly infectious hosts. Infectious power is most often blamed on gene or setting gaps, yet even cloned hosts vary.

In matched E. coli groups infected by a thread-like virus, spread in behaviour grew over time. That spread among equals shows plain chance at work. Such random spread can itself act as a survival trick, hedging a group's bets against a shaky future.
plos-pone-0011923:
Verena Ohms and co-workers studied in 2010 how zebra finches shape sound with their vocal tract, not just their sound source. Birdsong and human speech share striking parallels in how they are learned. Production may match too: human speech depends on the throat and mouth filtering the voice, and birds were long assumed to do far less of this.

The study examines how finches move their beak and throat structures while singing. Active shaping would mean the vocal tract acts as a tunable filter, as in human speech. That strengthens the case for songbirds as a model of vocal control, and it changes how their songs should be measured and taught to young birds in experiments.
plos-pone-0012023:
Zarir Udwadia, Lancelot Pinto, and Mukund Uplekar asked in 2010 whether private doctors in Mumbai treat tuberculosis any better than they did twenty years earlier. A study two decades before had exposed widespread poor TB practice among private practitioners, who handle much of India's TB care. Since then, the national program had advanced and tried to engage private doctors.

Repeating the check in the same city measures whether two decades of progress reached the private clinic. Persistent gaps between private habits and program standards matter because wrong regimens breed drug resistance. The comparison turns a suspicion about stalled change into documented evidence that policy can act on.
plos-pone-0012123:
Juan López-Ramos, Yukiko Tomioka, Masami Morimatsu, and colleagues studied learning in special transgenic mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. These mice carry a virus protein in the brain that shrinks the cerebellum and badly scrambles its structure, leaving the animals unsteady on their feet. Because the damage centers on the movement-coordination region, the mice serve as a model for testing which kinds of learning depend on it.

Tasks that needed coordinated movement were the ones the mice learned worst, more than other kinds of tasks. That pattern helps separate what the cerebellum truly does from what other brain regions can handle. Models like this guide research on human disorders where the cerebellum is damaged.
plos-pone-0012223:
Lesong Conteh, Edith Patouillard, Margaret Kweku, and co-authors priced preventive malaria treatment for Ghanaian children in PLOS ONE in 2010. The scheme gives young children full courses of malaria drugs at set times through the rainy season, whether or not they seem sick, in regions where malaria comes in waves. Two drug combinations were in use, at different prices and strength.

The team weighed what each option costs against the illness and death it prevents. For health ministries with small budgets, cost per case prevented is the number that decides what actually gets delivered. Their comparison gives Ghana, and countries copying the scheme, a factual basis for picking the better buy.
plos-pone-0012323:
Feng Zhang, Yanhua Hu, and Qingbo Xu compared two sibling hormone fragments on blood vessel cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Both come from the renin-angiotensin system, the body's blood pressure control circuit. The elder, angiotensin II, drives vessel disease, feeding high blood pressure and artery clogging, while its shorter sibling angiotensin-(1-7) protects the same vessels, a built-in counterweight.

On vessel muscle cells, the two push growth and migration in different directions, matching their opposing reputations. Migration and growth of these cells are the very steps that thicken artery walls. Strengthening the protective sibling, or mimicking it, is a strategy drug designers are actively weighing against the elder's damage.
plos-pone-0012423:
Cedar Chittenden, Jenny Jensen, David Ewart and colleagues asked whether young salmon now miss the peak of their food, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Spring blooms of tiny ocean plants near shore are starting earlier as the climate warms. Young salmon heading to sea depend on the creatures that graze those blooms, so a shift in timing could leave them hungry.

The authors weigh evidence that salmon migration timing has not kept pace with the earlier blooms. Hungry smolts would grow less and die more at sea, helping explain recent salmon declines. The timing idea links climate change to fishery losses through a testable chain that managers can monitor.
plos-pone-0012523:
Tinatin Brelidze, Anne Carlson, Douglas Davies and colleagues built a screen to find regulators of a brain ion channel, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. EAG1 channels pass potassium and appear in the brain, where they help set cell excitability; they also drive some cancers. Few good tools existed to find what turns these channels up or down.

Their screen pairs electrical recording with tryptophan fluorescence, a light signal from the channel itself, to spot regulators efficiently. A working screen is the gateway to drug discovery for this channel. Hits could yield leads for epilepsy, pain, or cancer, all fields where EAG1 shows up.
plos-pone-0012623:
Inoue, Li and Kurata built a computer method for splitting protein networks into meaningful groups. Proteins in a cell touch and bind each other in huge webs, and those webs hide the cell's working units. Their 2010 paper applies a diffusion model, which spreads a signal through the web step by step.

Clusters that emerge from the spread should match real functional groups, such as machines that copy DNA or build proteins. Better clustering helps biologists read network maps and guess what unknown proteins do. The method adds a tool for systems biology, the study of whole cell systems.
plos-pone-0012723:
Pirisinu, Di Bari, Marcon and co-authors built a new test for telling prion strains apart. Prions are rogue proteins that copy their own twisted shape, and strains differ in shape and behaviour. Their 2010 method measures how stable each strain's shape is when a protease attacks it.

The test covers both protease-sensitive and protease-resistant forms, which older methods often missed. telling strains apart matters for tracking mad cow style diseases in animals and people. A sharper test improves both food safety checks and basic prion science.  Stability readouts can be compared across labs with shared samples.
plos-pone-0329423:
Elisabeth Emanuel Graae and co-workers pool studies on whether a mother's weight before pregnancy raises her newborn's risk of a serious strep infection in the first days of life. Antibiotics during labor prevent many cases, but who counts as at risk is still debated. Their 2026 review gathers nineteen studies covering more than three point seven million women.

The pooled link was steady: each step up in body mass index nudged the odds of infection or of carrying the germ higher. At the heaviest levels, risk ran well above that of mothers at a healthy weight. One huge study found risk more than doubled for mothers in a high weight band. Adding weight to risk checklists could catch cases now missed.
plos-pone-0331823:
Shuangshuang Le and colleagues uncovered a cleanup routine that helps stomach cancer cells survive chemical stress. Cells use a selective recycling service to destroy damaged proteins one by one, guided by a gatekeeper protein in the recycling compartment's wall. The team found this gatekeeper is unusually abundant in stomach cancer and rises further when cells face oxidising chemicals.

The cargo turned out to be a protective protein that, once over-oxidised, becomes harmful baggage. Blocking the gatekeeper left the damaged protein piled up, tipped the cell's death switches toward dying, and made cancer cells far easier to kill with oxidants. The authors identify this disposal step as a key survival trick of gastric cancer and a possible weak point that future drugs could attack.
plos-pone-0332723:
Schema therapy treats deep personality patterns, and its theory has just been rewritten. Freideriki Carmen Mamali and colleagues present an international study plan, in PLOS One in 2026, to rebuild the therapy's questionnaires on the new theory and test whether its ideas hold across cultures.

Fresh drafts of three questionnaires, covering early life patterns, coping styles, and emotional modes, will be checked carefully for wording and meaning in each language. At least one hundred patients and one hundred non-patients per country will answer. The team will then test whether the concepts and their links behave the same everywhere, a universality the field has assumed but never proven.
plos-pone-0344623:
Feng Tang and colleagues predict crash risk at freeway exits. Their traffic safety study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. They studied twelve exit zones on two Chinese freeways. Cameras and image software pulled dozens of motion measures from video. The team tagged near-conflicts between cars, both behind and beside each other. Warnings were built in thirty-second blocks.

Four learning models were tested. The boosted-tree model did best. A tool that explains each warning ranked the top risk factors. Side conflicts lasted longer than rear ones. They also carried higher risk. Bad conflicts clustered within two hundred meters of the exit. Designers now know the exact stretch to fix first.
plos-pone-0344923:
Borui Yan and three co-workers asked how good freight links help farm regions grow past raw crops. They used data from thirty parts of China, from 2011 to 2022. High-grade freight means fast, sure, and cheap moves of goods. The team built a model of how such links lift farm work toward shops, brands, and food plants.

The lift was clear and held up in fresh tests. Part of it ran through the wider growth of each region. State cash for new tech helped. So did phone-based finance. Farm work rates and the town-country pay gap set how strong the lift was. One size of aid will not fit all.
plos-pone-0345123:
Rohollah Ramezani, Mohammad Reza Rabiei, and Mohammad Arashi develop a smarter estimation method for survival models where risk factors change over time. Standard survival models assume steady information flow, which breaks when patients risks evolve. Their method blends cautious shrinkage, which pulls wild estimates toward safe values, with a pre test of whether a simplifying assumption holds.

Theory shows the refined estimator stays fair when the assumption holds and tames variance when it nearly holds. Simulations and a classic liver disease data set backed the gains, beating both raw and penalised rivals. Clinicians modelling changing patient risks could get steadier risk estimates without giving up flexibility.
plos-pone-0346723:
Shiqi Liu and his team set out the plan for a study of heart scans. Some heart stents clog up again with time. The best checks are slow or use a tube in the artery. A scan-based method can gauge blood flow, but the maths takes too long. This 2026 paper is a plan, not a report of results.

The study will run at Beijing Anzhen Hospital and six more sites in China. It will train a deep learning tool to read the scans fast. Doctors will then check its calls against the tube-based test. The hope is a quick, safe way to spot a clogged stent.
plos-pone-0347123:
Neha Margret Issac and Rajakumar K. build a faster way for computers to find and sort cells on blood smear slides. Doctors read these slides to spot many blood diseases, but the cells vary in size, shape, and stain. Their 2026 paper adapts a well-known object-spotting system so its view adjusts to each cell's form.
