On slides marked by clinicians, the system sorted red cells, white cells, and platelets with high accuracy. It beat the base system it grew from and several newer rivals. It also ran fast enough for live use on strong hardware. Such a tool could back up busy labs and support quick first screening in remote care, where experts are scarce.
plos-pone-0347623:
Xiaolong Chen and colleagues mined cancer databases to study a sticky cell surface protein in bladder cancer. High levels of the protein marked more advanced stage, higher grade, and aggressive subtypes, and pointed to poorer outlook. Gene network tools traced links to cell shape shifting, immune surroundings, and drug response.

Tumours with high protein levels showed stronger signs of the shape shift that lets cancer spread, a reshaped immune mix, and marks of resistance to immune therapy. The protein also tied to chemical silencing of genes and to immune brake signals. A single marker that forecasts outlook and hints at treatment resistance could help sort patients for closer watch or new drug trials.
plos-pone-0348023:
Joanna Jadwiga Ilska, Fern McDonnell, and Jane Frances Ladlow ran the numbers on whether flat-faced dogs can simply be bred back to breathing properly. Bulldogs, French bulldogs, and pugs suffer a airway syndrome tied to their skull shape. Using a standard exercise-based breathing grade recorded for more than four thousand British dogs, plus pedigrees, the team estimated how much of the variation is inherited.

Breathing grade proved moderately heritable in every breed, and the related trait of pinched nostrils was heritable too, with the two genetically linked. Moderate heritability means selection can work: choosing parents with better grades should shift puppies toward easier breathing within breeds, without crossbreeding. The authors urge wider participation in the grading scheme so breeders have the data to act on.
plos-pone-0348123:
Tabea Thies, Philipp Buech, and Anne Hermes tested whether a speech-tracking technology can double as a breathing monitor, sparing speakers the chest bands normally used to record speech breathing. Electromagnetic articulography tracks tiny sensors on the body to follow speech movements. Their 2026 study recorded eighteen speakers producing sentences of varied length and complexity, comparing many sensor arrangements against the standard chest band signal.

The tracking method reliably captured inhales, exhales, and full breathing cycles. Horizontal distance measures worked best, especially pairing a sternum or rib sensor with one at the neck. Vertical measures wobbled more but never lost the breathing pattern. The authors propose the two-sensor setup as an easy add-on that folds breathing into speech research without extra gear.
plos-pone-0348523:
Paweł Chorab and Dorota Łozowicka examine a quiet source of error in ship design math: skipping middle slices when computing a hull's shape. Naval architects estimate underwater volume and the center of buoyancy by adding up cross-sections along the hull. Their 2026 study shows how leaving out intermediate sections distorts those numbers and compares classic calculation schemes.

Adding intermediate sections cut the numerical error in the worked examples. Sloppy geometry can mislead the stability checks that keep ships upright, so the fix matters beyond neatness. The authors propose a future search tool that picks section counts and placements automatically, weighing accuracy against computing cost. Better hull math means safer stability calls at the design stage.
plos-pone-0348623:
Wafaa A Mahmoud and colleagues surveyed medical students at a science and technology university in Jordan about how they study. Five hundred and fifty six students rated how often they use ten study habits, from rereading to self testing. Habits were grouped into proven active methods and common passive ones, then set beside self reported grades.

Just over half of students reported top grades. Use of proven methods rose step by step with grade level and raised the odds of top marks even after other factors were counted. Passive habits showed no such link. Because the survey is a snapshot, cause stays unproved, but teaching active methods early looks like a fair bet for schools.
plos-pone-0348823:
Emmanuel Nasinghe and co-authors set out a data science project in 2026 on tuberculosis in Kampala households, Uganda. The disease overlaps heavily with HIV there, many cases hide without symptoms, and it is hard to separate risks from the home, the germ, and the surroundings.

The team will use Makerere University computing power and records on patients and their household contacts to train learning models. Goals include spotting what drives spread inside homes and why treatment fails for some. The project is a plan rather than a result, aiming to turn routine health data into sharper targeting of testing and support.
plos-pone-0349023:
Ji-Young Son and Seung-Ho Han mapped the small arteries that pierce outward through the face, knowledge that surgeons need when they move living tissue flaps during reconstruction. Seven donated cadavers, fourteen half-faces, were examined with fine X-ray scanning and dissection. Every vessel branch at least half a millimetre wide was counted, measured at its origin, and plotted against fixed landmarks of the skull.

One hundred and thirty-four such vessels emerged from seven parent arteries. The facial artery's main trunk supplied the most and the thickest, appearing in every specimen. Maps showed distinct territories, and one branch spread widest while another packed vessels most densely near the nose. The authors offer their coordinate maps as a planning aid so flap surgeons can design around vessels they can actually expect to find.
plos-pone-0349223:
Xiao Liao and colleagues present STGAD, a system for spotting anomalies in streams of sensor data where many measurements move together, such as in servers or spacecraft. Nobody labels the failures in advance, so the system must learn what normal looks like and flag departures. Their design pits a generator against a critic in a training contest, with a transformer reading the time patterns.

At test time, each data window is compared with freshly generated normal versions, and the closest match leaves a residual that signals trouble. Two scores, from generation and from the critic, are fused with a threshold that adapts to each dataset. Tests spanned five benchmark sets, from server monitoring to aerospace telemetry, where the system also points to which variables went wrong.
plos-pone-0349423:
Kannika Damrongplasit and Kadir Atalay evaluated Thailand's unconditional cash grant for young children, using national survey data from 2019 and 2022 covering thousands of households. Their 2026 study matched grant-receiving families with similar non-recipients and compared early childhood development, learning materials, and children's screen habits, looking for both benefits and side effects of no-strings money.

Children in grant households developed modestly but measurably better. Yet those homes owned fewer children's books, even as children played more with homemade toys, and the children had more access to electronic devices with longer daily screen time. The authors conclude the grant works, but pairing it with nudges toward books and balanced screen habits would protect its gains.
plos-pone-0350023:
Robert Badgett, Sudha Xirasagar, and Hayrettin Okut ask whether strict copyright on widely used health questionnaires helps or harms science. Two famous tools, a burnout inventory and a mental status exam, charge royalties and forbid changes to their questions. The authors compared their citation patterns over time against four similar tools that are free to use and adapt.

If licensing fees and modification bans slow other researchers down, the restricted tools should gradually be cited less, relative to their topics, than the open ones. The comparison uses annual citation ratios drawn from the medical literature. The question matters for every field that measures people with standard scales: who owns a measuring stick shapes how much it gets used.
plos-pone-0350123:
Job Agba Opue led a team that turned a branch of pure math on supply chains. The math is semigroup theory, which studies one-way changes to a system. In their 2026 model, each shock or fix is one such change. Stack the changes up, and the math shows where the chain can break. It also shows which states are stable.

The team derived clear tests for total collapse. They found ways to spot spare capacity that can save a chain. Step-by-step methods prune the model down to those key parts. Test cases span factories, farm goods, and online sales. The authors say the tools turn vague talk of toughness into numbers planners can use.
plos-pone-0350223:
Peng Liu and co-authors charted acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in children and teenagers across poorer countries from 1990 to 2023 in work published in 2026, with projections to 2050. The cancer is the most common in childhood and often curable, yet outcomes split sharply by income.

Using global burden data, they counted new cases, deaths, and lost healthy years by income group. In 2023 the poorer countries saw tens of thousands of new cases and deaths, with boys hit harder. Rates per child fell while total cases rose with population. Workplace benzene and formaldehyde were the only modelled risks, a narrow slice of the story.
plos-pone-0350323:
Western Sweden's emergency departments swapped their triage system for a new one called WEST, and Samah Habbouche and colleagues studied how the change landed at the first two hospitals to adopt it. Their 2026 PLOS One study interviewed thirty-six triage nurses.

Nurses described the rollout stage by stage, comparing the new system's sorting rules with the old one's habits. Speed of adoption surprised even its supporters, and reports hinted at friction during the switch. The analysis used an innovation-spread framework, treating each department as its own social world. Lessons on training, timing, and nurse involvement should help the remaining departments adopt the system more smoothly.
plos-pone-0350623:
Decorative digital patterns are bulky to send and store, so Binmei Liu and colleagues built a compression method tuned for them. Their 2026 PLOS One paper mixes color grouping with a technique that flattens image data while keeping its local shape.

Colors are first grouped using the image's own color spread, then color and texture guide how the image is cut into pieces, and the flattening step adapts to each neighborhood. The method shrank files to about a sixth of their size while keeping measured quality high, with no clear visible loss. Large batches were handled quickly and with modest memory, suggesting use in design libraries and media sharing.
plos-pone-0350823:
Camilla Bjelland and colleagues reviewed a phone-based referral system for mothers in Ghana and Liberia in 2026. The system links rural clinics with district hospitals so women in labour emergencies reach care faster, a link that often decides survival.

The team combined interviews with dozens of rural and hospital staff in Liberia and a group discussion with midwives in Ghana. Workers said the system fit their daily routines and sped referrals, but shortages of phones, credit, and staff limited its use, and rollout stayed partial. The cross-country view shows what helps a simple mobile tool take hold in busy, low-resource maternity care.
plos-pone-0350923:
Andualem Addisu Birlie and colleagues mapped open defecation across Zambia and trained models to predict where it persists. Going outdoors instead of using a toilet spreads gut disease and pollutes water. A 2024 national survey covered close to thirteen thousand households. Map tools found clusters, while seven learning models raced to predict household practice from survey traits.

About twelve percent of households still practised open defecation. Hot spots clustered in southern, western, and eastern regions. A light boosting model predicted best among the seven. Maps plus prediction, the team argues, let sanitation programmes spend first where need and risk run highest, rather than spreading thin funds evenly.
plos-pone-0351023:
Chittaphone Vanhnollat and colleagues trapped mosquitoes across six provinces of Laos from 2021 to 2024 and screened them for flaviviruses, the family that includes dengue and Japanese encephalitis. Over twenty five hundred female mosquitoes from one hundred species were sorted into small pools and tested, with full gene reading for positive pools.

Gene reading recovered thirteen full virus genomes. One was Tembusu virus from a common mosquito type, closely matching a strain that harmed dolphins in Thailand. Twelve others were insect only viruses that do not infect people. Finding a mammal linked strain in Laos argues for wider virus watching beyond the two famous threats.
plos-pone-0351123:
The Antarctic scallop anchors food webs in the Southern Ocean, yet its genetic toolkit was nearly empty. Hye Jin Park and colleagues read the species' complete mitochondrial genome and built DNA markers for population studies, reported in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

The circular genome runs about fifteen thousand letters and holds the usual gene set minus one gene commonly missing in clams and scallops. Family tree analysis placed the scallop on its own well-supported branch, closest to a North Atlantic species. From the full DNA the team mined hundreds of thousands of short repeating markers and validated seven variable ones, giving future researchers tools to track scallop populations around Antarctica.
plos-pone-0351223:
Terahertz waves could carry the huge data loads of future 6G networks, but walls and human bodies block them easily. Tahniyat Aslam, Irfan Ahmed, and Sundus Ali modeled indoor terahertz uplinks with realistic three-dimensional antennas, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Most earlier work flattened antennas into two dimensions, ignoring how signals spread upward and downward. The new framework derives formulas for interference, coverage chances, and data capacity per area while people and walls block paths. Comparing the two antenna views shows where simplified models mislead designers. Indoor terahertz links, the authors argue, must be planned with the full geometry of rooms and bodies in mind.
plos-pone-0351323:
Some long stretches of RNA do not build proteins but still steer cancer, and Lu Pu and colleagues hunted for such molecules tied to survival in cancer of the womb lining. Their 2026 PLOS One study combined two large public cohorts holding hundreds of tumors.

Hundreds of these RNAs ran higher or lower in tumors than in healthy tissue. Thirty tracked with how long patients lived. Two stood out as critical: tumors behaved differently depending on their levels, and the pair connected to pathways known in cancer growth. The authors propose them as candidate warning markers, while noting lab work must confirm what the molecules actually do.
plos-pone-0351423:
A lichen called Usnea cornuta has a long folk medicine history, and Deepa Karki and colleagues gave it a modern laboratory workup. Their 2026 PLOS One study measured the extract's chemistry and tested it against oxidation, bacteria, and a diabetes-linked enzyme.

The extract proved rich in phenolic compounds and strongly quenched harmful free radicals. One fraction blocked the starch-digesting enzyme at very low doses. Chemical profiling named eleven compounds; computer docking suggested one, menegazziaic acid, binds the enzyme best, with favorable simulated behavior. The extract also halted staph bacteria in dish tests. The authors present the lichen as a candidate source for antioxidant and blood-sugar research.
plos-pone-0351523:
Chidiebele Petronilla Ojukwu led a team of six authors asking parents about children's physical activity, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Parents largely decide whether children join sports and active play. The team explored parents' satisfaction with current activity, their view of school-based options, the barriers they face, and the fixes they prefer.

Ojukwu's findings show what keeps children on the couch from the parent's seat: cost, time, safety, and access all feature in such accounts. Schools planning activity programs gain a parent-tested list of what would actually raise uptake. Children's activity is falling in many countries, with lifelong health effects. Listening to parents is a cheap, often skipped step toward reversing that trend.
plos-pone-0351623:
Gianna Vivaldo and co-authors modelled spring flow in a limestone karst aquifer in northwestern Tuscany, Italy. Karst systems react fast to weather yet hide complex plumbing, which makes them hard to manage under climate change. Their 2026 framework blends regression models with frequency analysis over eighteen years of flow, rain, and temperature records.

Weather alone could not explain the spring's long-term swings. Adding the system's short memory, about five days of carry-over, improved the models sharply. Frequency analysis pulled out yearly and half-yearly cycles whose strength waxes and wanes. Vivaldo and colleagues package the approach as decision support for groundwater managers who must plan around a reactive, partly hidden resource.
plos-pone-0351723:
McCulloch and colleagues modeled a fruit fly pest of blueberries in southern Georgia in a 2026 study. The spotted-wing fly lays eggs in ripe soft fruit, so growers need to know when numbers will rise or fall. Their computer model combined heat patterns with the timing of farmed berries and wild host plants nearby.

The standard run matched the early summer drop seen in trap counts from three seasons. Later parts of the season were harder to match, which showed the limits of using heat and host timing alone. Wild hosts that fruit in fall and winter helped keep flies going between berry seasons. The work gives growers a starting tool, while making clear where better local data are needed.
plos-pone-0351923:
Xiao Chen and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One climate paper. It forecasts Pacific Ocean surface heat weeks to months ahead. That window ties to the El Niño cycle, which shapes weather worldwide. Their model first splits daily heat records into two parts. One part is a smooth, slow trend. The other is a fast-changing remainder. Each part gets a branch suited to it. A learned gate then blends the outputs.

Tested on daily data from five watch regions, the model beat several deep learning rivals. It won at most one-to-three-month ranges. It also won under every El Niño phase, from onset to decay. Simple baselines still won at very short ranges, which the authors admit. They propose the approach as a base for richer ocean forecasts.
plos-pone-0352023:
Xiaodong Zhu and four colleagues test simple blood ratios as crystal balls for the sickest liver patients. Their 2026 study mines a large American intensive care database. Over eighteen hundred adults with cirrhosis at their first intensive care admission were included. Four measures built from red cell distribution width were examined. That width reflects how uneven a patient's red blood cells are, and it rises with inflammation. Outcomes were death within thirty days, ninety days, and a year.

Mortality was grim. Nearly a third died within a month, and almost half within a year. The red cell measures were tested for association with those outcomes after adjustment. Their predictive accuracy was graded with standard curves. Cheap, routine blood values that genuinely forecast survival would help intensive care teams enormously. Cirrhosis crises force fast triage decisions; a marker already sitting in every admission blood panel costs nothing extra to read.
plos-pone-0352323:
Croft and colleagues studied traffic pollution and hospital stays for lung infections in a 2026 paper. Doctors carefully confirmed whether each of more than four hundred patients had a viral infection, a bacterial one, or both. Pollution from traffic, including fine particles and gases, was tracked for the three weeks before each stay.

Links between pollution and admission were checked week by week before illness. The design let the team ask whether germ types respond to dirty air in the same way or on different schedules. Clearer answers could sharpen air quality warnings for people prone to chest infections. The careful case review by four doctors makes the infection labels unusually trustworthy for this kind of study.
plos-pone-0352423:
Suzuki and colleagues, in a 2026 study, hunt for blood signals that warn a COVID-19 patient is about to get worse. Samples were taken from infected patients before any downturn, then read with several deep molecular methods at once, covering proteins, fats, and other small molecules. Known warning signs, including an inflammation marker and white cell counts, held up in the data.

Beyond those, the team found a fresh panel of molecules that shifted before symptoms of decline appeared, and the panel tracked closely with established clinical and immune measures. One pattern stood out: several inflammation markers moved opposite to certain interferon types, the body's early virus alarms. The authors read that as a fingerprint of how this coronavirus muffles the alarm while inflammation builds. They present the panel as groundwork for early-warning tests and for research on the next pandemic virus.
plos-pone-0353123:
Ravneet Kaur and seven colleagues describe this 2026 PLOS One protocol for a pilot trial of a diet app for people with inflammatory bowel disease. The app, built together with patients, guides an anti-inflammatory diet and tracks eating. Forty patients at one center will be randomly assigned to use the app or receive usual care for sixty days, with the usual-care group crossing over halfway.

Because this is a protocol, it sets out measures rather than results. The main question is whether patients find the app usable and acceptable, judged by questionnaires and interviews. Secondary measures cover diet quality, urine markers of processed food intake, disease activity, quality of life, and stool and blood chemistry. The pilot will shape a larger trial and a template for judging diet apps in this disease.
plos-pone-0353423:
Salley and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a pilot study of a program called Talk With Me Baby, built into routine baby checkups. The words and back-and-forth talk a baby hears at home shape later school, health, and earning outcomes. The program coaches caregivers to talk more richly with their babies, but it had not been tested closely in rural or under-served clinics.

At least sixty-six caregiver and baby pairs will be recruited from two primary care clinics, starting when babies are two to six months old. Every family gets the coaching during regular checkups across a year. Before and after, the team will measure the home language setting with a recording tool that counts adult words and the turns of talk between adult and child. The pilot will show whether the program shifts caregiver talk in these clinics and will guide a larger trial.
plos-pone-0353523:
Lun Shen and seven colleagues published this 2026 study of artery plaque growth in the neck, a major stroke risk. Working from public gene data on plaque tissue, they hunted for genes tied to natural killer immune cells that track with worsening plaque, then checked the lead gene in single-cell data.

One gene, IGHG1, came out as the sole independent risk marker, and its levels ran higher in advanced plaques. It sat in pathways for immune attack and T cell signaling. Shen cautions that the gene usually belongs to antibody-making cells, so pinning down its true source needs more lab work.
plos-pone-0353723:
Gaurav Prakash, a single author, published this 2026 modeling paper proposing an earlier way to catch disease. Standard diagnostics wait for a measurement to cross a fixed line, yet illness often starts drifting earlier. Prakash models two meaningful measurements as a plane, then tracks whether a patient's values drift in the direction of disease, using synthetic data built from published trends.

His drift score flagged the pre-threshold group with patterns resembling early disease, even while single values still looked normal. Prakash presents the readable, unit-free metric as an idea needing real patient data before clinical claims.
plos-pone-0354123:
Hao Liu led a team of seven authors on this 2026 remote sensing study of benggang, a dramatic gully erosion form eating hillsides in southern China. Surface maps alone cannot show sinking or swelling ground. The team paired deep learning on sharp satellite photos with radar interferometry from ninety satellite passes over Wuhua County.

The photo model outlined eroded areas accurately, and the radar work resolved vertical movement of mere millimeters of movement per year into a smooth and continuous deformation map. Liu offers the combined watch as an early warning tool for geohazards.
plos-pone-0354423:
Kim and Cho, in a 2026 survey study, link poor sleep satisfaction to problem smartphone use among teenagers in South Korea. Heavy, hard-to-control phone use affects a sizable share of teens worldwide, and poor sleep is a suspected driver. The team asked whether anxiety and loneliness carry part of that effect.

Data came from nearly fifty thousand adolescents, sorted into general, at-risk, and high-risk users. High-risk teens used phones far longer each day and reported more anxiety and loneliness, as well as worse perceived health. Being female, long daily use, and low physical activity also tracked with risk. Tracing the pathways, the authors estimate anxiety carried about three tenths of the link between poor sleep and problem use, and loneliness about a sixth. They suggest that better sleep and support for anxious or lonely teens may cut problem use more than phone rules alone.
plos-pone-0354523:
Mehmet Emin Aksoy led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of how people learn basic life support, the emergency skills behind CPR. Trainees learned through lectures, a tablet game, or a virtual reality game, while a wearable head sensor tracked activity at the front of the brain during practice and testing.

Game-based practice engaged learners differently from lectures, and the virtual reality group showed brain patterns suggesting thriftier use of mental effort during the hands-on test. Aksoy argues training should be judged by brain measures as well as test scores when schools pick a format.
plos-pone-0354723:
Iris Pit and co-authors audited Europe's monitoring records for freshwater invertebrates, the small animals that signal river health. Rivers and lakes hold a rich share of species but face pollution, water extraction, and habitat loss. Their 2026 study gathered millions of records from twenty-eight countries for the early twenty-tens.

Records clustered in central Europe and England, leaving other regions and river types thin. Countries differed in sampling methods, reporting units, and how finely species were named. Those differences block clean Europe-wide trend estimates. Pit and colleagues argue that shared standards for naming and methods, plus better data exchange, are needed before biodiversity trends can be judged fairly across the continent.
plos-pone-0354823:
Xinyu Tian and co-authors developed a structured support programme for family caregivers of autistic children in China. Caregivers carry heavy, many-sided strain that can harm their health and the child's progress. Earlier structured programmes for this exact burden were scarce. Their 2026 development study blended family stress theory with evidence review and the team's own prior findings.

Expert panels refined the draft over two consultation rounds. The finished programme has three core modules covering stressors, how caregivers appraise them, and coping. Davydov, Goode, Sirota, and co-authors present GERP++, a method for finding parts of the human genome under selective constraint. Parts of DNA that stayed nearly unchanged across species are likely to do important jobs. Computer methods hunt for those conserved regions using comparative sequence data.

GERP++ computes constraint scores position by position, following a bottom-up approach. The team reports that a high fraction of the human genome shows such constraint. Those maps point researchers toward functional elements hidden outside protein-coding genes, including switches that control development and disease.  Conserved stretches also guide the search for harmful variants in patient genomes today.
pmc-3270023:
Salzman, Gawad, Wang, and co-authors report that circular RNAs are the main transcript form from hundreds of human genes. Most human gene transcripts are spliced into linear molecules that keep the genome's exon order. Deep RNA sequencing of normal and malignant human cells told a different story.

The team found transcripts from many genes in which the exons were joined in scrambled order, forming circles. Such circles turned out to be the predominant form for hundreds of genes across diverse cell types. The finding revealed a whole class of RNA whose roles researchers are still unravelling.
pmc-3326523:
Filippakopoulos, Picaud, Mangos, and co-authors analyse the human bromodomain family, a set of protein modules that read epigenetic marks. Bromodomains recognise a specific chemical tag on lysine, a key event in reading marks that control gene activity. The human genome holds dozens of them, grouped into eight families.

The team presents recognition studies and a large-scale structural analysis across the family. Comparing shapes reveals which members might be druggable. Their map guided drug hunters toward bromodomain blockers, a class since explored in cancer and inflammation.  Crystal structures in the paper gave chemists concrete pockets to aim compounds at.

Masella, Bartram, Truszkowski, and co-authors present PANDAseq, a tool for assembling paired-end Illumina reads. Researchers analyse microbial communities with paired-end reads, targeting pieces of the 16S rRNA gene. Public tools were needed to overlap and merge read pairs while fixing errors.

Many mismatches and uncalled bases can be corrected when the two reads overlap, yielding longer, cleaner sequences. PANDAseq performs that assembly efficiently for large datasets. Evans and Murshudov explain how to judge data quality and resolution in crystal work. Their paper sets out the new scaling program AIMLESS, which merges repeated diffraction readings into one dataset. Tests of refinement at different detail levels are checked against analyses from the scaling step itself.

Resolution decides how much detail a crystal structure can honestly claim. Overstating it builds false detail into models; understating it wastes good data. Sheldrick described crystal structure refinement with SHELXL in a 2015 paper. Refinement is the step where an initial crystal structure model is adjusted to fit the measured data as closely as possible. SHELXL is one of the most used programs for that task worldwide.

Its growth was closely tied to the CIF format, the standard framework for checking and storing crystal structures. Recent changes simplified key steps while keeping the program's power for hard cases. Good refinement is what turns raw diffraction into a structure others can trust and reuse. The paper serves as a guide for crystallographers who rely on the program daily.

When the methods agree, a causal claim gains strength; when they clash, the user gets a warning. Free shared tools like this raised the standard of work in the field and made results easier to check.
