Working in embryonic stem cells, the team found SMARCAD1 enriched at these viral relics. When its enzyme activity was lost, the retroviruses woke up and nearby genes were disturbed. The result names a guardian that keeps ancient viral DNA quiet during early development. It adds a layer to how stem cells protect their genomes.
pmc-6651423:
Nathan Kelley, Devon Jeltema, and Yanhui Duan gave an overview of the NLRP3 inflammasome in 2019. This protein machine is a core part of innate immunity. It switches on an enzyme that releases two powerful inflammatory signals.

The review explains the two-step process: a priming signal, then a trigger from infection or cell damage. When control fails, the machine drives diseases from gout to Alzheimer disease. Blockers are in development for several of them. New readers get the activation logic, the regulators, and the disease list in one organized account.
pmc-6769923:
Luca Pinzi and Giulio Rastelli reviewed molecular docking in drug discovery in 2019. Docking predicts how a small molecule fits into a protein's binding pocket. It is a core computer method for finding new drug candidates.

The review traces how docking grew from rigid fitting to flexible, physics-aware scoring. It covers screening huge libraries, refining hits, and reading structure-activity patterns. Limits are plain too, since scores remain rough guides, not proof. Medicinal chemists read it for a balanced view of where the method shines and where experiments must decide. Case examples from real drug projects show where docking scores matched later experiments and where they failed.
price-new-geology-1923:
In 1923 George McCready Price published a geology textbook with a startling claim at its center. Price argued that the earth is young and that Noah's Flood, not slow change over ages, shaped the rock layers. He wrote against the view, then held by most geologists, that the same slow forces still at work today explain the past.

Price lays out his case layer by layer, reading fossils and strata as records left by one great flood. Later writers on creation and the Flood built on his scheme, which is why the book is often called the founding text of flood geology. It also shows the sharp clash between faith and science in its day.
principle-of-relativity-1923:
Methuen issued The Principle of Relativity in 1923, in W. Perrett and G. B. Jeffery's translation. Inside stand the primary papers of relativity by its makers. H. A. Lorentz and Albert Einstein represent the theory's first steps. H. Minkowski contributes Space and Time, his famed address on the new geometry of physics.

H. Weyl's Gravitation and Electricity carries the story into general relativity. Notes by Arnold Sommerfeld help readers through the hard parts. The volume let English readers study the sources, not just summaries. It fixed the canon of early relativity in one binding. Students still use it to meet the founders directly. Few source books match its lineup.
proudhon-general-idea-revolution-robinso:
John Beverley Robinson published his translation of Proudhon's General Idea of the Revolution in the Nineteenth Century in 1923. Proudhon wrote the work in 1851, from a French prison cell, as Louis Napoleon tightened his grip. It is his fullest plan for a free society.

Proudhon proposed ending rule by the state and letting work and trade run by free pact. He called for free credit, shared banks, and loose unions of towns and workshops. Robinson, an American writer, kept the case clear in English. The book links Proudhon's early attack on property to the shared, local plans that later rebels took up across Europe.
radin-the-winnebago-tribe-1923:
Radin's great monograph on the Winnebago, now called Ho-Chunk, appeared in 1923 in the annual report of the Bureau of American Ethnology. It was the fullest statement of his years of fieldwork with the tribe in Wisconsin and Nebraska.

The study centers on the medicine rite, a major ceremony taught in secret and passed down at great cost. Radin also describes the night-spirits society and prints autobiographies of native thinkers in their own words. His method treated Winnebago men as authors, not just informants. The monograph remains a foundation for the study of Native American religion.
rasaprakasasudhakara-1923-1923: Rasaprakasasudhakara, 1923. The Sanskrit alchemical text. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it.
rattray-ashanti-1923:
Robert Sutherland Rattray wrote Ashanti in 1923, the foundational ethnography of the Ashanti people of the Gold Coast. Rattray served as the colonial government's own anthropologist in what is now Ghana, recording law and religion at first hand for years. The Golden Stool, soul of the nation, abusua kinship, gods, shrines, and courts fill his account.

Ashanti priests, queen mothers, and elders speak through his pages, explaining custom in their own terms to the reader. Rattray's respect for his sources and his care with their words made the book a model of its kind. A century on, Ashanti remains a first source for the kingdom's religion, law, and social order.
richet-thirty-years-psychical-research-1:
Charles Richet looks back on a life's hunt in Thirty Years of Psychical Research, his book of 1923. Richet had won the top prize in the science of the body. He gave the field its French name, metapsychics. Here he sums three decades of sittings, tests, and famed seers from his own notes and the work of peers he trusts.

He grants fraud in bulk, yet holds a strange core stands firm. His calm, grave tone gives the claim weight. The book is the field's own tale of its first age. No sum since skips it.
robson-fixed-stars-and-constellations-19:
Vivian Robson was a British astrologer and librarian whose Fixed Stars and Constellations in Astrology appeared in 1923. The book gathers the lore of the fixed stars, the bright stars beyond the planets, into one compendium. It became the standard modern reference for stellar astrology.

Robson lists each star's position, nature, and reputed effects on health, fortune, and character, drawn from Ptolemy and the long tradition after him. He sorts a scattered inheritance of Greek, Arab, and modern claims into usable order. Astrologers still reach for Robson first when a chart raises a question about the fixed stars.
rowlands-mona-antiqua-restaurata-1723:
Henry Rowlands, a priest on the isle of Anglesey in Wales, wrote this study of the isle's old remains, first printed in 1723. The text here is from the 1766 second edition. Anglesey, called Mona in Latin, is rich in stone works from deep time.

Rowlands read the stone rings and tombs of Mona as druid shrines and graves. He built the first druid based view of the isle's past from its own ground. His scheme taught readers to see great stones as temples, a view that held for years. His maps and plates of the sites still have worth today.
saadi-gulistan-ross-1823:
James Ross published his translation of Saadi's Gulistan in 1823, the first English version of the most famous Persian prose classic. This text follows the 1890 Camelot reprint of Ross's work. Saadi wrote the Gulistan, meaning The Rose Garden, in 1258, after years of travel.

Eight chapters of short tales and verses treat kings, dervishes, lovers, and schoolboys with equal wit. A story may end in a laugh, a proverb, or a sudden sting of moral judgment. Persian speakers have memorized its lines for seven centuries, and Ross first opened that garden to English readers. Its humor keeps the moral lessons from ever feeling heavy.
santayana-scepticism-animal-faith-1923:
George Santayana published Scepticism and Animal Faith in 1923, the start of his mature system. Santayana pushes doubt to its limit, questioning even memory and the past. What survives is animal faith: the body's trust that a world exists and can be known in part. Knowledge, he says, is faith mediated by symbols.

He distinguishes essences, the pure characters of things, from matter and truth. The book is a modern classic of epistemology, the study of knowledge. Santayana's wit and calm style carry hard arguments lightly. Later volumes built the full system of The Realms of Being. This first volume can stand alone.
shaker-summary-view-1823:
Calvin Green and Seth Y. Wells wrote A Summary View of the Millennial Church in 1823. The work gives the first official account of Shaker faith. The United Society of Believers speaks here in its own voice.

Mother Ann Lee, the sect's founder, stands at the account's heart. Celibacy, shared goods, and the dance of worship mark Shaker life. The authors write at the height of their society's growth and fame. Their calm self-portrait explains a faith many outsiders found strange. Readers meet American communal religion drawn by its own leading hands. The book also serves historians as the Shakers' own yardstick of belief.
shakespeare-complete-works-1623:
William Shakespeare's plays and poems fill this complete works text, drawn from the First Folio canon of 1623. Fellow actors saved the plays in that folio seven years after his death. Project Gutenberg's standard text makes the whole set easy to search and read.

Inside are the great tragedies, the comedies, the histories, and the late romances. Hamlet, Macbeth, Lear, Falstaff, and Rosalind all speak in these pages. Sonnets and long poems sit beside the plays in one vast store. No single book in English holds so much of the tongue. Teachers reach for it for almost any age of English.
shakespeare-macbeth-1623:
William Shakespeare's Macbeth first reached print in the First Folio of 1623. The short, fierce tragedy tracks ambition and guilt in old Scotland. Three witches hail Macbeth as a future king and plant a dark seed.

Macbeth and his wife murder King Duncan to seize the throne. Guilt dogs them both, in sleepless nights and a spot of imagined blood. More murders follow, and Birnam Wood comes at last to Dunsinane. The play shows how a brave man can rot from one foul choice. Stage and screen return to its witches and daggers on stages yearly, in every land and tongue.
shakespeare-the-tempest-1623:
William Shakespeare's The Tempest first reached print in the First Folio of 1623. Most readers take it as his last solo play. Prospero, a duke turned mage, rules a lone island with his daughter Miranda.

A storm Prospero raises wrecks his old foes' ship on his shore. His sprite Ariel and the wild Caliban serve and chafe under his rule. Young Ferdinand and Miranda fall in love at first sight on the beach. Prospero tests them, forgives his foes, and gives up his magic staff. The play blends wonder, mercy, and a fond farewell to art.
shaw-saint-joan-1923:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Saint Joan in 1923, soon after the Catholic Church made Joan of Arc a saint. Shaw, then in his sixties, treated Joan not as a plaster saint but as a practical, stubborn genius. He called the play a chronicle play in six scenes and an epilogue.

The action follows Joan from Domrémy, where her voices send her to the French court, through her victories and capture. Church and state join to try her for heresy, and she is burned at the stake. An epilogue set years later shows her judges regretting their work. Shaw argues that institutions destroy the very saints they later honor.
sinclair-uncanny-stories-1923:
May Sinclair brought new thought on the mind to the ghost tale in Uncanny Stories, her set from 1923. She knew the work of Freud and his peers well. Her ghosts grow from guilt, grief, and wants long held down in the self.

Lovers parted by death meet in odd ways. A man's past sins take shape and dog him. Sinclair asks if the shade is real or a trick of a hurt mind. She leaves both doors ajar. The set marks a new, sharp turn for the old ghost tale. Sinclair helped found a clinic for mind care in London in her day. That work gave her tales a depth few ghost scribes could match.
spr-proceedings-vol33-1923:
Parts eighty five through eighty eight form volume thirty three, printed in 1923. The Society for Psychical Research spreads four parts across this single year. Telepathy experiments continue, now a tradition with its own classics. Reports on trance sittings take the largest share, as they long had.

Investigators compare new mediums against the great Piper record. Apparition cases, each with its witnesses and documents, keep their place. The society prints criticism from members who doubt the whole enterprise. Volume thirty three shows the archive in its last full decade. The debate of 1882 to 1930 nears its close here. Its files outlasted every verdict offered on them.
stevens-harmonium-1923:
Wallace Stevens published Harmonium in 1923, his first book of poems. Stevens was an insurance executive in Hartford who wrote poetry on the side. The poems play with lush language, strange images, and bright wit. Sunday Morning, The Emperor of Ice-Cream, and Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird are among them.

Stevens pits imagination against plain reality and finds joy on the side of imagination. Florida scenes, music, and food recur in sensuous detail. The book sold poorly at first and Stevens wrote little for years. Later readers raised it to classic status. It remains a dazzling start to a major poetic career.
the-phrenological-journal-and-miscellany: The Phrenological Journal and Miscellany, 1823. The Edinburgh journal. This book preserves that periodical. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. The archive guards it with care.
thelma-pg3823: Marie Corelli's Thelma is a tender romance of Norway. An English gentleman loves a pure Norwegian maiden amid fjords and snow. The bestselling novel enchanted millions of readers. Passion in the land of the midnight sun.
tob-0123:
William Reed argued in The Phantom of the Poles, published in 1906, that the earth is hollow and open at both poles. Explorers' reports of open water, warm winds, and birds flying north past the ice became his proof. Beyond the rim, he claimed, lies a warm inner world.

Reed answered objections with care and built his case like a lawyer. Later writers on the hollow earth treated his book as their bible. Science has long settled the matter against him: ships and planes have crossed both poles. The book survives as the most argued, and most enjoyable, statement of a lost theory.
tob-10623:
Ancient Egyptian priests carved the Book of Gates on tomb walls in the New Kingdom, the age of Egypt's empire. It maps the night voyage of the sun god Ra through the underworld. Tomb scenes pair its text with rich pictures of gods and beings.

Ra's boat passes twelve gates, one for each hour of night, each guarded by beings he must name and pass. Along the way the dead are judged and foes of order are punished, until the sun rises renewed. Alongside the Book of the Dead, it is a chief source for how Egyptians pictured the afterlife.
tob-10823:
H. P. Blavatsky edited Lucifer, a Theosophical magazine whose provocative title meant light-bringer, not the devil of popular fear. Volume one gathers the movement's monthly output at its combative start. Essays on occult philosophy, Eastern religion, and the hidden side of science fill its pages.

Readers watch Theosophy talking to itself and to its critics month by month: manifestos, reviews, correspondence, and defenses of unpopular ideas. A magazine preserves what books smooth over, including fashions, quarrels, and enthusiasms of a young movement. For historians of modern occultism, the first volume of Lucifer is primary evidence of how Blavatsky presented her cause to the Victorian public.
tob-11023:
Vatsyayana composed the Kama Sutra in ancient India as a guide to kama, pleasure, one of the proper aims of life. Shivaram Parashuram Bhide's translation presents the full Sanskrit work in English. Most people know its fame as a book about love, but its range is far wider.

Large parts treat gracious living: how to furnish a home, arrange a day, choose friends, and manage a household. Other parts cover courtship, marriage, and the conduct expected of lovers. Vatsyayana treats pleasure with system and frank good sense, as a skill to be learned like any art.
tob-11123:
Readers who open Bhide's translation of Vatsyayana's Kama Sutra often meet a duplicate copy of the classic held elsewhere in the library. The Sanskrit original dates from ancient India and treats pleasure as a rightful aim of human life, alongside duty and gain. Its fame rests on candor, but its method is orderly.

Section by section it covers the arts of living well, from music and games to courtship and marriage customs. It advises on household harmony and on the duties partners owe each other. Behind the notorious reputation stands a serious, humane attempt to describe how love fits into a well-run life.
tob-13323:
William Benham's English version of Thomas a Kempis carried the Imitation of Christ to generations of readers. Kempis, a fifteenth-century monk, wrote for people who wanted a serious inner life without leaving the world behind. His four books are built from short chapters meant for daily reading.

The counsel is steady: prize humility, distrust praise, bear wrongs patiently, and turn the heart toward Christ. Later chapters prepare the reader for Communion with unusual warmth. Churches and empires have risen and fallen since Kempis wrote, yet his quiet voice still finds readers who open the book a page at a time.
tob-4023:
Voltaire published Candide in 1759, dragging his cheerful hero through war, earthquake, plague, and the Inquisition. Candide has been taught by Dr. Pangloss that this is the best of all possible worlds and all is for the best. Reality disagrees, repeatedly and violently, across three continents and a parade of disasters.

Pangloss keeps theorizing; companions keep suffering, dying, and occasionally returning from apparent death to suffer again. Voltaire aims his satire at optimistic philosophy, religious cruelty, and war's glory alike. The little book ends in a garden with its famous practical conclusion: we must cultivate our garden. Few novels so funny are so angry underneath.
tob-4123:
Volume eight of the Sacred Books of the East, in Kashinath Trimbak Telang's 1882 translation, prints the Bhagavad-Gita with two companions from the Mahabharata. The Sanatsugatiya and the Anugita both return to the Gita's themes in plainer teaching form. Telang equips the three with notes and a learned introduction.

Krishna's battlefield counsel needs no summary here; the value lies in the company it keeps. The companion texts show how the epic itself pondered action, duty, and release long after the war. Vedanta students gain the Gita with its native context restored. Verified from the 1919 edition, the volume serves study better than devotion alone.
tob-4223:
Agrippa's Three Books of Occult Philosophy return in a modern annotated translation, checked from the 1919 edition record. The 1533 original organized magic into natural, celestial, and ceremonial books. Annotations in this version guide today's readers through names, sources, and rites that Agrippa left bare.

Readers meet the full Renaissance system: herbs and stones with virtues, numbers and stars with powers, spirits with ranks and seals. The notes separate Agrippa's text from later editors' growth. For students who find the old English hard going, the annotated form offers the magus made newly accessible, without trimming his system down.
toomer-cane-1923:
Jean Toomer published Cane in 1923, mixing short stories, poems, and a short play in one book. The first part is set in rural Georgia, among cane fields and small towns. Later parts move to Washington and Chicago. Black life in the South and the North stands at the center throughout.

Many pieces follow young women and men caught between love, work, and loss. The writing is brief, musical, and full of sharp images of land and sky. Cane won praise at the time and later became a key work of the Harlem Renaissance. It still shapes how writers blend forms to tell a shared story.
torreblanca-daemonologia-1623:
Francisco Torreblanca Villalpando was a Spanish jurist whose Daemonologia appeared in 1623. Its full Latin title promises a treatise on magic natural, demonic, licit, and illicit, sorted into kinds. Torreblanca wrote for a Spain where the Inquisition watched occult practice closely.

He divides wonders into those God allows, those nature hides, and those demons fake, and assigns each its lawful response. His care in sorting licit natural magic from forbidden demonic arts shows the period's legal mind at its sharpest. The book is a prime source for Spanish demonology in the age of the great trials.
torreblanca-daemonologia-latin-1623:
Francisco Torreblanca Villalpando, a Spanish jurist, published his Daemonologia in Latin in 1623. Four books treat magic in its kinds: natural, demonic, licit, and illicit. The work is the Spanish law's systematic word on the devil and his works, late in the great age of demonology.

Torreblanca sorts spells and wonders by their causes and their legality. A judge's habits rule the whole: define, divide, decide. Spanish inquisitors and courts could consult him on hard cases. His demonology is complete and orderly rather than sensational. It shows Spanish legal thought giving the subject its last full system before the long skepticism set in.
un-ga-res-23:
Treaties should be on the public record, and Resolution 23 of the General Assembly built that rule for the new United Nations in February 1946. Under Article 102 of the Charter, treaties would now be filed with the UN and printed by it. A stopgap plan had run since the Charter took force. Deals were filed for the time being. States were asked to send in recent deals left out of the League of Nations treaty books.

The text then looks to states outside the UN. It finds it a matter of plain use that deals sent in freely by non-members should also be printed, where the League books lack them. Out of such house rules grew the UN Treaty Series, still the chief public shelf of world pacts.
un-ga-res-56-223:
Guatemala's peace was six years old, and still thin, when the General Assembly passed Resolution 56/223 in December 2001. The Verification Mission in Guatemala had its term stretched through 2001 by a vote of the year before. The state had restated its pledge to put the peace deals into full force. Yet core parts of those deals, the text stresses, still waited to be done.

A fresh timetable for the work, to run through 2004, had been agreed by the follow-up team. Both sides had asked the UN to back the firming of peace to 2003. The mission's twelfth report on human rights is weighed. So is the truth report of the Commission for Historical Clarification, which had laid the war's crimes on the record.
un-ga-res-a-69-23:
A just peace for Palestine is urged in Resolution A/69/23, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the core votes of the conflict: partition in 1947, and the Security Council texts of 1967 and 1973. It notes, with worry, two grim counts. Sixty-seven years had passed since partition. Forty-seven years had passed since Israel took the Palestinian land in 1967.

The fixed duty of the UN toward the question of Palestine is stated again. The two-state vision, backed by the Security Council, frames the goal: Israel and Palestine side by side, in peace, within safe and known borders. The Secretary-General's report on the last vote is weighed. The record's catalog year of 1967 is the year of the taking, not of this vote.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 23, adopted on 10 February 1946 at the twenty-eighth plenary meeting, set up the filing and printing of treaties under Article 102 of the Charter. Members had already been sending in recent treaties not found in the League of Nations series, and the Assembly now ordered lasting rules for the work.

The Secretary-General was told to draft detailed regulations. He was told to invite members to send in their pre-Charter treaties for filing and printing. He was to register new ones as they came. Non-member states could also send treaties in by choice. But the text bars that path for Spain, whose government the Assembly viewed as born of Axis support.

Resolution 56/223, adopted by the General Assembly on 24 December 2001, renews the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala for another year of overseeing the peace accords. The decision rests on the mission's most recent verification report and on updates from the Secretary-General and Guatemala's peace structures.

The mission is extended through 31 December 2002, and the Secretary-General is asked to report on the mission's future beyond that date. Because an agreed timetable for finishing the peace process ran to the end of 2004, the Assembly treated continued verification as part of that schedule rather than an open-ended stay. The renewal kept international witnesses in place while Guatemala worked through the last stages of its postwar settlement.

General Assembly resolution 69/23 (2014), 'Peaceful settlement of the question of Palestine,' is the Assembly's comprehensive annual statement on the conflict. It notes that 67 years had passed since the 1947 partition resolution. It notes that 47 years had passed since the 1967 occupation began. It reaffirms the United Nations' permanent responsibility for the question.

The resolution restates the Assembly's positions. Israeli settlements and the separation wall in the occupied territory are illegal. Territory cannot be acquired by war. A settlement must rest on the two-State solution, the Madrid terms of reference, the Arab Peace Initiative, and the Quartet road map. It deplores the July–August 2014 Gaza conflict and its heavy civilian toll. It calls for a durable cease-fire and open crossings. It urges renewed international effort toward a final peace treaty. The text functions as the Assembly's standing brief on the conflict's legal and political terms.
un-sc-res-1023: For the year 1995, the catalog lists Resolution 1023 among the Security Council's formal decisions. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-123:
Resolution 123, adopted on 21 February 1957, concerns the dispute between India and Pakistan, the long-running question that included the status of Kashmir. The vote was ten to none, with the Soviet Union abstaining. The Council recalls its earlier resolutions on the question and those of the UN Commission for India and Pakistan.

The Council asks its President, the representative of Sweden, to meet with the governments of India and Pakistan and test any proposals that might help settle the dispute. He is to visit the subcontinent for this purpose and report back by 15 April 1957. India and Pakistan are invited to work with him, and UN staff are told to give him the help he asks for.
un-sc-res-1323:
War in the Democratic Republic of the Congo had slowed but not stopped by late 2000. On 13 October 2000 the Security Council extended MONUC, its mission in the Congo. The Council restated the sovereignty and independence of the Congo. It deplored the fighting that still went on. It also noted the lack of cooperation with the United Nations.

The extension ran only until 15 December 2000. The Secretary-General's latest report guided the choice of that short term. The Council voiced deep concern about suffering and rights abuses. It also condemned the illegal taking of the Congo's natural resources. The mission's future would depend on real progress toward peace.
un-sc-res-1423:
With Resolution 1423, adopted on 12 July 2002, the Council turned to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The vote came late, after a dispute over shielding peacekeepers from the new International Criminal Court. A separate vote that day settled that dispute. The NATO-led Stabilisation Force, SFOR, still guarded the Dayton peace.

The text extends the United Nations Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina until 31 December 2002. That mission ran the International Police Task Force. States in SFOR may keep the force in place for twelve more months under one command. SFOR may use all needed means to enforce the military side of the peace deal and to defend itself.
un-sc-res-1523:
Western Sahara opened the Council's peacekeeping year in 2004. On 30 January 2004 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 30 April 2004. It recalled the peace plan it had backed in July 2003. The Secretary-General had to report before the mandate ended. The Council stayed seized of the matter. The text is brief and follows the mission's usual renewal form.

Even so, the renewal mattered on the ground. MINURSO's observers kept watch over the ceasefire line. Its staff kept the referendum plan on file for a vote that never came. Each extension signaled that the Council had not given up on a settlement. The dispute between Morocco and the Polisario Front remained frozen.
un-sc-res-1623:
Afghanistan's security force was renewed for a year on 13 September 2005. The Council restated its line of texts from 1386 (2001) onward. Kabul's government worked with the International Security Assistance Force while holding prime duty for the country's safety. Extending central rule, disarming fighters, and fighting the narcotics trade all remained unfinished tasks. The Bonn Agreement's plan for the force to grow beyond Kabul still guided the work.

The Council extended the force's authorization for twelve months beyond 13 October 2005. The states serving in it were authorized to take all necessary measures to carry out its mandate. The need to strengthen the force was recognized, and its work with the Afghan army and police was backed. The force's leadership had to report to the Council each quarter through the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-1723:
The Council's vote on 28 November 2006 produced Resolution 1723 on Iraq. A national unity government had formed that May. Iraqi forces had taken charge of security in two southern provinces. The prime minister asked in writing for foreign troops to stay another year.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the multinational force mandate until 31 December 2007. The force stays at Iraq's request and can be ended early if Baghdad asks. A review is due by mid-June 2007. The oil-revenue fund and its outside monitors get the same extension. The text backs national reconciliation and urges armed groups to join politics instead.
un-sc-res-1823:
Rwanda's remaining arms restrictions were ended by the Security Council on 10 July 2008. The Rwanda sanctions committee had reported at the end of 2007, and its chairman briefed the Council in May 2008. Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo had signed the Nairobi communiqué in November 2007. A peace conference for the Kivu provinces had met at Goma in January 2008.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminated the prohibitions set by paragraphs 9 and 10 of resolution 1011 (1995). Those clauses had required notice of arms deliveries to Rwanda and barred supply to non-government forces. The Council also dissolved the committee created by resolution 918 (1994) on Rwanda. It stressed that states in the region still had to work with the Congo sanctions committee and its experts. Arms delivered in the region, it warned, must not be diverted to illegal armed groups.
un-sc-res-1923:
Chad and the Central African Republic are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1923, adopted on 25 May 2010. Chad's government had asked the United Nations mission to leave. A January deal had warmed ties between Chad and Sudan, with a joint border force deployed. Chad pledged to take over guarding civilians in its east.

The Council extends the mission, called MINURCAT, one last time, until 31 December 2010. Its troops fall to 2,200, and all staff must be out by year's end. Early withdrawals start by 15 July, with the final pull-out from 15 October. Until then the mission trains the camp police unit and may still answer direct threats to civilians nearby.
un-sc-res-2023:
Resolution 2023 on Eritrea was adopted on 5 December 2011. Monitors found that Eritrea still funded and trained armed groups, including Al-Shabaab. A planned bomb attack on an African Union summit in Addis Ababa was also laid at its door. Qatar had placed observers on the Djibouti border, and Eritrea had pulled back there.

The Council condemns the breaches of its earlier sanctions. It orders Eritrea to stop taxing its overseas citizens by threats and fraud to fund armed groups. Firms in Eritrea's mining sector must take care that their money does not fuel abuses. Targeted sanctions may follow for those who meet the listing tests. States must report within 120 days on the steps they take.
un-sc-res-23: A United Nations commission was studying clashes on Greece's northern borders in 1947. On 18 April 1947 the Security Council decided to keep a smaller team in the area. The subsidiary group would have one member from each state on the commission. It would carry out the tasks the commission set for it. The arrangement lasted until the Council decided otherwise. The one-paragraph text kept eyes on a tense frontier in the early Cold War.
un-sc-res-323:
Namibia's own voice carried the Council's argument on 6 December 1972. The Secretary-General's representative had consulted the territory's people under resolution 319 (1972). Their views, heard inside Namibia, ran strongly one way. South Africa still gave no clear answer on self-determination for the territory. The World Court's 1971 opinion had declared its presence illegal.

The Council noted with satisfaction that Namibians had spoken clearly in their own land. Most of those asked wanted the homelands policy ended at once. They wanted the South African administration out, national independence, and the territory kept whole. The Council solemnly restated the Namibian people's right to self-determination, independence, and territorial integrity. Any plan for Namibia had to rest on that right. The Secretary-General was invited to press his efforts in close consultation, and South Africa was called again to cooperate fully with him.
un-sc-res-423: Holding number 423 in the Council series, this resolution carries a 1978 date in the library catalog. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1023, adopted unanimously on 22 November 1995, responds to the Basic Agreement on Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Sirmium. The agreement was signed ten days earlier by the Government of Croatia and local Serb representatives. The Council repeats that these territories, known as Sector East, are integral parts of Croatia.

The Council welcomes the agreement. It notes that it asks the United Nations to establish a transitional administration. It asks it to authorize an appropriate international force for the region. It says it stands ready to consider that request quickly. It asks the Secretary-General to stay in close contact with all concerned. It stresses that both sides must cooperate fully. They must avoid military activity. They must guarantee the safety and freedom of movement of the UNCRO peacekeeping operation.

Security Council resolution 123, adopted on 21 February 1957 by 10 votes to none, with 1 abstention, turns again to the India-Pakistan question, the dispute over Kashmir. It asks the President of the Council, then the representative of Sweden, to examine with the two governments any proposals likely to help settle the dispute. He is to visit the subcontinent for that purpose, and report back by 15 April 1957. India and Pakistan are invited to cooperate with him.

Congo's UN mission gained two more months in the autumn of 2000. On 13 October, the Council adopted Resolution 1323. Fighting in the Second Congo War still raged. The parties showed little will to work with the UN. The peace dialogue had stalled as well. Reports told of the country's wealth being looted.

One short clause does the work of the text. It extends the mandate of MONUC to 15 December 2000. The mission backed the Lusaka peace process on the ground. The short bridge kept a small force alive. The Council weighed a bigger deployment at the same time. That larger force came the next year, as the war's fronts froze.

Bosnia's peace process is renewed on two tracks by Resolution 1423, adopted on 12 July 2002. The Dayton Peace Agreement was being implemented, a new High Representative had arrived in May, and Bosnia had just joined the Council of Europe. Refugee returns remained crucial. The UN Mission, UNMIBH, was nearing its end, with an EU Police Mission set to take over on 1 January 2003.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes the multinational stabilization force, SFOR, for a further planned 12 months. The force has power to enforce the military annexes of the peace deal and control Bosnian airspace. It extends UNMIBH, including the International Police Task Force, to 31 December 2002 as its final period. It restates full support for the High Representative's authority, including binding decisions, and reminds the parties that continued support depends on their compliance, above all with the Yugoslavia tribunal.

Morocco's pushback against the peace plan hangs over this text of 2004. On 30 January, the Council adopted Resolution 1523 without dissent. It recalls the Council's past Sahara texts. Resolution 1495 of July 2003 stands out among them. That text backed the envoy's plan as the best political path.

The mandate of MINURSO now runs to 30 April 2004. A report from the Secretary-General is due before that term ends. By early 2004, the plan had stalled in place. Morocco balked at its vote clauses most of all. The three-month stretch kept the mission and its truce watch alive. The Council kept hunting for a way forward.

Resolution 1623, passed on 13 September 2005, keeps the NATO-led force in Afghanistan for one more year. The force had spread far past Kabul, as the Bonn pact of 2001 had planned. Afghans hold the chief duty for law and order in their own land. They work side by side with the force. Named tasks range wide: armed bands must be broken up, courts and police rebuilt, and Kabul's writ spread to all parts of the land.

The force won twelve more months on the ground. The frame stayed the same as in past years. The Council backed the land's unity and free rule. It recalled its anti-terror texts. It treated the Bonn and Berlin pledges as the map from a fallen regime to a working state.

Iraq's multinational force stays for another year in Resolution 1723, adopted on 28 November 2006. A national unity government had formed with a reconciliation programme. Iraqi forces had taken over security in Muthanna and Dhi Qar provinces. Iraq's Prime Minister asked in an annexed letter to keep the force.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council notes the force is present at Iraq's request and extends its mandate, as set out in Resolution 1546 (2004), until 31 December 2007. The mandate must be reviewed by 15 June 2007, or earlier at Iraq's request, and ends sooner if Baghdad asks. The arrangements channelling oil and gas export proceeds into the Development Fund for Iraq, monitored by the International Advisory and Monitoring Board, are extended to 31 December 2007. The Secretary-General must report quarterly on the UN Assistance Mission for Iraq, UNAMI, as must the United States for the force.

Resolution 1823, adopted on 10 July 2008, closes out the arms embargo imposed on Rwanda during its catastrophe. The embargo dated to May 1994, in the middle of the genocide, and had been adjusted several times as Rwanda stabilized. The committee overseeing it had reported at the end of 2007 and again in May 2008.

The Council ended the remaining embargo measures and dissolved the Rwanda sanctions committee. At the same time it stressed that states in the region had to keep arms delivered to them from leaking to illegal armed groups, especially in neighboring Congo. The decision marked a formal end to an emergency regime created fourteen years earlier, while acknowledging how porous the region's arms flows remained.

Chad's mission is wound down on the government's own timetable in Resolution 1923, adopted on 25 May 2010. Chad had asked MINURCAT to leave, then reconsidered, and months of consultations followed. Chad and Sudan had normalized relations in January 2010 and deployed a joint border force, and Chad committed in writing to take over protection of civilians in the east.

The Council extends MINURCAT until 31 December 2010 as a drawdown mandate. Its military component is cut to 2,200 personnel, surplus troops leave by 15 July 2010, and all uniformed and civilian components withdraw by 31 December 2010. Chad assumes full responsibility for protecting refugees, displaced persons, and aid workers. Benchmarks cover camp demilitarization and the capacity of its authorities, monitored monthly by a joint Chad-UN working group. MINURCAT keeps mentoring the Détachement intégré de sécurité and may still respond to imminent threats to civilians nearby.

Eritrea's sanctions reach its diaspora tax and mining income in Resolution 2023, adopted on 5 December 2011. The Monitoring Group's July 2011 report found Eritrea supported armed groups including Al-Shabaab, and condemned a planned January 2011 terrorist attack on the African Union summit in Addis Ababa. Eritrea had withdrawn from the Djibouti border area after Qatari observers deployed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemns Eritrea's violations of Resolutions 1844, 1862, and 1907 and demands it stop destabilization, including travel facilitation for armed groups. It orders Eritrea to cease collecting the diaspora tax through extortion, threats, or fraud. It tells states to hold accountable those collecting it on their territory. Concerned that mining revenue may fund violations, it directs states to promote due diligence by firms in Eritrea's mining sector and expands the Monitoring Group to cover the measures. It repeats the demand for information on missing Djiboutian combatants.

Resolution 223, adopted unanimously on 21 June 1966, takes up the application of Guyana for membership in the United Nations. The South American country had become independent from Britain less than a month earlier, in May 1966. Joining the UN was a standard early step for the many new states appearing in that decade.

The Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Guyana, and the text ends there. That single line mattered because the Charter requires the Council's recommendation before the Assembly can vote a country in. The resolution records Guyana's formal arrival on the world stage, weeks after independence, as a sovereign state on the northeastern coast of South America.

Greece's northern borders saw raids and gunfire after the Second World War. A Council commission had been sent in December 1946 to investigate. Resolution 23, adopted on 18 April 1947, kept a foothold for that inquiry. Nine members voted yes. Poland and the Soviet Union abstained.

The commission was told to maintain a smaller standing group in the area. Each commission member would supply one representative. The group would perform whatever tasks the commission assigned. The measure applied until the Council decided otherwise. Behind the dry wording lay a bitter dispute. Greece blamed its communist neighbors for aiding guerrillas. The case was an early East-West flashpoint at the UN.

Resolution 323, adopted on 6 December 1972 by thirteen votes to none with one abstention, reports what Namibians told the UN when finally asked. The Secretary-General's representative had consulted people inside the territory. Their views, the Council noted, had come through clearly: an overwhelming majority wanted the homelands policy abolished at once, South Africa's administration withdrawn, and a single independent Namibia with its territory intact.

The Council recorded that verdict with satisfaction. It reaffirmed the UN's special responsibility for the territory and the people's right to self-determination, citing the World Court's 1971 ruling that South Africa must leave. The consultations gave the UN's legal claim a democratic answer to match, quoted in Namibia debates for years.

Southern Rhodesia's illegal regime tried in 1978 to settle the conflict on its own terms. Its plan, called an internal settlement, would keep power with the white minority. At the same time, its forces attacked neighboring states and executed captured fighters. Resolution 423 was adopted on 14 March 1978.

The Council condemned every attempt by the regime to hold minority power. Such attempts blocked independence for Zimbabwe. Any internal settlement made under the regime was declared illegal and unacceptable. All states were told to refuse it recognition. Ending the regime came first, the text says. Its army and police had to be replaced. Free and fair elections would then follow, on universal adult suffrage and under United Nations supervision. Britain was pressed to act, and a report was due by 15 April 1978.
un-un-res-first-report-of-the-secretary-:
Late 1999 brought a bigger United Nations mission to Sierra Leone, and this first report of the Secretary-General, document S/1999/1223, opens its record. The new mission, UNAMSIL, replaced the small observer team as the Lomé peace deal took hold. Thousands of troops were now tasked with guarding the peace.

The report describes the mission's setup, its first deployments, and the mood among former fighters. It covers disarmament camps, aid work, and the risks posed by armed holdouts. The text marks the start of one of the largest peacekeeping efforts of its era.
undset-the-bridal-wreath-kristin-lavrans:
Sigrid Undset opens her medieval trilogy with The Bridal Wreath, given here in Charles Archer's 1923 English version. Kristin Lavransdatter, a farmer's daughter in fourteenth-century Norway, loves a man her family rejects. She defies her father to marry him anyway.

Young Kristin moves from a sheltered childhood to secret meetings and a troubled wedding. Undset fills the tale with rich detail on farms, faith, and daily life long ago. Love and guilt shape every choice Kristin makes. The trilogy later helped earn Undset the Nobel Prize, and its fame rests heavily on this strong opening volume.
veblen-absentee-ownership-1923:
Absentee Ownership, published in 1923, is Thorstein Veblen's last book, subtitled the case of America. The great critic of business returns to his lifelong target: owners who profit without work. He weighs the waste their control imposes on the whole country.

Veblen sets industry, the making of goods, against business, the making of money by managing scarcity and prices. Absentee owners, he argues, hold back production to protect earnings, and America suffers the difference. His prose is sardonic, looping, and remorseless. The book closes his long critique of American business life with undiminished bite. It appeared six years before his death.
webster-duchess-malfi-1623:
John Webster wrote The Duchess of Malfi around 1613, drawing on an Italian tale of a widowed duchess murdered by her brothers. The play was performed by the King's Men and printed in 1623. Webster, a London coachmaker's son, wrote only a handful of plays, but two of them are masterpieces.

The Duchess secretly marries her steward, Antonio, and bears his children while hiding the marriage for years. Her brothers, a cardinal and the twisted Ferdinand, hire the malcontent Bosola to spy on her. Discovery leads to imprisonment, madness, and murder staged with grim theatrical invention. The play mixes horror with real pity, and many call it the crown of Jacobean tragedy.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol23:
Volume XXIII of the Journal of Discourses appeared at Liverpool in 1883, deep into the set's long run. Sermons by leading elders fill the pages, reported word for word as the Journal always promised its readers. The speakers teach a church under legal siege, and quiet resolve rings through the talks.

Yet everyday counsel still shares space with defense of the faith, since the pulpit served both needs each week. The printed volumes let Saints abroad stand, in effect, in the tabernacle with the Utah congregations. Volume XXIII continues the doctrinal record toward its close, three volumes from the end of the whole set.
